title: A framework for measuring the quality of business process simulation models
abstract: Business Process Simulation (BPS) is an approach to analyze the performance of business processes under different scenarios. For example, BPS allows us to estimate the impact of adding one or more resources on the cycle time of a process. The starting point of BPS is a process model annotated with simulation parameters (a BPS model). BPS models may be manually designed, based on information collected from stakeholders and from empirical observations, or automatically discovered from historical execution data. Regardless of its provenance, a key question when using a BPS model is how to assess its quality. In particular, in a setting where we are able to produce multiple alternative BPS models of the same process, this question becomes: How to determine which model is better, to what extent, and in what respect? In this context, this article studies the question of how to measure the quality of a BPS model with respect to its ability to accurately replicate the observed behavior of a process. Rather than pursuing a one-size-fits-all approach, the article recognizes that a process covers multiple perspectives. Accordingly, the article outlines a framework that can be instantiated in different ways to yield quality measures that tackle different process perspectives. The article defines a number of concrete quality measures and evaluates these measures with respect to their ability to discern the impact of controlled perturbations on a BPS model, and their ability to uncover the relative strengths and weaknesses of two approaches for automated discovery of BPS models. The evaluation shows that the proposed measures not only capture how close a BPS model is to the observed behavior, but they also help us to identify the sources of discrepancies.
venue: Information Systems
human_qa_notes: Clear, well-structured, no OCR issues; QA2 scored 0 because the paper addresses general business-process-simulation quality assessment (loan application, call-centre, academic-credential, procure-to-pay processes), not a software-engineering-specific context.
human_research_question: How can the quality of a Business Process Simulation (BPS) model be measured with respect to its ability to accurately replicate observed process behavior, across multiple process perspectives (control-flow, temporal, resource, congestion)?
human_main_finding: The proposed multi-perspective framework and its instantiated distance measures (e.g., NGD, CFLD, AED, RED, CED, CWD, CAR, CTD) can discern the impact of controlled perturbations on BPS models and reveal the comparative strengths/weaknesses of two automated BPS discovery techniques (SIMOD vs. ServiceMiner); the proposed NGD measure matches CFLD's discriminative power at much lower computational cost (Kendall correlation of 1.0).
human_limitations: The framework only applies to BPS models that can generate event logs (not e.g. system-dynamics models), treats the actual event log as ground truth (assuming it fully represents process behavior), and the evaluation is limited to 29 synthetic and 8 real-life discovered BPS models across a few domains, limiting internal/external/construct/ecological validity generalization.

title: A note on two-stage software testing by two teams
abstract: This paper reports our experience of software reliability evaluation in the actual software development which employs somewhat uncommon testing procedure. The procedure can be called as a two-stage testing by two teams. First we discuss the problems underlying the software testing. We explain the concept of the procedure of the two-stage testing by two teams, and then, a stochastic model which traces the procedure is derived. The model analyzes a data set which were obtained from the real testing activity. By using the result of data analysis, we show some numerical illustrations for the software reliability assessment and the evaluation of the skill level of the test teams.

title: Detection and correction process modeling considering the time dependency
abstract: Most of the models for software reliability analysis are based on reliability growth models which deal with the fault detection process only. In this paper, some useful approaches to the modeling of both software fault detection and fault correction processes are discussed. Since the estimation of model parameters in software testing is essential to give accurate prediction and help make the right decision about software release, the problem of estimating the parameters is addressed. Taking into account the dependency between the fault correction process and the fault detection process, a new explicit formula for the likelihood function is derived and the maximum likelihood estimates are obtained under various time delay assumptions. An actual set of data from a software development project is used as an illustrative example. A Monte Carlo simulation is carried out to compare the predictive capability between the LSE method and the MLE method
venue: Proceedings 12th Pacific Rim International Symposium on Dependable Computing Prdc 2006

human_main_finding: Using a new explicit likelihood function that accounts for the dependency between fault detection and fault correction processes, MLE parameter estimates give more accurate and stable predictions (lower mean relative error) of future fault detection/correction behavior than least-squares estimates, confirmed on a real dataset and via Monte Carlo simulation of 120 datasets.

title: Process discovery: Automated approach for block discovery
abstract: Process mining is a set of techniques helping enterprises to avoid process modeling which is a time-consuming and error prone task. Process mining includes three topics: process discovery, conformance checking, and enhancement (IEEE Task Force on Process Mining: Process Mining Manifesto, 2012). The principle of process discovery is to extract information from event logs to capture the business process as it is being executed. Several techniques in literature (a algorithm, a+ algorithm and others) can be applied to discover a process model from a workflow log. However, as the amount of information grows exponentially, the log files (input of a process discovery algorithm) get bigger. In fact, classical techniques, which inspect relation between each couple of tasks will have problem dealing with big data. To this end, we introduced in (Boushaba et al., 2013) a new approach aiming to extract a block of tasks from event logs. In this paper, we present a new algorithm, based on a matrix representation, to detect a block of tasks. In addition, we develop an application to automate our technique.
venue: Enase 2014 Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Evaluation of Novel Approaches to Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text; case study uses only a small illustrative toy log, not real-world data; no validation metrics, threats-to-validity, or reproducibility statement.
human_research_question: How can a matrix-based algorithm efficiently detect blocks of tasks (sets of activities with equivalent behavior) in event logs to support faster, more scalable process discovery than existing methods?
human_main_finding: The proposed matrix-based block discovery algorithm (using an indirect succession matrix and logical similarity operator) detects succession, parallel, XOR, and loop patterns and constructs a Petri net iteratively; the authors claim O(n^2) complexity, making it more efficient than the alpha algorithm for large event logs.
human_limitations: The authors state the illustrative case study log "is not representative for real-life event log in terms of size and complexity"; future work is needed to handle partial/incomplete logs.

title: An Intelligent Methodology to Enhance Requirements Engineering in Multidisciplinary Projects
authors: Salmani, Ali; Imani, Alireza; Bahrehvar, Majid; Duffett-Leger, Linda; Moshirpour, Mohammad
abstract: The multidisciplinary nature of a team has been identified as one of the success criteria of both user-centric approaches and agile methods. Stakeholder involvement is considered to be essential for agile processes in order to meet project objectives and ensure results are aligned with stakeholder expectations. However, establishing a collaborative process involving designers, programmers, stakeholders, and users can be challenging; particularly during the requirements engineering stage. Agile methodologies, such as scrum, offer a powerful way of effectively managing software projects and generates a great deal of useful data through tools such as Jira and GitHub. The aim of this research is two folds: 1) analyze the project data from aforementioned sources using process mining techniques to discover deficiencies in the software development process, and 2) propose an automated effort estimation process to address the identified challenges in this study and provide decision support in the development process. This approach is applied to a case study of a virtual healthcare intervention system. The results are indicative that these enhancements helped boost the decision-making and release planning processes by providing the development team a more clear picture, which ultimately mitigated the number of change requests.
venue: 2022 IEEE Canadian Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering (CCECE)
human_qa_notes: Concrete real-world case study (Robin's Nest health platform) with clear objectives and SE/agile context, but no reproducible dataset details (no case/event counts), no explicitly named PM discovery algorithm actually applied, no formal threats-to-validity discussion, no data/code availability, and no process-model quality metrics.
human_research_question: How can process mining insights from Jira/GitHub data be used to identify deficiencies in multidisciplinary agile requirements engineering, and can an automated effort-estimation tool reduce change requests and improve release planning?
human_main_finding: Communication gaps and lack of domain knowledge among multidisciplinary stakeholders caused high rework rates and requirement changes; an NLP (BERT)-based effort-estimation decision-support tool helped reduce the backlog of remaining user stories.
human_limitations: Plurality of stakeholders and non-technical stakeholders' lack of software engineering knowledge are cited as causes of inefficiency; authors plan to adopt formal process mining tools (ProM, Disco) in future work, implying the current analysis was not based on standard PM discovery techniques.

title: Modeling and predicting software failure costs
abstract: For software, the costs of failures are not clearly understood. Often, these costs disappear in the costs of testing, the general developments costs, or the operating expenses. In a general manufacturing context, the British standard BS-6143-2:1990 classifies quality-related costs into prevention costs, appraisal costs, and failure costs. It furthermore recommends to identify the activities carried out within each of these categories, and to measure the costs connected with the activities. The standard thus presents a framework for recording and structuring costs once they have occurred. In this paper, we propose an approach for structuring the information on internal and external software failure costs such that their development over time can be represented by stochastic models. Based on these models, future failure costs can be predicted. In two case studies we show how the approach was applied in an industrial software development project.
venue: Proceedings International Computer Software and Applications Conference
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction; no formal threats-to-validity section, though authors acknowledge the constant-event-rate assumption was 'overly simplistic' in discussion.
human_research_question: How can internal and external software failure costs be structured and modeled using continuous-time Markov chain / Markov reward models to predict future costs?
human_main_finding: Using CTMC/Markov reward models built from activities, events and trigger probabilities, the approach successfully predicted internal and external failure costs in two industrial case studies, with most actual costs falling within the 95% prediction intervals.
human_limitations: Authors note the assumption of constant event rates was overly simplistic since fault detection rates change over time; future work is needed on parameter estimation without prior release data and on combining the model with appraisal costs.

title: Use of combined system dependability and software reliability growth models
abstract: This paper describes how MEADEP, a system level dependability prediction tool, and CASRE, a software reliability growth prediction tool can be used together to predict system reliability (probability of failure in a given time interval), availability (proportion of time service is available), and performability (reward-weighted availability). The system includes COTS hardware, COTS software, radar, and communication gateways. The performability metric also accounts for capacity changes as processors in a cluster fail and recover. The Littlewood Verall and Geometric model is used to predict reliability growth from software test data this prediction is integrated into a system level Markov model that incorporates hardware failures and recoveries, redundancy, coverage failures, and capacity. The results of the combined model can be used to predict the contribution of additional testing upon availability and a variety of other figures of merit that support management decisions.
venue: International Journal of Reliability Quality and Safety Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction; combines system-level Markov dependability model with software reliability growth models (Littlewood-Verrall, Geometric); explicit limitations section discusses test-data quality and the heisenbug/randomness assumption, but no data/code availability and no fitness/precision-style model quality metric is reported (only availability/downtime figures).
human_research_question: How can system-level Markov dependability models be combined with software reliability growth models (Littlewood-Verrall, Geometric) to predict system availability/reliability and support test-time-vs-redundancy tradeoff decisions?
human_main_finding: Combining software reliability growth models with a system-level Markov dependability model (applied to an FAA air-traffic-control STARS example) shows diminishing returns from additional testing on system availability; e.g., ~900 extra hours of RDP testing reduces yearly downtime by only ~0.45 hours, letting managers trade off testing against redundancy/hardware reliability.
human_limitations: Authors note validity depends on proper operational-profile-based test data gathering, and the heisenbug/stochastic-failure assumption does not cover deterministic failures such as design flaws or security issues.

title: Extension of a Simulation Software to Incorporate Quality-Related Factors in Investigations on Software Engineering Economics
abstract: The economics of software engineering [B. W. Boehm, Software Engineering Economics, Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, 1981] are strongly influenced by the way how software development processes are performed. Simulations give valuable insights in the performance of these processes. In order to research the economics of software engineering, a process analysis studio (PAS) was developed and presented [D. Kuhlen and A. Speck, Business process analysis by model checking, in Proc. 5th Int. Symp. Data-Driven Process Discovery and Analysis SIMPDA, eds. P. Ceravolo and S. Rinderle-Ma, 2015; D. Kuhlen and A. Speck, The way of designing a simulation software in order to evaluate the economic performance in software development, in ICCMS ’17 Proc. 8th Int. Conf. Computer Modeling and Simulation, Int. Conf. Proc. Series by ACM, 2016; D. Kuhlen, Kostensenkungspotenzialfunktion der Softwareproduktion, dissertation, Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel, 2019]. This simulation software was built to analyze the capacitive configurations of the software production. It helps to assess the impact of different configurations on the process output. However, this research emphasizes the impact of quality-related factors (QRFs) on the process output. This paper presents a proposal how to extend the simulation software model in order to facilitate qualitative analysis. In order to facilitate the understanding of the model and the evaluation of the contribution, offered by the proposal, Prolog codes are used.
venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering

QA4=1: software-process simulation (PAS) is formally named; system dynamics appears in related work but is not the proposed technique. QA5=0: 'experiment' is SWI-Prolog queries showing the extended meta-model can mention quality; the PAS extension is not implemented or run on SE projects (authors say it still 'has to be changed').

title: Intervention of knowledge flows in software process mining projects
authors: Urrea-Contreras, Silvia Jaqueline; Astorga-Vargas, María Angélica; Flores-Rios, Brenda L.; Ibarra-Esquer, Jorge E.; González-Navarro, Félix Fernando
abstract: Knowledge flows permit to analyze the type and sources of knowledge, and the way in which knowledge flows or is managed within an organization. This paper presents how a knowledge flow approach implemented in a process mining project, which analyzes process instances, supports the categorization of the different types and assets of knowledge stored in the repositories of software development organizations. In addition, it provides information for the roles involved in improvement cycles to make strategic decisions based on the types of mining (process discovery, conformance checking and process improvement). We present the implementation of the intervention methodology for the identification of processes, flows and types of knowledge with the objective of strengthening and validating the compliance of software processes. These results were validated with an experience report on the analysis of knowledge flows in a Mexican software development company implementing a Process Mining project.
venue: 2022 IEEE Mexican International Conference on Computer Science (ENC)
human_qa_notes: Clear case study/experience report with real SME company data (roles, tools, 315h) and named PM algorithms (alpha, heuristic, fuzzy, genetic); no formal threats-to-validity section, no shared data/code, no fitness/precision metrics reported.
human_research_question: How can a knowledge-flow analysis approach (based on the SECI/knowledge-cycle model) be integrated into a software process mining project to identify knowledge types, sources, and flows among roles, in order to strengthen and validate compliance of software processes?
human_main_finding: An intervention methodology combining knowledge-flow analysis (SECI model) with process mining phases (audit, tool identification, KM deployment, follow-up) was applied in a real Mexican software development company; the four SECI knowledge-creation flows (socialization, externalization, combination, internalization) were successfully identified around a process mining project using Jira, SIMIo and GitHub, validating the approach via an experience report and lessons learned.
human_limitations: Authors note the main limitation is that organizational repositories were not interconnected, requiring considerable manual effort (several weeks) to build the event log; results are based on a single company case study.

title: Online Discovery of Simulation Models for Evolving Business Processes
abstract: Business Process Simulation (BPS) refers to techniques designed to replicate the dynamic behavior of a business process. Many approaches have been proposed to automatically discover simulation models from historical event logs, reducing the cost and time to manually design them. However, in dynamic business environments, organizations continuously refine their processes to enhance efficiency, reduce costs, and improve customer satisfaction. Existing techniques to process simulation discovery lack adaptability to real-time operational changes. In this paper, we propose a streaming process simulation discovery technique that integrates Incremental Process Discovery with Online Machine Learning methods. This technique prioritizes recent data while preserving historical information, ensuring adaptation to evolving process dynamics. Experiments conducted on four different event logs demonstrate the importance in simulation of giving more weight to recent data while retaining historical knowledge. Our technique not only produces more stable simulations but also exhibits robustness in handling concept drift, as highlighted in one of the use cases.
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
human_qa_notes: Clear technique paper (incremental process discovery + Hoeffding Adaptive Trees for online BPS discovery) with public BPIC logs and GitHub tool link; but domain is general business-process simulation (loan/purchasing/pharmacy), not software-engineering specific.
human_research_question: How can business process simulation models be incrementally discovered/updated from streaming event data so they adapt to concept drift in evolving processes while retaining useful historical information?
human_main_finding: The proposed online discovery technique (Inductive Miner + incremental process discovery + Hoeffding Adaptive Trees) produces simulation models that are more accurate and stable over time than single-large-batch or last-small-batch baselines, achieving the best results in 75% of tested metric/log combinations across four event logs including one with a documented concept drift.
human_limitations: Authors acknowledge that the underlying incremental process discovery method does not remove unobserved behavior from the model (reducing readability) and that trace-completion detection via domain knowledge/timeout can be a threat to validity in some settings.

title: Software reliability estimation method based on Markov usage models using Importance Sampling
abstract: Importance sampling (IS) is a change-of-measure technique for speeding up the simulation of rare events in stochastic systems. In this paper, we presented an approach uses Importance Sampling technique for efficient estimation of software reliability via Markov software usage models in statistical testing. By suitable changes of the probabilities of state transitions during test, an iterative method based on the Ali-Silvey distance is proposed for this choice, and an unbiased reliability estimator with zero variance is obtained. A learning algorithm for the computation of optimal transition probabilities of the Markov chain usage model is also presented and experimental results of this algorithm are reported.
venue: 2012 IEEE 5th International Conference on Advanced Computational Intelligence Icaci 2012
human_qa_notes: OCR extraction has garbled math symbols/subscripts (e.g. mangled equations, 'vr' for pi) but the methodology and results remain assessable; no explicit threats-to-validity section or data/code availability statement found.
human_research_question: How can Importance Sampling applied to a Markov software usage model produce an unbiased, low-variance estimator of software reliability while directing more test effort toward error-prone but infrequently used operations?
human_main_finding: The proposed importance-sampling learning algorithm (based on the Ali-Silvey/Kullback-Leibler distance) for optimizing Markov usage-model transition probabilities yields a reliability estimator with lower variance (8.32e-4) than the standard method (5.21e-3) and simulated annealing (1.683e-3), while giving more testing weight to critical low-frequency operations.
human_limitations: The approach is restricted to Markov (memoryless) usage models with manageable state-space size to avoid state-space explosion, and the zero-variance estimator is not fully achieved in practice due to statistical estimation error from finite sampling; authors note future work on non-Markov models, larger state spaces, and formal convergence proofs.

title: Process minding: Closing the big data gap
abstract: This study investigates how different ways of receiving peer written corrective feedback (WCF) affect learners’ opportunities to actively engage in negotiation of form in tandem virtual encounters. Two types of WCF are compared, namely direct WCF plus oral metalinguistic explanation and indirect WCF plus oral prompt. During a telecollaboration programme between Italian students of English and US students of Italian, the participants (n = 16) were given several tasks to complete in dyads, including that of providing feedback on written compositions produced by their partner in the target language. The eight dyads were divided into two groups which received the same instructions for the activities, with the exception of instructions on how to provide WCF to their partner. The data of six dyads – three from each group – were analysed with regard to the quality of language-related episodes. The data analysis showed that indirect WCF plus oral prompt was more effective in leading the NNSs to actively engage with negotiation of form during the discussion phase. This result will be discussed together with other findings which emerged from the analysis, with the aim to provide useful insights on how to promote focus on form when implementing peer-review activities in telecollaboration programmes.
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics

title: Process Mining Software Repositories from Student Projects in an Undergraduate Software Engineering Course
abstract: An undergraduate level Software Engineering courses generally consists of a team-based semester long project and emphasizes on both technical and managerial skills. Software Engineering is a practice-oriented and applied discipline and hence there is an emphasis on hands-on development, process, usage of tools in addition to theory and basic concepts. We present an approach for mining the process data (process mining) from software repositories archiving data generated as a result of constructing software by student teams in an educational setting. We present an application of mining three software repositories: team wiki (used during requirement engineering), version control system (development and maintenance) and issue tracking system (corrective and adaptive maintenance) in the context of an undergraduate Software Engineering course. We propose visualizations, metrics and algorithms to provide an insight into practices and procedures followed during various phases of a software development life-cycle. The proposed visualizations and metrics (learning analytics) provide a multi-faceted view to the instructor serving as a feedback tool on development process and quality by students. We mine the event logs produced by software repositories and derive insights such as degree of individual contributions in a team, quality of commit messages, intensity and consistency of commit activities, bug fixing process trend and quality, component and developer entropy, process compliance and verification. We present our empirical analysis on a software repository dataset consisting of 19 teams of 5 members each and discuss challenges, limitations and recommendations.
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE Companion 2014)
human_qa_notes: Well-structured case-study/experience-report paper with detailed dataset description and self-critique of metric limitations (entropy, gaming risk); no fitness/precision-style process-model quality metrics reported and no public dataset/code release.
human_research_question: How can process mining of Wiki, version-control, and issue-tracking event logs from student teams in an undergraduate SE course give instructors visibility into development-process quality (workload distribution, commit quality, bug-fixing efficiency) beyond what is visible from the product alone?
human_main_finding: Applying process mining (via Disco/Fuzzy Miner) and custom metrics (component/developer entropy, bug-fixing score, commit-message quality) to Wiki, VCS, and ITS logs from 19 student teams reveals large, previously invisible variation in process quality between teams, giving instructors actionable, non-product-based feedback and grading signals.
human_limitations: Authors note the entropy-based metrics capture diversity rather than intensity of contribution, and that all proposed metrics can be gamed by redundant/needless commits or bug reports, so should be used cautiously for grading.

title: Cutting the software building efforts in continuous integration by semi-supervised online AUC optimization
abstract: Continuous Integration (CI) systems aim to provide quick feedback on the success of the code changes by keeping on building the entire systems upon code changes are committed. However, building the entire software system is usually resource and time consuming. Thus, build outcome prediction is usually employed to distinguish the successful builds from the failed ones to cut the building efforts on those successful builds that do not result in any immediate action of the developer. Nevertheless, build outcome prediction in CI is challenging since the learner should be able to learn from a stream of build events with and without the build outcome labels and provide immediate prediction on the next build event. Also, the distribution of the successful and the failed builds are often highly imbalanced. Unfortunately, the existing methods fail to address these challenges well. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a semi-supervised online AUC optimization method for CI build outcome prediction. Experiments indicate that our method is able to cut the software building efforts by effectively identify the successful builds, and it outperforms the existing methods that elaborate to address part of these challenges.
venue: Ijcai International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence
human_qa_notes: Clean extraction of a full IJCAI-18 paper; QA4 scored 0 because SOLA is semi-supervised online AUC/ML (stochastic gradient/saddle-point is SGD, not a named PM or stochastic-process technique); QA8 scored 1 because AUC is a closely analogous ranking/accuracy metric; QA7 scored 0 because the Madeyski & Kawalerowicz (2017) CI dataset is cited but no code or data URL is provided. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (CI build-outcome prediction, not process mining or stochastic process modeling).
human_research_question: How can a semi-supervised online AUC optimization method (SOLA) jointly handle streaming CI events, scarce build-outcome labels, class imbalance, and suspiciousness ranking so that likely-successful builds can be skipped and CI build effort reduced?
human_main_finding: On eight GitHub/CI projects from the Madeyski & Kawalerowicz continuous-defect-prediction dataset, SOLA attains mean AUC 0.783, beating Hoeffding Tree (0.551), OMR (0.539) and online AUC-only SOLAM (0.741), matching the batch upper bound SAMULT (0.782) while cutting model-update time by more than 97% versus batch learning, indicating that addressing the four CI prediction challenges together reduces wasted successful-build effort.
human_limitations: Evaluation uses only eight open-source Java projects; authors note that results may not generalize to closed-source or non-Java systems and plan broader experiments and richer (e.g. deep) features.

title: Representing software usage models with stochastic automata networks
abstract: The benefits of usage models in the statistical testing of software have been recognized by the software engineering community and discrete state formalisms have been largely used to describe such usage models of software. The Markov Chains formalism (MC) is a natural choice to do so. However, in this paper we suggest the use of a more sophisticated discrete state formalism, the Stochastic Automata Networks (SAN). In many problems of the performance evaluation area, the SAN models present advantages over MC models. Therefore, it seems natural to us to verify similar advantages in the modeling of usage models.This paper presents a case study of building a software usage model using SAN formalism. A software tool called DOCSEDITOR is modeled using MC and SAN. The models are compared in terms of number of states, scalability, and readability. It is not the objective of this paper to present a full framework to develop and analyse usage models with SAN, but just to show some evident advantages of the use of SAN instead of MC. In order to do this, the conclusion points out the indexes than can be computed from both models and suggests the next steps on future work.
venue: ACM International Conference Proceeding Series
human_qa_notes: Text clean (no OCR issues); solid detailed case study but limited to a single small internally-developed tool and no public data/code release or formal quality metrics.
human_research_question: Can Stochastic Automata Networks (SAN) offer modeling advantages (fewer states, better scalability/readability) over Markov chains for representing software usage models used in statistical testing?
human_main_finding: A case study modeling the DocsEditor tool with both Markov chains (53 states) and SAN (5 automata, 324 combined states but only 53 reachable) showed SAN can make implicit features (e.g., node type) explicit without state explosion, offering more modular, scalable, and maintainable usage models for statistical software testing.
human_limitations: The study is described as a "preliminary" and "first case study" using a relatively simple target application, focused mainly on the modeling process rather than a full framework for analysis; a full SAN-based framework and testing on more complex applications remain future work.

title: Software Reliability Assessment: An Architectural and Component Impact Analysis
abstract: In the software landscape, understanding component impacts on system reliability is pivotal, especially given the unique complexities of modern software systems. This paper presents a model tailored for software reliability assessment. Our approach introduces the ‘component influence’ to measure a single component's effect on overall system reliability. Additionally, we adapt a state transition model to cater to the diverse architectures of software systems. Using a discrete-time Markov chain, we predict software reliability. We tested our model on an actual software system, finding it notably accurate and superior to existing methods. Our work offers a promising direction for those venturing into software reliability enhancement.
venue: Tsinghua Science and Technology
human_qa_notes: Detailed, well-structured reliability-modeling paper with an explicit dedicated Threats-to-Validity section (4.4); not a process-mining paper, no code/data repository provided, and reported accuracy/deviation metrics are reliability-prediction accuracy rather than PM-style fitness/precision metrics.
human_research_question: How can a 'component influence' metric combined with a global state-transition model (based on a discrete-time Markov chain) more accurately assess component-based software system reliability than existing architecture-based methods, while accounting for the diversity of software architectural styles?
human_main_finding: On a benchmark bank-transaction software system case study, the proposed component-influence + Markov-chain reliability model achieved a reliability estimate of 0.853 versus an actual measured reliability of 0.865 (1.39% deviation), outperforming six existing reliability-assessment methods (Cheung, Xie et al., Li and Hoang, Xue et al., Lo et al., Wang et al.) in accuracy.
human_limitations: Authors' own Threats to Validity section notes: the weight coefficients (alpha1, alpha2) may not generalize across all software systems; components are assumed independent, which may not hold; the model has only been validated on limited system types/architectures; comparison is limited to three classic reliability models; and predictive power across broader scenarios needs further evaluation.

title: Generating event logs with workload-dependent speeds from simulation models
abstract: Generating Event Logs with Workload-Dependent Speeds from Simulation Models Joyce Nakatumba, Michael Westergaard, and Wil M.P. van der Aalst Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands {jnakatum,m.westergaard,w.m.p.v.d.aalst}@tue.nl Abstract. Both simulation and process mining can be used to analyze operational business processes. Simulation is model-driven and very use- ful because diﬀerent scenarios can be explored by changing the model’s parameters. Process mining is driven by event
venue: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
human_qa_notes: Well-described CPN simulation model plus a real-life event log (324 cases, 19805 events, 15 resources, 175 activities) with regression fit statistics (r, R2); no formal threats-to-validity section and no explicit code/data release statement.
human_research_question: How can workload-dependent processing speeds of resources be incorporated into simulation models and learned from event logs using process mining, and does workload measurably affect resource processing speed in real life?
human_main_finding: Simulation experiments (colored Petri nets) and regression analysis of a real-life municipal permit-handling event log both confirm that resource workload (queue length and 'how busy' measures) significantly affects processing speed, following a Yerkes-Dodson-like relationship; ignoring this yields unrealistic simulation results.
human_limitations: The model only captures the first half of the Yerkes-Dodson curve (busier resources work faster) and does not model other resource behaviors such as multitasking, part-time availability, or batch working, which the authors address only in separate earlier work.

title: Supporting software evolution actions with process mining
abstract: There are several forces driving software evolution. One is the business process (BP) misalignment, i.e., when the behavior of the information systems supporting the BPs, or its users, is not aligned with the intended behavior of the BPs identified during the requirement engineering phase. Process Mining (PM) is an essential strategy for BP alignment evaluation. Nevertheless, PM initiatives do not usually focus on connecting BP alignment misfits with concrete software requirements for software evolution. This paper provides initial insights into how PM can support software evolution actions by considering research questions posed during a PM initiative. We exemplify this idea by analyzing administrative procedures within an Electronic Document Management System, providing action guides for its evolution obtained from the PM initiative.
venue: Cibse 2023 Xxvi Ibero American Conference on Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text; process mining used is general/exploratory (Disco tool, PRICED methodology) without a specific named discovery algorithm (no alpha/inductive/heuristic/conformance-checking explicitly applied), so QA4 scored 0; no data/code replication package or fitness/precision metrics reported.
human_research_question: How can process mining findings obtained during a PM initiative be systematically connected to concrete software evolution actions for the information system supporting the analyzed business process?
human_main_finding: Applying the PRICED process-mining methodology to a university Electronic Document Management System (EXPE+) revealed process-alignment deviations and data-quality challenges (non-standardized/process-independent activity names, missing timestamps, missing end-of-process events) that map to concrete software evolution actions such as renaming/standardizing activities and enforcing timestamp logging.
human_limitations: Authors state this is only an initial/exploratory experience with a single EDMS case, findings are not generalizable, and further validation with business experts and additional cases is needed.

title: Combination of process mining and simulation techniques for business process redesign: A methodological approach
abstract: International audienceOrganizations of all sizes are currently supporting their performance on information systems that record the real execution of their business processes in event logs. Process mining tools analyze the log to provide insight on the real problems of the process, as part of the diagnostic phase. Nonetheless, to complete the lifecycle of a process, the latter has to be redesigned, a task for which simulation techniques can be used in combination with process mining, in order to evaluate different improvement alternatives before they are put in practice. In this context, the current work presents a methodological approach to the integration of process mining and simulation techniques in a process redesign project
venue: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
human_qa_notes: Rigorous applied case study combining process mining (alpha mining, Petri nets) with simulation and decision trees on a real procurement dataset; no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, no data/code shared, and reported metrics are business KPIs (cycle time) rather than PM fitness/precision.
human_research_question: How can process mining and business process simulation techniques be methodologically combined (extending BPtrends and Maruster's approach) to support a complete business process redesign lifecycle, from project understanding through as-is analysis, to-be redesign, and implementation?
human_main_finding: Applying the proposed four-phase methodology (understanding, as-is analysis via process/data mining, to-be redesign via simulation, implementation) to a university procurement process (15,091 orders, cleaned to 8,987) identified the purchase-requisition-approval subprocess as the main bottleneck; simulation of combined redesign alternatives (removing an approval step and adding a 5-day approval rule) reduced mean cycle time from 50.7 to about 35 days.
human_limitations: Authors state the methodology needs to be validated in other case studies through the implementation phase to assess whether it meets expected results, and that further research is needed on how different event log sources (ERP/WFMS/CRM) affect required extraction and cleansing steps.

title: Model-driven safety modeling and analysis of embedded parallel software
abstract: This paper focuses on model-driven safety modeling and analysis of embedded parallel software. Firstly, analyze safety requirements of embedded parallel software and summarize potential safety risks because of software concurrency. Secondly, according to potential safety risks, extend AADL language which include increasing attribute of safety level, describing specific concurrency error type and error propagation to establish AADL safety model. Then use FMEA and Markov chain approaches to analyze and evaluate its safety. Finally, do an instance analysis with a flight control system software.
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Software Engineering and Service Sciences Icsess
human_qa_notes: Illustrative model-driven safety-analysis example (AADL extended with Markov chain/FMEA) on a flight-control system; no real dataset, no threats-to-validity discussion, and no reproducibility artifacts.
human_research_question: How can AADL be extended to model safety risks of embedded parallel software (concurrency errors) and how can FMEA and Markov chain analysis be used to quantitatively evaluate safety levels of such systems?
human_main_finding: Extending AADL's error-model annex with concurrency-specific error types and safety-level attributes, then mapping the resulting error model to a Markov chain, allows automatic (OSATE-generated) FMEA tables and computation of stable-state safety-level probabilities; illustrated on a flight-control system example where the probability of the software being in a catastrophic state was computed as ~4.08e-5.
human_limitations: not stated

title: A stratification and sampling model for bellwether moving window
abstract: An effective method for finding the relevant number (window size) and the elapsed time (window age) of recently completed projects has proven elusive in software effort estimation.Although these two parameters significantly affect the prediction accuracy, there is no effective method to stratify and sample chronological projects to improve prediction performance of software effort estimation models.Exemplary projects (Bellwether) representing the training set have been empirically validated to improve the prediction accuracy in the domain of software defect prediction.However, the concept of Bellwether and its effect have not been empirically proven in software effort estimation as a method of selecting exemplary/relevant projects with defined window size and age.In view of this, we introduce a novel method for selecting relevant and recently completed projects referred to as Bellwether moving window for improving the software effort prediction accuracy.We first sort and cluster a pool of N projects and apply statistical stratification based on Markov chain modeling to select the Bellwether moving window.We evaluate the proposed approach using the baseline Automatically Transformed Linear Model on the ISBSG dataset.Results show that (1) Bellwether effect exist in software effort estimation dataset, (2) the Bellwether moving window with a window size of 82 to 84 projects and window age of 1.5 to 2 years resulted in an improved prediction accuracy than the traditional approach.
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering Seke
human_qa_notes: Text is clean and readable overall (only minor OCR artifacts in probability equations); no code/data availability statement is given beyond naming the licensed ISBSG dataset, so QA7 scored 0.
human_research_question: Does a 'Bellwether effect' exist in software effort estimation, and can a Markov-chain-based stratification/sampling method determine an effective window size and age for a Bellwether moving window that improves prediction accuracy over a growing-portfolio baseline?
human_main_finding: Using Markov chain Monte Carlo-based stratification and sampling on the ISBSG dataset, the study empirically confirms a Bellwether effect in software effort estimation and identifies an optimal Bellwether moving window of 82-84 projects with an age of 1.5-2 years (Gaussian weighting), which significantly outperforms the traditional growing-portfolio approach (Welch t-test p<0.05, Glass's Delta=0.627).
human_limitations: The study relies on a single release of the ISBSG dataset restricted to a single industry sector (a convenience sample), so results may not generalize to other chronological datasets; authors plan to validate the method on other datasets (e.g., a Finnish dataset) in future work.

title: Distributed process discovery and conformance checking
abstract: Process mining techniques have matured over the last decade and more and more organization started to use this new technology. The two most important types of process mining are process discovery (i.e., learning a process model from example behavior recorded in an event log) and conformance checking (i.e., comparing modeled behavior with observed behavior). Process mining is motivated by the availability of event data. However, as event logs become larger (say terabytes), performance becomes a concern. The only way to handle larger applications while ensuring acceptable response times, is to distribute analysis over a network of computers (e.g., multicore systems, grids, and clouds). This paper provides an overview of the different ways in which process mining problems can be distributed. We identify three types of distribution: replication, a horizontal partitioning of the event log, and a vertical partitioning of the event log. These types are discussed in the context of both procedural (e.g., Petri nets) and declarative process models. Most challenging is the horizontal partitioning of event logs in the context of procedural models. Therefore, a new approach to decompose Petri nets and associated event logs is presented. This approach illustrates that process mining problems can be distributed in various ways
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Formal/theoretical position paper (van der Aalst) using only toy illustrative examples, no real event log, case study, or SE-specific context; no threats-to-validity discussion and no shared data/code, though fitness/precision/generalization are formally defined.
human_research_question: How can process discovery and conformance checking be decomposed and distributed across computing nodes (via vertical/horizontal partitioning of event logs and 'passages' of a process model) to handle large-scale event logs, for both procedural (Petri net) and declarative process models?
human_main_finding: The paper introduces the notion of 'passages' to decompose Petri-net-based conformance checking (and, under a known causal structure, process discovery) into independent subproblems that can each be solved on a sublog/net-fragment and then merged, proving that a log is perfectly fitting a workflow net iff each decomposed sublog is perfectly fitting its corresponding net fragment.
human_limitations: The paper notes horizontal distribution of procedural (Petri-net) models is much more challenging than vertical distribution or declarative models, and provides no empirical performance evaluation on real large event logs -- only illustrative toy examples.

title: Unearthing open source decision-making processes: A case study of python enhancement proposals
abstract: Good governance practices are pivotal to the success of Open Source Software (OSS) projects. However, the decision‐making processes that are made available to stakeholders are at times incomplete and may remain buried and hidden in large amounts of software repository data. This work bridges this gap by unearthing enacted decision‐making processes available for Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) from 1.54 million email messages that embody decisions made during the evolution of the Python language. This work employs a design science approach in operationalizing a framework called DeMaP miner that is used to discover hidden processes using information retrieval and information extraction techniques. It also uses process mining techniques to visualize the processes, and comparative structural analysis techniques to compare different decision processes. The work identifies a richer set of decision‐making activities than those reported on the Python website and in prior research work (48 new decision activities, 199 new pathways and 6 new stages). The extracted decision process has been positively evaluated by a prominent member of the Python steering council. The extracted process can be used for process compliance checking and process improvement in OSS communities. Additionally, the DeMaP Miner framework can be extended and customized to suit other OSS projects, such as the OpenJDK project.
venue: Software Practice and Experience
human_qa_notes: Long SPE paper; extraction is clean aside from Wiley download watermarks. QA7=1: DeMaP Miner source is on GitHub (https://github.com/sharmapn/DeMaPMiner); data available from the corresponding author on request. QA8=1: framework accuracy 82% on 200 sentences with TP/TN/FP/FN, plus Cohen's kappa (0.67–0.78) and Fleiss 0.73 — treated as closely analogous to precision/F1. Process models are visualized (Disco) but fitness/precision of the mined nets are not reported.
human_research_question: What enacted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) decision-making process can be mined from 1.54 million mailing-list emails, how does it differ from advertised/prior models, and how do Process, Informational and Standards Track PEP processes compare?
human_main_finding: DeMaP Miner (IR/NLP + process-mining visualization) on 463 PEPs / 89,914 decision-related emails (1995–2018) yields an enacted process with 48 new decision sub-states, 199 new pathways and 6 new stages (e.g. consensus formation, polling, voting) versus advertised PEP-1/prior state models; Standards Track PEPs are substantially more complex than Process/Informational PEPs; extraction accuracy 82% and a Python Steering Council member judged the mined model useful.
human_limitations: Single OSS community (Python) and mixed meritocracy/dictatorship era ending at BDFL resignation (2018); manual concept coding on 30 PEPs; NLP/ClausIE misses some triples and negation; off-list IRC/Twitter/F2F decisions unobserved; Disco maps are huge (61 activities, 235 paths) so figures show only a subset of paths; framework not yet applied to non-numbered-proposal projects (Apache, Linux, Perl).

title: Software reliability considering the superposition of non-homogeneous poisson processes in the presence of a covariate
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a Bayesian analysis to the superposition of nonhomogeneous Poisson process in the presence of a covariate x. Posterior summaries of interest are obtained using Markov chain Monte Carlo Methods. A numerical example is given.
venue: Statistics
human_qa_notes: OCR/text-extraction noise from a poor scan of a technical-report (garbled symbols, mixed-up characters) made some equations hard to read, but did not obscure the overall methodology and conclusions.
human_research_question: Can a Bayesian (MCMC/Gibbs-sampling) approach for the superposition of non-homogeneous Poisson processes, extended to include a covariate, better model software reliability/failure data than the same model without the covariate?
human_main_finding: Using Gibbs sampling/Metropolis-Hastings MCMC on simulated software failure data, the superposition model including the covariate produced better posterior fit and a favorable Bayes-factor comparison than the model without the covariate.

title: DevOps workflow verification and duration prediction using non-Markovian stochastic Petri nets
abstract: In this paper, we provide a non‐Markovian Stochastic Petri Net (SPN) model for DevOps workflow specification, and we determine how business processes are carried out. After describing our model semantics, we show how general properties related to liveness and safety can be checked. After that, we provide several extensions on SPNs (SPN) the notation and expressivity to check some specific properties related to actors' (Developers and Operators) availability, interactions between the actors, and execution failures detection linked to the DevOps steps. Next, we validate the proposed model relevance with MATLAB simulation through a specific DevOps case study. Finally, we propose a truncated density function to anticipate the delays related to the DevOps business process overall steps.
venue: Journal of Software Evolution and Process
human_qa_notes: Formal/technical stochastic Petri net paper with a detailed illustrative case study (Geldzin DevOps workflow) and simulation via TimeNET, but no dedicated threats-to-validity section and no public code/data repository for the proposed NM-WSPN model itself (only the case study's tools/blog reference are public).
human_research_question: How can a non-Markovian stochastic Petri net extension (NM-WSPN) formally specify, verify (liveness/boundedness/soundness), and predict duration/delay risk of DevOps workflows, capturing dynamic interactions between developer and operator actors?
human_main_finding: Applying the proposed NM-WSPN model to the Geldzin DevOps case study (steps 9-17 of a real CI/CD pipeline) revealed a blocking state (CardM15) and identified transition Tr14 as the primary source of delay; density-truncation-based prediction estimated delay margins and confidence intervals for critical transitions (e.g., ~60% probability of continuous delay under an exponential firing-time distribution for transition Tr21).
human_limitations: The model assumes independence between activity durations, is demonstrated on a single illustrative case study rather than broad empirical validation, and future work is needed to add resource-sharing constraints and dynamic real-time verification capabilities; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

title: An empirical study of the evolution of GitHub actions workflows
abstract: CI/CD practices play a significant role during collaborative software development by automating time-consuming and repetitive tasks such as testing, building, quality checking, dependency and security management. GitHub Actions, the CI/CD tool integrated into GitHub, allows repository maintainers to automate development workflows. We conducted a mixed methods analysis of GitHub Actions workflow changes over time. Through a preliminary qualitative analysis of 439 modified workflow files we identified seven types of conceptual changes to workflows. Next, we performed a quantitative analysis over 49K+ GitHub repositories totaling 267K+ workflow change histories and 3.4M+ workflow file versions from November 2019 to August 2025. This analysis revealed that repositories contain a median of three workflow files, and 7.3% of all workflow files are being changed every week. The changes made to workflows tend to be small, with about three-quarters containing only a single change. The large majority of the observed changes have to do with task configuration and task specification in workflow jobs. We did not find any conclusive evidence of the effect of LLM coding tools or other major technological changes on workflow creation and workflow maintenance frequency. Our findings highlight the need for improved tooling to support fine-grained maintenance tasks, such as a broader adoption of dependency management and AI-based support for ensuring and sustaining workflow security and quality.
venue: Journal of Systems and Software
human_qa_notes: Clean arXiv extraction of a large mixed-methods MSR paper; explicit RQs, Zenodo dataset/code (QA7=1), and a full Wohlin-style threats section (QA6=1). QA4 scored 0: no named process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique (descriptive mining of YAML workflow diffs). QA8 scored 0: results are frequencies/medians/%, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE-style quality metrics. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (CI/CD configuration evolution, not PM/stochastic SE modeling).
human_research_question: How frequently and in which conceptual/syntactic ways do GitHub Actions workflow files change over time, and is there evidence that LLM coding tools or other major technological shifts have changed workflow creation or maintenance frequency?
human_main_finding: On 236,775 workflow histories from 47,488 popular GitHub repositories (Nov 2019–Aug 2025), repositories have a median of three workflow files and about 7.3% of files change each week; ~79% of changesets are modification-only and ~80% of edits concentrate in job steps (task specification/configuration); Dependabot (69%) and Renovate (21%) drive many Action version updates toward more secure pinning; before/after tests found no conclusive effect of LLM tools on change frequency.
human_limitations: Dataset is restricted to active, popular GitHub repos (≥300 stars and commits); 11.54% of histories with invalid YAML were dropped; only the primary branch is observed (squash merges can hide fine-grained changes); LLM-impact analysis is a coarse before/after design that cannot reliably detect agent use.

title: An iterative decision-making scheme for markov decision processes and its application to self-adaptive systems
abstract: Software is often governed by and thus adapts to phenomena that occur at runtime. Unlike traditional decision problems, where a decision-making model is determined for reasoning, the adaptation logic of such software is concerned with empirical data and is subject to practical constraints. We present an Iterative Decision-Making Scheme (IDMS) that infers both point and interval estimates for the undetermined transition probabilities in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) based on sampled data, and iteratively computes a confidently optimal scheduler from a given finite subset of schedulers. The most important feature of IDMS is the flexibility for adjusting the criterion of confident optimality and the sample size within the iteration, leading to a tradeoff between accuracy, data usage and computational overhead. We apply IDMS to an existing self-adaptation framework Rainbow and conduct a case study using a Rainbow system to demonstrate the flexibility of IDMS
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Rigorous formal/simulation study on self-adaptive systems (Rainbow framework) with explicit statement that Matlab source code and data are publicly available; no formal threats-to-validity discussion and no process-mining-style quality metrics (this is an MDP decision-accuracy study, not process discovery).
human_research_question: How can an iterative decision-making scheme infer point and interval estimates of transition probabilities in a Markov Decision Process from runtime data and trade off accuracy, data usage, and computational overhead when selecting a confidently optimal scheduler for self-adaptive systems?
human_main_finding: The proposed Iterative Decision-Making Scheme (IDMS), embedded into the Rainbow self-adaptation framework, flexibly trades off accuracy, data usage, and computational overhead, achieving higher correctness rates than simple point estimation (especially for larger sample sizes), as shown via Monte Carlo simulation on a Rainbow-based example system.
human_limitations: Future work is needed to automatically adjust the confident-optimality criterion and sample size based on given metric priorities, and to generalize the value-iteration method so it can synthesize a scheduler without requiring a predefined, restricted subset of schedulers.

title: Mining constraints for event-based monitoring in systems of systems
abstract: The full behavior of software-intensive systems of systems (SoS) emerges during operation only. Runtime monitoring approaches have thus been proposed to detect deviations from the expected behavior. They commonly rely on temporal logic or domain-specific languages to formally define requirements, which are then checked by analyzing the stream of monitored events and event data. Some approaches also allow developers to generate constraints from declarative specifications of the expected behavior. However, independent of the approach, deep domain knowledge is required to specify the desired behavior. This knowledge is often not accessible in SoS environments with multiple development teams independently working on different, heterogeneous systems. In this New Ideas Paper we thus describe an approach that automatically mines constraints for runtime monitoring from event logs recorded in SoS. Our approach builds on ideas from specification mining, process mining, and machine learning to mine different types of constraints on event occurrence, event timing, and event data. The approach further presents the mined constraints to users in an existing constraint language and it ranks the constraints using different criteria. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by applying it to event logs from a real-world industrial SoS.
venue: Ase 2017 Proceedings of the 32nd IEEE ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text, no OCR issues; explicit 'Threats to Validity' section present (New Ideas paper with preliminary evaluation).
human_research_question: How can constraints for runtime monitoring of systems-of-systems be automatically mined from event logs, combining ideas from specification mining, process mining and machine learning?
human_main_finding: A four-step approach (sequence trees, feature vectors, decision tree/rule learning, ranking) automatically mined 43 candidate constraints from real industrial event logs of an automation systems-of-systems; engineers rated 11 of the top 15 ranked constraints as useful for monitoring.
human_limitations: Authors note the preliminary evaluation used small event logs from only one system, scalability was not tested at larger scale, generalizability to other systems remains to be investigated, and the learning step requires labeled valid/invalid event logs which may not always be available.

title: Probabilistic Model Checking GitHub Repositories for Software Project Analysis
abstract: GitHub serves as a platform for collaborative software development, where contributors engage, evolve projects, and shape the community. This study presents a novel approach to analyzing GitHub activity that departs from traditional methods. Using Discrete-Time Markov Chains and probabilistic Computation Tree Logic for model checking, we aim to uncover temporal dynamics, probabilities, and key factors influencing project behavior. By explicitly modeling state transitions, our approach provides transparency and explainability for sequential properties. The application of our method to five repositories demonstrates its feasibility and scalability and provides insights into the long-term probabilities of various activities. In particular, the analysis provides valuable perspectives for project managers to optimize team dynamics and resource allocation. The query specifications developed for model checking allow users to generate and execute queries for specific aspects, demonstrating scalability beyond the queries we present. In conclusion, our analysis provides an understanding of GitHub repository properties, branch management, and subscriber behavior. We anticipate its applicability to various open-source projects, revealing trends among contributors based on the unique characteristics of repositories.
venue: Applied Sciences Switzerland
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction, high confidence; data availability statement says raw data will be made available only on request (not open by default), and no fitness/precision/error metric is reported (only probabilistic query outputs specific to this study), so QA7 and QA8 scored 0.
human_research_question: How can Discrete-Time Markov Chain modeling combined with probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (pCTL) model checking be used to quantitatively and transparently analyze GitHub repository activity, branch management, and participant collaboration patterns?
human_main_finding: Applying DTMC-based probabilistic model checking (via PRISM) to five OSLabs GitHub repositories reveals repository-specific action rates, branch-usage patterns, pull-request processing speed, and participant contribution/merge dynamics, offering an interpretable alternative to black-box time-series/ML methods for informing project-management decisions.
human_limitations: Authors note the method may face challenges with repositories having complex multi-level branching strategies and could encounter state-explosion issues at larger scale (tested feasible up to ~400 participants); the study focuses on small/medium team projects rather than large-scale open-source projects.

title: Formal modeling and analysis of probabilistic real-time systems
abstract: Real-time systems usually involve a subtle interaction of a number of distributed components and have a high degree of parallelism, which makes their performance analysis quite complex. Thus, traditional techniques, such as simulation, or state-based formal methods usually fail to produce reasonable results. The main limitation of these approaches may be overcome by conducting the performance analysis of real-time systems using higher-order-logic theorem proving. This chapter is mainly oriented towards this emerging trend and it provides the details about analyzing both functional and performance related properties of real-time systems using a higher-order-logic theorem prover (HOL). For illustration purposes, the Stop-and-Wait protocol, which is a classical example of real-time systems, has been considered as a case-study.
venue: Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing

title: A stochastic approach to security software quality management
venue: 25th European Modeling and Simulation Symposium Emss 2013
human_qa_notes: Practitioner conference paper combining Six Sigma DMAIC, Monte Carlo simulation and OSDC; demonstration is a 'hypothetical scenario' built on a real published reliability dataset (Lyu 1996, Dataset ODC4), with predicted-vs-actual validation tables.
human_research_question: How can a stochastic approach combining Six Sigma DMAIC, Monte Carlo simulation, and Orthogonal Security Defect Classification improve security software quality/risk management for ongoing projects, overcoming the limitations of conventional analytic risk models?
human_main_finding: The stochastic DMAIC + Monte Carlo + OSDC method accurately predicted total defect counts (0% error) and reliability risk levels using real published failure data mapped to a hypothetical security-software scenario, correctly flagging an unstable testing process and later verifying that a proposed improvement plan would bring the process within target Six Sigma quality levels.

title: Optimal version-upgrade problem based on stochastic differential equations for Open Source Software
abstract: The current software development environment has been changing into new development paradigms such as concurrent distributed development environment and the so-called open source project by using network computing technologies. New distributed development paradigm typified by such open source project will evolve at a rapid pace in the future. Especially, OSS (Open Source Software) systems which serve as key components of critical infrastructures in the society are still ever-expanding now. We focus on OSS developed under open source project. In this paper, we propose a software reliability growth model based on stochastic differential equations in order to consider the active state of the open source project. Especially, we assume that the software failure intensity depends on the time, and the software fault-report phenomena on the bug tracking system keep an irregular state. Also, we analyze actual software fault count data to show numerical examples of software reliability assessment for the OSS. Moreover, it has been necessary to manage the software development process in terms of reliability, effort, and version-upgrade time. In this paper, we find the optimal total version-upgrade time based on the total expected software maintenance effort. We show that the proposed model can assist improvement of quality for OSS systems developed under the open source project.
venue: Icqr 2007 Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Quality and Reliability

title: Leveraging process mining techniques for up-To-date resource profiles
abstract: Keeping an up-to-date overview of the knowledge and skills available in an organization is a difficult task. Looking at this problem we propose the use of data, that already exists in the\norganization’s information systems, as a means to keep user knowledge profiles up to date. To extract the required information from these information systems, we suggest the use of process mining. We illustrate the current state of our research and the end goals we aim to reach with it. We state a general\nresearch question. We then apply this to a software development setting, applying knowledge gained during an ongoing case study at a software development company.
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Short workshop 'radar'/research-in-progress paper describing a design-science research plan; most QA criteria score 0 because no concrete dataset, named PM technique, or empirical results are yet presented (work is at the problem-identification/objectives stage); text extraction itself is clean with no OCR issues.
human_research_question: Can employee knowledge/skill profiles be kept up to date automatically using process mining applied to data already captured in organizational information systems (time registration, SCRUM boards, version control)?
human_main_finding: This research-in-progress (design science) paper proposes leveraging process mining on existing information-system logs to automatically maintain up-to-date employee knowledge/skill profiles for team selection, illustrated through an ongoing case study at software company Cegeka; no empirical results are yet reported, only research design and anticipated challenges.
human_limitations: Authors themselves flag: (1) available log data may be too fine-grained to map to skills/knowledge, (2) version-control logs lack a clear notion of activities (coding vs. commit time), and (3) knowledge/skill levels are subjective, making objective validation of resulting profiles difficult.

title: Software process simulation modeling: preliminary results from an updated systematic review
authors: Chao Gao; Shu Jiang; Guoping Rong
abstract: Software Process Simulation Modeling (SPSM) has raised research interest since 1980s. However, it is observed that SPSM studies published in the ICSSP community may have dropped in recent years. The objective of this research is to update the recent status of this area. We conducted a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) using the QGS-based search strategy. The review identified 74 primary studies in the past five years (2008-2012). This paper presents the preliminary results from this updated SLR by answering the first four research questions. Based on the findings from this updated review, it can be concluded that in terms of the number of SPSM studies found in the overall software engineering community, there is no significant change (drop) compared to the former review stage (1998-2007).
venue: Proceedings of the 2014 International Conference on Software and System Process
human_qa_notes: This is itself a rigorous systematic literature review (SLR) with a reproducible QGS-based search protocol and kappa-checked screening, but it studies software process SIMULATION modeling (not process mining) and reports no process-model fitness/precision metrics; no dedicated threats-to-validity section for the SLR itself.
human_research_question: What is the state-of-the-art of software process simulation modeling (SPSM) research from 2008-2012 -- purposes, simulation paradigms, tools, and problem domains -- compared to the prior 1998-2007 review period?
human_main_finding: An updated SLR of 74 primary studies (2008-2012) found no significant change in the overall volume of SPSM research in the SE community versus 1998-2007, although ProSim/ICSSP-specific publications declined; System Dynamics and Discrete-Event Simulation remain the dominant paradigms, hybrid simulation is increasingly used, but many Category-A studies still lack industry-scale validation.
human_limitations: The authors note that many software process simulation model/simulator studies fail to trial their models on industry-scale problems, and that limitations of the paradigms/methods used are still rarely discussed in the reviewed literature; space limits also meant only RQ1-RQ4 of the planned six research questions were reported.

title: Better reasoning about software engineering activities
abstract: Software management oracles often contain numerous subjective features. At each subjective point, a range of behaviors is possible. Stochastic simulation samples a subset of the possible behaviors. After many such stochastic simulations, the TAR2 treatment learner can find control actions that have (usually) the same impact despite the subjectivity of the oracle.
venue: Proceedings 16th Annual International Conference on Automated Software Engineering Ase 2001
human_qa_notes: ASE 2001 submission extract; some mojibake (smart quotes, math glyphs) but the argument is fully readable. QA3=1: CMM2 source (Paulk et al., pp. 125–191), encoding size (55 items, 27 actions, 79/150 edges), chance ranges 0.7X–1.3X, 2000/4000 runs and treatment-search settings are specified. QA7=0: 'full model available via email from the authors' is not a public archive. QA8=0: outcomes are class-worth ratios and treatment rankings, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE/RMSE.
human_research_question: In data-starved early-lifecycle SE, can stochastic simulation of a subjective CMM level-2 knowledge model, summarized by the TAR2 treatment learner, identify a small set of management actions that improve the odds of cheap, high-chance projects (the 'minimal management question')?
human_main_finding: 2000 random JANE walks over an encoded CMM2 oracle, classified into cost×chance bands and summarized by TAR2, yield a handful of high-leverage treatments (notably lowering cost of using requirements, formal milestone reviews, and good unit testing) that raise 'worth' from 1.0 to about 1.28–1.44; most of the 27 candidate CMM2 actions can be ignored. Treatments remained stable when the sample was doubled to 4000 runs.
human_limitations: CMM2 is not universally accepted and the authors' subjective encoding may diverge from the SEI text; results come from simulated behaviour of that oracle, not field project data; random-search coverage is only checked by doubling N; a particular project may need fixed bindings that were not empirically validated. External-validity threats are discussed in §4.
