title: Probabilistic Approach to Predicting Risk in Software Projects Using Software Repository Data
abstract: Although the factors that need to be focused on for a successful software project appear to be difficult to define, risk management has become one of the key activities for achieving such success because significant risk is involved in each software development phase. Software project failures are often a result of insufficient and ineffective risk information regarding the future. To overcome this, software risk prediction should be performed in advance to allow project managers insight into providing more valuable information for decision making, such as scope coverage, resource allocation, and schedule changes. In this research, we propose a risk prediction model from the perspective of quality using a software repository. We evaluated the risk threat level by mapping some defect attributes that exist in the defect lifecycle, defined their risk threat transition states, and applied a Markov chain for predicting the potential risk level. We evaluated the proposed approach using practical real-industry mobile software projects. The experimental results confirm that our approach is applicable to software threat risk estimation.
venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text; strong real-industry case study with a dedicated Limitations section, though no fitness/precision-style model-quality metric and dataset/code not publicly released.
human_research_question: Can a Markov-chain-based risk prediction model, built from defect severity/frequency attributes mined from a software repository, accurately estimate and predict future software project risk levels?
human_main_finding: A Markov chain-based Risk Prediction Model (RPM), built from defect severity/frequency data of real industrial mobile software projects, effectively estimated and predicted future risk-threat levels, with predicted probabilities aligning with observed defect-risk trends over the project lifecycle.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly discuss human/tester bias in severity assessment, limited applicability to small-scale or non-platform-based projects with insufficient defect volume, and inapplicability when the test team changes mid-project.

title: Mining Software Process Lines
abstract: There is a vast growth of generated event data being collected and stored by organizations. Within the field of Process Mining, this data has been used to discover, analyze and enhance processes from different domains. For this purpose there are hundreds of techniques available in different tools. These techniques are mostly focused on single processes. On the other hand, there are several proposals for dealing with multiple processes. Under different names, such as: configurable process models, process families or process lines, processes are characterized by capturing commonalities and variability between (similar) process models. These approaches have shown to be useful for organizations that have multiple variants of a given process, e.g., reducing redundancy and maintenance time. In this research proposal, we are developing a framework that allows the use of Process Mining techniques in families of processes within the software development domain (i.e., Software Process Lines).
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Software Engineering Companion (ICSE '16)
human_qa_notes: This is a doctoral-symposium/work-in-progress paper (ICSE 2016 Companion) describing an ongoing research proposal rather than a completed empirical study; most of the described framework (conformance, enhancement phases, full evaluation) is future work, and no code/data repository or threats-to-validity section is provided.
human_research_question: How can process mining techniques (discovery, conformance, enhancement) be extended to work with Software Process Lines (families of related process variants) rather than single processes, particularly to help small software enterprises (SSEs) capture and improve their real, often-undocumented development processes?
human_main_finding: This work-in-progress paper proposes an end-to-end Process Mining framework (discovery, conformance, enhancement) for Software Process Lines and reports a prototype discovery algorithm ('v-algorithm', implemented as a ProM plug-in) already applied to event logs extracted from 2 of 5 target Chilean small software enterprises via a descriptive case study, with results manually compared to the companies' known processes; conformance and enhancement components remain future work.
human_limitations: The paper is explicitly an early-stage/ongoing research proposal without full empirical validation: only 2 of 5 target companies had event logs extracted so far, conformance/enhancement prototypes are not yet built, and planned evaluation with company stakeholders had not yet been conducted at time of writing.

title: Discrete and continuous time high-order markov models for software reliability assessment
abstract: Due to the critical challenges and complexity of modern software systems developed over the last decade, there has arisen an ever increasing attention to look for products with high reliability at reasonable costs. Software development process moves toward component-based design, and architecture based approach in software reliability modeling is widely used. However, in lots of models for software reliability assessment the assumption of independent software runs is a simplification of real software behaviour. This paper describes two software reliability models that use high-order Markov chains thus taking into account dependencies among software component runs for more accurate software reliability assessment. The efficiency and accuracy of developed models is investigated by the example of several software products. It is shown that using the software reliability models based on the high-order Markov chains results in the software reliability assessment accuracy up to 10–20%.
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Real software systems (developed by one of the authors) are used for validation with named high-order Markov chain techniques and AIC/BIC order-selection criteria, but the datasets/logs themselves are not shared or fully described for independent reproduction; no formal threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: Can discrete- and continuous-time high-order Markov chain models, which account for dependencies among software component runs, provide more accurate software reliability assessment than standard first-order Markov chain models?
human_main_finding: High-order Markov chain models increase software reliability assessment accuracy by up to 6% (discrete-time) and 10-20% (continuous-time) compared to first-order models, by better capturing interdependence among software component runs; the optimal chain order is determined via AIC/BIC criteria.
human_limitations: Practical aspects of estimating model input parameters and studying how reliability depends on software characteristics (component count, variables per component, component cohesion, etc.) are explicitly deferred to future work.

title: Experiences in discovering, modeling, and reenacting open source software development processes
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Full text is clean and complete; NetBeans public artifacts and dated URLs (Issuezilla, XTest, QA graphs) are specified well enough for QA3=1, and the authors did discover/model/re-enact a real process (QA5=1); QA6/QA7/QA8 scored 0 because challenges are discussed without a threats-to-validity framing, no research dataset/code is released, and conformance is only informal role/artifact/tool reconciliation (no fitness/precision).
human_research_question: Can software processes of large global OSSD projects (illustrated on the NetBeans requirements-and-release process) be discovered, modeled, and re-enacted from publicly observable Web information spaces using a process meta-model and reference model?
human_main_finding: A bottom-up Web-artifact discovery strategy guided by the Mi–Scacchi meta-model produced informal (use cases, rich hypermedia, flow graphs) and formal PML models of the NetBeans requirements-and-release process that could be compiled into navigable re-enactments; walkthroughs surfaced practical issues such as release-manager overload and duplicated testing work across four agent types.
human_limitations: Private communications are unobservable; ethnographic discovery does not scale across many projects; assembling control-flow and activity hierarchy from heterogeneous artifacts remains largely manual; process prescriptions may not match actual enactment; demonstration is concentrated on one NetBeans process (Mozilla/Apache mentioned only as further cases).

title: Software safety assessment based on a subordinated Markov chain
abstract: Abstract Software safety can be defined as the property such that no situation inducing a hazard (dangerous condition) is created during the intended period under a specified environment when the software executes a predetermined function. In this paper, by considering the correlation in regard to the impact of software faults a new software safety assessment model based on a subordinated Markov chain is proposed. The goodness‐of‐fit is investigated for the software fault detection data observed in the actual test process, and we show the effectiveness of the proposed model in software safety evaluation. © 2004 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Electron Comm Jpn Pt 3, 87(5): 24–32, 2004; Published online in Wiley InterScience ( www.interscience.wiley.com ). DOI 10.1002/ecjc.10097
venue: International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction with formulas well preserved; no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, typical of a mathematical modeling paper.
human_research_question: How can software safety be assessed by modeling correlated types of software errors (critical/major/minor) using a subordinated Markov chain (NHPP + DTMC), and does this model fit and predict data better than existing independent-NHPP-based models?
human_main_finding: Using real testing data on critical/major/minor software errors from the Shuttle Ground System, the proposed subordinated Markov chain model achieved better AIC and prediction accuracy (SAE) than two existing superposed NHPP models, yielding a more optimistic (higher) software safety estimate.
human_limitations: Authors note that Newton's method for estimating LPe parameters can yield invalid (negative) parameter values, and that DTMC estimation under grouped data is harder than under fully observed transition data; future work will extend the model to the software release problem.

title: Mining Issue Trackers: Concepts and Techniques
abstract: An issue tracker is a software tool used by organisations to interact with users and manage various aspects of the software development lifecycle. With the rise of agile methodologies, issue trackers have become popular in open and closed-source settings alike. Internal and external stakeholders report, manage, and discuss "issues", which represent different information such as requirements and maintenance tasks. Issue trackers can quickly become complex ecosystems, with dozens of projects, hundreds of users, thousands of issues, and often millions of issue evolutions. Finding and understanding the relevant issues for the task at hand and keeping an overview becomes difficult with time. Moreover, managing issue workflows for diverse projects becomes more difficult as organisations grow, and more stakeholders get involved. To help address these difficulties, software and requirements engineering research have suggested automated techniques based on mining issue tracking data. Given the vast amount of textual data in issue trackers, many of these techniques leverage natural language processing. This chapter discusses four major use cases for algorithmically analysing issue data to assist stakeholders with the complexity and heterogeneity of information in issue trackers. The chapter is accompanied by a follow-along demonstration package with JupyterNotebooks.
venue: Handbook on Natural Language Processing for Requirements Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean book-chapter extraction (arXiv v2); survey/tutorial with Jupyter demonstrations on public Jira data rather than a single empirical study. QA4/QA8 scored 0: techniques are NLP/embeddings/link analysis, not a named process-mining or stochastic-modeling method, and the chapter's own demos report cosine similarity and sentiment rather than fitness/precision/F1. QA6 scored 0: 'Pitfalls and Takeaways' discuss NLP false positives, not study threats to validity. QA7 scored 1 (Zenodo notebooks + Jira dataset DOI + LYNX GitHub). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (MSR/NLP on issue trackers, not PM/stochastic SE modeling).
human_research_question: How can NLP and mining techniques applied to issue-tracker content, metadata, discussions, evolution histories, and issue links help stakeholders analyse requirements quality, issue evolution, comments, and traceability in large heterogeneous issue repositories?
human_main_finding: Four demonstrated use cases on public Jira data (including the Montgomery et al. 2.7M-issue dataset) show that lexical/POS/hypernym methods can flag subjective language and nominalisations in user stories, description edits often reduce sentiment toward more technical wording, comment mining can surface suggested field updates, and TF-IDF vs BERT embeddings distinguish Cloner links (highest similarity) while Duplicate links are not reliably separable from other types by text similarity alone.
human_limitations: Issue text is heterogeneous and often low-quality (false-positive ambiguity detections; 'Story' issues that are not true user stories; sentiment tools sensitive to URLs/log dumps); typed issue-link classification remains an open problem (cited macro-F1 still modest); the chapter is a methods survey with illustrative analyses rather than a controlled experiment.

title: Systematic mapping study on process mining in agile software development
abstract: 18th International Conference on Software Process Improvement and Capability Determination, SPICE 2018; Tessaloniki; Greece; 9 October 2018 through 10 October 2018Process mining is a process management technique that allows for the analysis of business processes based on the event logs and its aim is to discover, monitor and improve executed processes by extracting knowledge from event logs readily available in information systems. The popularity of agile software development methods has been increasing in the software development field over the last two decades and many software organizations develop software using agile methods. Process mining can provide complementary tools to Agile organizations for process management. Process mining can be used to discover agile processes followed by agile teams to establish the baselines and to determine the fidelity or they can be used to obtain feedback to improve agility. Despite the potential benefit of using process mining for agile software development, there is a lack of research that systematically analyzes the usage of process mining in agile software development. This paper presents a systematic mapping study on usage of process mining in agile software development approaches. The aim is to find out the usage areas of process mining in agile software development, explore commonly used algorithms, data sources, data collection mechanisms, analysis techniques and tools. The study has shown us that process mining is used in Agile software development especially for the purpose of process discovery from task tracking applications. We also observed that source code repositories are main data sources for process mining, a diversity of algorithms are used for analysis of collected data and ProM is the most widely used analysis tool for process mining
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
human_qa_notes: Clean text; this is a systematic mapping (secondary) study, not an empirical case study on its own event-log data, so QA5 scored 0; no explicit threats-to-validity/limitations-of-the-review discussion (QA6=0), though search/selection methodology is reproducibly described (QA7=1).
human_research_question: What is the current state of research on the application of process mining in agile software development, including usage areas, purposes, footprint data sources, algorithms, and tools?
human_main_finding: The mapping study identified 25 relevant papers showing process mining in agile contexts is used mainly for process discovery (via issue trackers and software repositories), with conformance checking and improvement as secondary purposes; ProM is the dominant tool and diverse algorithms (alpha, heuristic, fuzzy, genetic miners) are used, while data collection and concept drift remain key open challenges.
human_limitations: not stated

title: Probabilistic Learning of Temporal Uncertainties in Business Processes
venue: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
human_qa_notes: Rigorous, reproducible experimental paper (public code/datasets, proper scoring-rule evaluation, explicit discussion of overfitting/limitations); however it is a generic business-process-simulation paper (datasets: repair shop, PCR testing lab, bank loan process) with no explicit software-engineering context, so QA2 is not met.
human_research_question: Can a non-parametric probabilistic learner (DR-BART) better model the temporal uncertainty (multi-peaked, context-dependent distributions) of activity processing and waiting times in data-driven business process simulation than traditional single-peaked/resource-differentiated parametric distributions?
human_main_finding: DR-BART models trained with well-chosen feature encodings outperformed traditional parametric and resource-differentiated probabilistic models on two of three datasets (artificial repair-shop and real-world PCR testing logs) in log-likelihood and CRPS, though a resource-differentiated approach still won on the large real-world BPIC-2017 bank loan dataset; too few or too many features, and too many training iterations, caused overfitting and degraded performance.
human_limitations: Authors note DR-BART is prone to overfitting and computationally expensive (some BPIC-2017 models failed to train or were infeasible within a week), and that the business process simulator used is simplified, simulating cases independently and ignoring shared-resource contention across concurrently running cases.

title: Holistic discovery of decision models from process execution data
abstract: Abstract The analysis of business processes is a multifaceted problem that is comprised of analysing both activities’ workflow, as well as the decisions that are made throughout that workflow. In process mining, the automated discovery of process models from event data, a strong emphasis can be found towards discovering this workflow, as well as how data influences that workflow, i.e., decision point analysis. Nonetheless, the data that is pertaining to the activities in the workflow does not necessarily correlate with the control flow. Decisions that influence variables that are used by activities can also impact other variables used later in the workflow without interfering with the order in which activities are executed. Discovering this has not been addressed in literature, as current decision mining techniques still rely on control flow. To address this, Process Mining Integrating Decisions (P-MInD) is proposed. It relies on uncovering the influence of activities on their variables and connects them by making use of sequence dependencies present in the data. Furthermore, it allows to find autocorrelations, as well to incorporate case variables. This allows to establish a holistic image of the decision layer, captured with Decision Model and Notation (DMN), that is consistent with the discovered control flow. Furthermore, decision model conformance checking, i.e., the matching of event logs with holistic models, is proposed to offer a way to verify whether the models are corresponding with the behaviour that is present in the current system. P-MInD is implemented and used on real-life data to verify its effectiveness.
venue: Knowledge Based Systems
human_qa_notes: Strong decision-mining paper (P-MInD) with real BPI Challenge 2017 case study, public dataset and open-source ProM/GitHub implementation; domain is general business process (loan application), not SE-specific, and there is no formal threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: How can decision models be discovered from process execution data in a way that captures the full 'holistic' decision layer (variable-activity relationships, autocorrelations, loops, case attributes) independently of, yet consistent with, the control-flow model, and how can such discovered decision models be checked for conformance?
human_main_finding: P-MInD, using variable-activity pairs and shifts, discovers holistic Decision Requirements Graphs from event logs that are independent of but consistent with the control flow, capturing autocorrelations, loops, and case attributes; applied to the BPI Challenge 2017 log it uncovers decisions (e.g., credit-score assignment) invisible to control-flow-based approaches, and a conformance-checking extension can compare decision models discovered from different event logs.
human_limitations: Authors note that a high number of resulting trace clusters can make results hard for users to interpret, and that a benchmarked alternative decision-mining technique could not be used for comparison because it cannot handle loops and had only been validated on synthetic, loop-free data.

title: International Workshops on Business Process Management, BPM 2020
abstract: Purpose Although Business Process Management (BPM) is a critical issue and small- and medium-sized family firms (SMFFs) frequently adopt process organization, very little literature focuses on the processes by which family firms remain distinctive (Chrisman et al. , 2016) or on their approach to BPM. The current research aims to fill this gap by analyzing dynamic companies’ attitudes to process-driven ability that concern exploitative as well as explorative processes. The purpose of this paper is to identify which kinds of dimensions may build an ambidextrous state in BPM in SMFFs, also favored by entrepreneurial IT capabilities and influenced by a stable but changeable context. Design/methodology/approach The authors referred to vom Brocke et al.’s (2014) study as it allows a focus on BPM research in the context of SMFFs. Then, the authors adapted the framework to the context of SMFFs. In addition, an empirical analysis has been made for applying the framework’s principles on effective BPM requirements to SMFFs. In the research, the authors applied grounded theory, according to which observation and theorization are linked by circularity, as they represent moments being managed simultaneously. The theorization emerged in different moments of the empirical surveys, influencing the next data gathering and the data gathering was the object of a de-structured matching and analysis process. Findings Specific cultural and cognitive aspects, values and abilities affect the company behavior of SMFFs in terms of BPM, and this is influenced by the connection between the family and the business. Therefore, it confirms that the family is a missing variable in organizational research (Dyer, 2006) also in BPM. A good BPM permits the definition of business abilities of running the current processes, along with of acclimatizing the company to a changeable context. In regard to the exploitative and explorative strengths typical of organizational ambidexterity, the research favors, respectively, transactional excellence with a focus on net cost reduction and transformational excellence based on net revenue generation. This approach requires consideration of the difference between external and internal contingencies as well as of the different processes to manage. However, despite IT-based BPM tools and the new era of IT-based process thinking, technology appropriation is only one of our dimensions, and each dimension plays a role in good BPM behavior; only a combination of dimensions favors effective and flexible BPM. Research limitations/implications The research contributes to the literature on BPM through theoretical implications, in particular two main implications. First, the research emphasizes the impact of familiness on good BPM practice. Family appears to be a missing variable in organizational research on BPM, even though familiness affects process specificity and mechanisms. Second, the research is based on certain category dimensions that characterize management models common in the literature, allowing the application of BPM in FFs by taking advantage of their confidence and adaptability. Limitations are related to different points of view on the model’s scope and design, the recipient and the research method. Practical implications The research has two main practical implications, representing managerial potential, that improve the significance and originality of the research in internal and external contexts. In the internal context, this permits a new BPM mind-set. Originality/value The research is original for the following two reasons. First, when FF complexity grows and/or new organizational issues emerge, FFs are faced with two challenges: an increased number of complex processes to handle, along with a lack of IT-based BPM for organizational ambidexterity. In such a context, this research can suggest a solution. Second, the research is based on dimensions that have been widely characterized in general management models. For this reason, FFs may already be familiar with these dimensions. In addition, the model strongly valorizes the familiness impact on BPM development and takes into consideration the context awareness of the company.
venue: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing

title: Bayesian inference for nonhomogeneous Poisson processes in software reliability models assuming nonmonotonic intensity functions
abstract: Abstract When analysing reliability data from a repairable system e.g. a car, a fridge, etc, reliability specialists are interested in the full life history of a system so that they may identify problems that have affected its life and apply solutions, if possible, to other new systems so that these new systems do not suffer from the same problems. The basis of reliability analysis is to understand how systems are failing by modeling their life history so that prediction of the likely future reliability of systems is possible. This is the basis of reliability growth (development) testing where systems under development are tested to find latent design and manufacturing defects so that they can be eliminated from the full‐scale production system. The simplest way of identifying structure in the system's life history is to plot the data. Three plots are commonly used: plotting failures on a time line; plotting the failure number against cumulative time, and plotting an estimate of the intensity, the rate of occurrence of failures (ROCOF) against cumulative time. These plots appear in Ascher and Feingold [31] and Crowder et al . [61] among others. These plots will help to identify structure such as an increase or decrease in the interfailure times of a system over time (more commonly known as reliability growth and reliability decay); evidence of cycles in the data—these may be short or long cycles; periods of high or low reliability (again related to usage); gaps in the time stream (due to change in the reporting mechanism, management, etc) and outliers (possible abnormal operating conditions). This review lists the intensity functions and their associated expected number of failures, which is the mean value parameter of the nonhomogeneous Poisson process (NHPP). The simplest and best known intensities, those based on mortality rates, those based on hazards of well‐known probability distributions, the software related intensities, and those based on differential equations and extensions are discussed under their appropriate classification headings.
venue: Computational Statistics and Data Analysis
human_qa_notes: Purely theoretical/statistical paper validated only on a simulated numerical example (not real SE data), no discussion of validity threats or code availability; OCR badly garbles the equations, though prose and tables are legible enough to judge most criteria.
human_research_question: How can Bayesian inference via MCMC (Gibbs sampling/Metropolis-Hastings) be used to fit nonhomogeneous Poisson process software reliability models with nonmonotonic (e.g., bathtub-shaped) intensity functions, and how can competing models be discriminated using Bayesian model-selection criteria?
human_main_finding: Using MCMC to fit an exponentiated-Weibull NHPP intensity function recovers nonmonotonic (bathtub) failure-intensity shapes accurately on a simulated dataset, and Bayes factors computed from estimated marginal likelihoods show this model is strongly preferred over two superposition-of-Musa-Okumoto alternatives for the simulated bathtub data.
human_limitations: not stated

title: Towards automated conformance checking of ebBP-ST choreographies and corresponding WS-BPEL based orchestrations
abstract: Web Services technologies are a natural candidate for Business-to-Business integration (B2Bi). For crossorganizational processes, the concepts of “choreography” and “orchestration” are important. The term choreography denotes a model of a global view over message exchange scenarios, whereas the term orchestration focuses on models of the local implementation. While WS-BPEL is already kind of a de-facto standard in the field of orchestration languages, there does not exist a standard choreography language. We propose the usage of ebXML BPSS (ebBP) in order to provide choreography modeling at the business level. A frequent problem is to ensure and enforce the consistency and conformance of choreography and orchestration models which is often referred to as “conformance checking”. In this paper we examine a way to check the conformance between ebBP-ST (a subset of ebBP) choreographies and corresponding WS-BPEL based implementations. To achieve this check well-known and approved model checking methods and tools are used: First ebBP-ST choreographies are directly transformed into the process algebra CCS. Second, the low level WS-BPEL processes are analyzed for code blocks that implement choreography elements and the sequence of these code blocks is then mapped to CCS, too. Afterwards these formalized representations will be checked for bisimulation equivalence in order to reveal inconsistencies between the choreography and their implementations.
venue: Seke 2011 Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean extraction. QA2=0: running example is a B2B purchase choreography (quote request/accept), not a software-engineering development process. QA4=1 because conformance checking / weak bisimulation / CCS are formally named, but this is model-checking equivalence of ebBP-ST vs WS-BPEL, not event-log process-mining conformance. QA5=0: only a 'towards' method plus 'preliminary' CWB checks on the toy use case and injected faults; no systematic empirical evaluation.
human_research_question: How can conformance between ebBP-ST choreographies and corresponding WS-BPEL control-process orchestrations be checked automatically by transforming both to CCS and testing weak bisimulation?
human_main_finding: Authors give algorithms that map well-formed binary ebBP-ST shared-state choreographies and WS-BPEL implementation patterns to CCS, then use the Edinburgh Concurrency Workbench to decide weak bisimulation; they argue the backend-driven B2Bi architecture requires this stricter notion rather than incoming/outgoing trace refinement. Only preliminary CWB applicability is claimed.
human_limitations: Restricted to well-formed binary ebBP-ST (no forks/joins, no overlapping shared states); BPEL must follow known ebBP implementation patterns rather than arbitrary processes; no public tool/data and no quantitative quality metrics; authors themselves list ongoing work on relaxing BPEL structure and usability (highlighting mismatches in the original models).

title: Characterization of operational failures from a business data processing SaaS platform
abstract: This paper characterizes operational failures of a production Custom Package Good Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform. Events log collected over 283 days of in-field operation are used to characterize platform failures. The characterization is performed by estimating (i) common failure types of the platform, (ii) key factors impacting platform failures, (iii) failure rate, and (iv) how user workload (files submitted for processing) impacts on the failure rate. The major findings are: (i) 34.1% of failures are caused by unexpected values in customers' data, (ii) nearly 33% of the failures are because of timeout, and (iii) the failure rate increases if the workload intensity (transactions/second) increases, while there is no statistical evidence of being influenced by the workload volume (size of users' data). Finally, the paper presents the lessons learned and how the findings and the implemented analysis tool allow platform developers to improve platform code, system settings and customer management.
venue: 36th International Conference on Software Engineering ICSE Companion 2014 Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Rigorous empirical/statistical case study of a production SaaS platform's operational failures (MTBF, Laplace/Mann-Kendall trend tests, distribution fitting); no dedicated threats-to-validity section and underlying data/LOC counts are kept confidential, limiting reproducibility.
human_research_question: What are the common causes of operational failures in a production business-data-processing SaaS platform, and how do workload intensity and workload volume affect the platform's failure rate?
human_main_finding: Analysis of 283 days of operational logs from a production CPG SaaS platform found that 34.1% of failures stem from unexpected values in customer data and 32.7% from timeouts; failure rate increases with workload intensity (not workload volume) and is largely insensitive to software upgrades, with failure inter-arrival times fitting a Fatigue Life distribution that becomes exponential once timeout failures are removed.
human_limitations: The authors note the findings are based on a single, specific SaaS platform, so generalizability to other systems is not established, and that 29.8% of failures could not be diagnosed because they produced only empty log entries, a data-quality limitation of the underlying logs used in the study.

title: Analysis of software repositories using process mining
abstract: This study conducts a comparative analysis of Artificial Intelligence (AI) software and traditional GitHub repositories, focusing on workflow efficiency and sentiment dynamics.Using process mining and sentiment analysis techniques, we examine repositories from eight prominent projects, encompassing diverse datasets of issues and pull requests filtered for relevance and consistency.Our findings reveal that AI software repositories exhibit different workflow patterns and sentiment dynamics compared to traditional repositories.Sentiment analysis uncovers that contributors to AI software repositories experience more positive sentiment dynamics, likely reflecting structured workflows and collaborative tools.Conversely, traditional repositories exhibit longer resolution times and more fluctuating sentiment patterns, which may indicate higher complexity or less automation.These insights provide valuable recommendations for optimizing repository management, fostering contributor satisfaction, and improving collaborative software development environments.
venue: Smart Innovation Systems and Technologies
human_qa_notes: Clean text; solid real open-source case study but no specific named discovery algorithm (only generic "DISCO tool"/"process mining"), no limitations/threats-to-validity discussion, and no fitness/precision metrics reported.
human_research_question: What does mining the Google Chromium Issue Tracker's event logs with process mining reveal about inefficiencies and inconsistencies in the software bug-resolution process?
human_main_finding: Process mining of ~23,800 Chromium bug reports (using the Disco tool) revealed process inefficiencies such as fixed issues rarely being verified, frequent rework/reassignment, duplicate-status rework, and priority-handling inconsistencies (23 issues with invalid priorities), indicating the actual bug-resolution process deviates from the intended design.
human_limitations: not stated

title: Reducing user input requests to improve IT support ticket resolution process
abstract: Management and maintenance of IT infrastructure resources such as hardware, software and network is an integral part of software development and maintenance projects. Service management ensures that the tickets submitted by users, i.e. software developers, are serviced within the agreed resolution times. Failure to meet those times induces penalty on the service provider. To prevent a spurious penalty on the service provider, non-working hours such as waiting for user inputs are not included in the measured resolution time, that is, a service level clock pauses its timing. Nevertheless, the user interactions slow down the resolution process, that is, add to user experienced resolution time and degrade user experience. Therefore, this work is motivated by the need to analyze and reduce user input requests in tickets’ life cycle.\u3cbr/\u3e\u3cbr/\u3eTo address this problem, we analyze user input requests and investigate their impact on user experienced resolution time. We distinguish between input requests of two types: real, seeking information from the user to process the ticket and tactical, when no information is asked but the user input request is raised merely to pause the service level clock. Next, we propose a system that preempts a user at the time of ticket submission to provide additional information that the analyst, a person responsible for servicing the ticket, is likely to ask, thus reducing real user input requests. Further, we propose a detection system to identify tactical user input requests.\u3cbr/\u3e\u3cbr/\u3eTo evaluate the approach, we conducted a case study in a large global IT company. We observed that around 57% of the tickets have user input requests in the life cycle, causing user experienced resolution time to be almost twice as long as the measured service resolution time. The proposed preemptive system preempts the information needs with an average accuracy of 94–99% across five cross validations while traditional approaches such as logistic regression and naive Bayes have accuracy in the range of 50–60%. The detection system identifies around 15% of the total user input requests as tactical. Therefore, the proposed solution can efficiently bring down the number of user input requests and, hence, improve the user-experienced resolution time
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Very thorough empirical process-mining + ML case study (Empirical Software Engineering journal) with a dedicated Threats-to-Validity section (Sec. 11) and survey triangulation; raw ticket data itself is confidential/not shared (company policy), though keyword lists, process models, and anonymized survey results were published on GitHub; QA8=0 because reported precision/recall are for ML classifiers, not process-model conformance metrics.
human_research_question: How can process mining and machine learning be used to analyze and reduce real and tactical (non-information-seeking) user input requests in IT support ticket resolution, thereby shortening the gap between measured service-level resolution time and user-experienced resolution time?
human_main_finding: Process mining of 593,497 real IT support tickets from a large global IT company showed 57% of tickets have at least one 'Awaiting User Input' state, making user-experienced resolution time roughly double the measured service-level time; an SVM-based preemptive model achieved 94-99% accuracy (vs 50-60% for naive Bayes/logistic regression baselines) at anticipating needed information, and a rule-based detection model identified about 15% of input requests as tactical.
human_limitations: Authors' Threats to Validity section notes: findings on tactical requests may not generalize to organizations with different characteristics (external validity); the preemptive model was evaluated on held-out test data, not in live production (conclusion validity); and communication occurring outside the ticketing system (phone/chat) was not observable, potentially affecting the preemptive model (construct validity).

title: Business process analysis of programmer job role in software development using process mining
abstract: In software development, the contribution of each role is needed to run the business process according to the expected goals. This research was conducted to identify the programmer’s contribution in the software engineering course. Based on the record of commit data through collaboration tools, it was found that programmers contributed less when compared to project managers and analysts. So, it is necessary to discover the programmer’s workflow. Process mining techniques were used in this study to obtain a flow based on the event log generated by the collaboration tools. The results of this study were on average; each team carried out 4-6 activities. Based on SEQUAL framework, whether syntactic, semantic, or pragmatic, there are issues that occur, including deadlocks, lack of synchronization, superfluous activity, labeling issues, line crossing, and crooked alignment. Handling the quality issue of the process can improve the role of programmers and all members of the software development team.
venue: Procedia Computer Science
human_ft_notes: PDF em no-ok/ não utilizado para QA/extração — Business process analysis of programmer job role in software development. Decisão alterada de include para exclude (2026-08-13).

title: Assessing process-centered software engineering environments
authors: Vincenzo Ambriola; Reidar Conradi; Alfonso Fuggetta
abstract: Process-centered software engineering environments (PSEEs) are the most recent generation of environments supporting software development activities. They exploit an representation of the process (called the process model that specifies how to carry out software development activities, the roles and tasks of software developers, and how to use and control software development tools. A process model is therefore a vehicle to better understand and communicate the process. If it is expressed in a formal notation, it can be used to support a variety of activities such as process analysis, process simulation, and process enactment. PSEEs provide automatic support for these activities. They exploit languages based on different paradigms, such as Petri nets and rule-based systems. They include facilities to edit and analyze process models. By enacting the process model, a PSEE provides a variety of services, such as assistance for software developers, automation of routine tasks, invocation and control of software development tools, and enforcement of mandatory rules and practices. Several PSEEs have been developed, both as research projects and as commercial products. The initial deployment and exploitation of this technology have made it possible to produce a significant amount of experiences, comments, evaluations, and feedback. We still lack, however, consistent and comprehensive assessment methods that can be used to collect and organize this information. This article aims at contributing to the definition of such methods, by providing a systematic comparison grid and by accomplishing an initial evaluation of the state of the art in the field. This evaluation takes into account the systems that have been developed by the authors in the past five years, as well as the main characteristics of other well-known environments
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
human_qa_notes: Clean TOSEM 1997 survey/assessment of PSEE technology (OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1). QA4 scored 1 because SLANG/SPADE Petri nets (ER nets) and related PMLs are formally named; this is process modeling/enactment, not process mining (pm_technique=other). QA3/QA5/QA7/QA8 scored 0: no reproducible event log or dataset, no new empirical validation (industrial notes cite prior work; authors admit industrial experience is still limited), no artefacts, no fitness/precision-style metrics (Sutton 'fitness' here means human followability). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (1990s PSEE survey, not PM or stochastic modeling of SE processes).
human_research_question: How can process-centered software engineering environments (PSEEs) and their process-modeling languages be systematically compared, and what is the state of the art when OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1 and related systems are assessed on a shared grid covering PML technology, architecture, and industrial experience?
human_main_finding: A three-part assessment grid applied to OIKOS, EPOS, SPADE-1 and related PSEEs shows that Petri-net and rule-based PMLs can support process analysis, simulation and enactment, but industrial uptake is constrained by low process-maturity (CMM 1–2 organisations need comprehension/simulation more than enactment), lack of incremental introduction strategies, and the trade-off between advanced research platforms and commercially interoperable technology.
human_limitations: Authors state that industrial use of the three research prototypes remains limited and ISPW reference examples are insufficient for real evaluation; the grid needs refinement for early lifecycle phases, user interfaces and metaprocesses; no shared reference PSEE architecture exists, making comparative assessment inherently biased.

title: Extending hybrid CSP with probability and stochasticity
abstract: Probabilistic and stochastic behavior are omnipresent in computer controlled systems, in particular, so-called safety-critical hybrid systems, because of fundamental properties of nature, uncertain environments, or simplifications to overcome complexity. Tightly intertwining discrete, continuous and stochastic dynamics complicates modelling, analysis and verification of stochastic hybrid systems SHSs. In the literature, this issue has been extensively investigated, but unfortunately it still remains challenging as no promising general solutions are available yet. In this paper, we give our effort by proposing a general compositional approach for modelling and verification of SHSs. First, we extend Hybrid CSP HCSP, a very expressive and process algebra-like formal modeling language for hybrid systems, by introducing probability and stochasticity to model SHSs, which is called stochastic HCSP SHCSP. To this end, ordinary differential equations ODEs are generalized by stochastic differential equations SDEs and non-deterministic choice is replaced by probabilistic choice. Then, we extend Hybrid Hoare Logic HHL to specify and reason about SHCSP processes. We demonstrate our approach by an example from real-world.
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Purely theoretical formal-methods paper (extension of Hybrid CSP with stochastic differential equations and an extended Hoare Logic); only a toy illustrative aircraft example is used, with no real case study, dataset, reproducibility artifact, or threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: How can Hybrid CSP be extended with probabilistic choice and stochastic differential equations to model stochastic hybrid systems (SHCSP), and how can Hybrid Hoare Logic be extended to formally specify and verify probability-related properties of such processes?
human_main_finding: The paper defines Stochastic HCSP (SHCSP) with a well-defined operational semantics (proven measurable and adapted to a Markov-time filtration) and a compositional Hoare-Logic-based proof system for reasoning about probability of properties, illustrated on an aircraft flight-path safety example.
human_limitations: Not explicitly stated; the authors note as motivation that existing probabilistic model-checking techniques for SHSs do not scale (e.g., for SDEs with more than two variables), but do not present a limitations section evaluating their own deductive approach's scope or restrictions.

title: SSRGM: Software strong reliability growth model based on failure loss
abstract: Failures that exist in software cause tremendous damage and bring large amount of loss. Thus the research of software trustworthiness has been attracted much attention from all over the world. By considering the impact of failure loss, the traditional definition of software reliability is redefined in this paper and improved to software strong reliability. Based on this new definition and traditional J-M model, a new model called SSRGM is proposed along with its mathematical relationship and implementation based on Markov Chain. Besides, through experiment and analysis, the conclusion that this model is correct and effective is drawn.
venue: Proceedings International Symposium on Parallel Architectures Algorithms and Programming Paap
human_qa_notes: Text extraction generally clean aside from minor OCR/ligature artifacts in some formulas; no dedicated threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: How can software reliability growth modeling be improved by incorporating failure loss (severity) into the traditional J-M Markov model, creating a new 'software strong reliability' measure (SSRGM)?
human_main_finding: The authors propose SSRGM, extending the J-M Markov reliability model with failure loss speed instead of failure time; applied to the NTDS dataset, the model's predicted total failure loss (76.5) approximated the actual value (56), which the authors interpret as validating correctness and effectiveness.
human_limitations: Authors acknowledge that the experimental data used (NTDS) was originally collected for traditional reliability models, not failure-loss models, making it difficult to fully verify their model's effectiveness; collecting appropriate failure-loss data is noted as future work.

title: Towards Organizational Digital Twins: Process Enhancement by Object-Centric Simulation
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: This is a PhD doctoral-consortium research-plan abstract, not a completed empirical study; most concrete claims (conformance/similarity/cycle-time evaluation) reference a separate companion publication [3] rather than being presented in full here, and the domain (order-to-cash business processes / digital twins) is not software-engineering-specific, so QA2 and QA3 scored 0.
human_research_question: How can object-centric process mining be combined with discrete-event simulation to build executable object-centric process simulation (OCim) models that support automated process enhancement and organizational digital twins?
human_main_finding: The thesis proposes a framework (object generation, behavioral modeling, performance/resource modeling) for object-centric process simulation; a proof-of-concept discovering OCim models from event data showed empirical validity via conformance, object-similarity, and cycle-time measures, though components such as attribute-sensitive object generation, refined behavioral/resource modeling, and recommender systems remain open future work.
human_limitations: Authors acknowledge shortcomings in their proof-of-concept (simple stochastic routing based on flattened logs, object-type-flattened performance modeling, a data model that does not explicitly capture object relations) that future work will address.

title: Model-based scheduling analysis for software projects
abstract: We show how to compute optimal policies for the scheduling of software development projects under uncertainty. Our approach is based on a stochastic scheduling model that explicitly captures the strong feedback between the tasks in software development ("ripple effects"). We apply reinforcement learning to the optimization problem. For a selected sample project, we compute the optimal policy, simulate the project, and analyze the task assignments that are made by the optimal policy. From the analysis of the simulated schedules, we derive tentative, generic scheduling guidelines. The guidelines prioritize certain tasks based on the characteristics of the software architecture, and assign tasks according to the past performance of the developers.
venue: Proceedings International Computer Software and Applications Conference
human_qa_notes: Well-described stochastic (MDP/reinforcement-learning) scheduling model, but the demonstrated instance uses hypothetical/illustrative probability distributions rather than a described real dataset, and no threats-to-validity, reproducibility, or PM-style quality metrics are reported.
human_research_question: How can optimal dynamic scheduling policies be computed for software development projects under uncertainty and task-coupling feedback ("ripple effects"), modeled as a Markov decision process solved via reinforcement learning?
human_main_finding: Reinforcement learning (Sarsa) computed near-optimal dynamic scheduling policies for a stochastic software-project MDP with millions of states; simulating a sample 8-component/3-team project 500,000 times showed the optimal dynamic policy substantially outperforms the best static "list" policy (which mis-assigns tasks in over half of simulations, causing up to 20% longer completion times), and let the authors derive tentative generic scheduling heuristics (balance workload, exploit specialization, adapt dynamically).
human_limitations: Authors describe the derived scheduling guidelines as "very tentative" and note they are still running more case studies to check under which conditions the guidelines hold.

title: DATA-DRIVEN SIMULATION-BASED ANALYSIS OF COLLABORATIVE BUSINESS PROCESSES IN DISTRIBUTED ENVIRONMENTS
venue: Simulation Series
human_qa_notes: Single synthetic example (retailer-supplier procurement) generated because no real information system yet supports the paper's new XES Distributed-Simulation extension; no formal threats-to-validity section and no public dataset/code link.
human_research_question: How can Process Mining and Distributed Simulation (HLA) be jointly used, via a low-code approach, to build federated simulators for predictive analysis of business-process collaborations across independent organizations that each have only partial visibility of the overall process?
human_main_finding: The proposed distributed, low-code Predictive Process Mining approach discovers per-participant BPMN collaboration models from event logs and combines them with an HLA-based federated simulation; on a synthetic retailer-supplier case study, simulated task service/waiting times and overall process elapsed time closely matched the values derived from log analysis.
human_limitations: The authors note that the required XES Distributed-Simulation extension is not yet supported by real process-aware information systems, forcing use of synthetic logs for evaluation, and that future work is needed to unify the prototype into a single ProM plugin and extend it to real-time/digital-twin scenarios.

title: Uncertainty, risk, and information value in software requirements and architecture
abstract: Uncertainty complicates early requirements and architecture decisions and may expose a software project to significant risk. Yet software architects lack support for evaluating uncertainty, its impact on risk, and the value of reducing uncertainty before making critical decisions. We propose to apply decision analysis and multi-objective optimisation techniques to provide such support. We present a systematic method allowing software architects to describe uncertainty about the impact of alternatives on stakeholders' goals; to calculate the consequences of uncertainty through Monte-Carlo simulation; to shortlist candidate architectures based on expected costs, benefits and risks; and to assess the value of obtaining additional information before deciding. We demonstrate our method on the design of a system for coordinating emergency response teams. Our approach highlights the need for requirements engineering and software cost estimation methods to disclose uncertainty instead of hiding it.
venue: Proceedings International Conference on Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean ICSE'14 extraction; Monte-Carlo simulation is formally named (QA4=1) and applied to the published SAS/GuideArch architecture case. QA8 scored 0: reported quantities are expected net benefit, loss probability, project-failure risk and EVTPI/EVPPI, not process-model quality or predictive accuracy metrics. QA6 scored 1 via the Evaluation section (model falsifiability, elicitation bias, scalability, applicability) even without a 'Threats to Validity' heading. Tool/models claimed at cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/e.letier/sdda (QA7=1).
human_research_question: How can statistical decision analysis — eliciting parameter uncertainty as probability distributions, propagating it with Monte-Carlo simulation, shortlisting architectures on expected net benefit versus risk, and computing expected value of information — support early software requirements and architecture decisions?
human_main_finding: Reanalysing the SAS emergency-response architecture model (6,912 candidates, 175 uncertain parameters), Monte-Carlo simulation plus a resolution-margin Pareto strip shortlists nine architectures with higher expected net benefit and much lower project-failure risk than GuideArch's top ten; EVTPI is only 0.25% of best ENB, so further reducing parameter uncertainty has little decision value given the current (non-falsifiable) utility model.
human_limitations: Authors themselves stress that the SAS utility/contribution model is not falsifiable, so rankings and information-value estimates cannot be empirically validated; the method does not yet treat model (structural) uncertainty; expert probability-elicitation methods have not been evaluated in software engineering; political/governance barriers to honest uncertainty reporting remain untested.

title: An exploratory study of process enactment as input to software process improvement
abstract: Software process improvement has been a focus of industry for many years. To assist the procedure and implementation of software process improvement we provide a software process recovery method based on mining project enactment data. The goal of process recovery is to improve the quality of a planned software process. We investigate the enactment of a planned software process from the view of understanding the appropriateness and fitness for purpose of the process model from the viewpoint of the project managers in the context of a small software development organization. We collected empirical data from this organization and then applied our method to a pilot case study. The main contribution of our work is to provide a methodology of software process model recovery which supports software process improvement.
venue: Proceedings International Conference on Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean OCR/text extraction; a genuine pilot case study with real industrial project data, an explicit alpha-algorithm-based mining method, and an explicit limitations subsection, but no fitness/precision-style quality metrics and no shared dataset or code.
human_research_question: Can process mining of low-level project task enactment data reveal gaps between a predefined software process model (an ISO 12207-based Electronic Process Guide) and how a project team actually executed the process, in a way that is directly comparable to (and useful for improving) the predefined model?
human_main_finding: Mining task-level enactment data from a pilot database-development project (using an alpha-algorithm-inspired causal-relation method plus expert task classification verified via Kappa=0.808) recovered a higher-level process pattern directly comparable to the predefined EPG model and revealed concrete deviations (skipped process elements, different process start/end points), demonstrating the approach's usefulness as input to software process improvement.
human_limitations: The method cannot classify or use tasks that do not map cleanly to a single predefined process element ('noise' tasks are excluded), and the approach lacks clear guidance on when/how to split larger projects into modules for analysis.

title: Change your history: Learning from event logs to improve processes
abstract: The abundance of event data enables new forms of analysis that facilitate process improvement. Process mining provides a novel set of tools to discover the real process, to detect deviations from some normative process, and to analyze bottlenecks and waste. The lion's share of process mining focuses on the “as-is” situation rather than the “to-be” situation. Clearly, analysis should aim at actionable insights and concrete suggestions for improvement However, state-of-the-art techniques do not allow for this. Techniques like simulation can be used to do “what-if” analysis but are not driven by event data, and as a result, improvements can be very unrealistic. Techniques for predictive analytics and combinatorial optimization are data-driven but mostly focus on well-structured decision problems. Operational processes within complex organizations cannot be mapped onto a simulation model or simple decision problem. This paper provides a novel approach based on event logs as used by process mining techniques. Instead of trying to create or modify process models, this approach works directly on the event log itself. It aims to “improve history” rather than speculate about a highly uncertain future. By showing concrete improvements in terms of partly modified event logs, the stakeholders can learn from earlier mistakes and inefficiencies. This is similar to analyzing a soccer match to improve a team's performance in the next game. This paper introduces the idea using event logs in conjunction with flexible “compatibility” and “utility” notions. An initial prototype -serving as a proof-of-concept- was realized as a ProM plug-in and tested on real-life event logs.
venue: Proceedings of the 2015 IEEE 19th International Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work in Design Cscwd 2015

title: ARCH-COMP25 Category Report: Stochastic Models
abstract: This report is concerned with a friendly competition for formal verification and policy synthesis of stochastic models. The main goal of the report is to introduce new benchmarks and their properties within this category and recommend next steps toward next year’s edition of the competition. In particular, this report introduces three recently developed software tools, a new water distribution network benchmark, and a collection of simplified benchmarks intended to facilitate further comparisons among tools that were previously not directly comparable. This friendly competition took place as part of the workshop Applied Verification for Continuous and Hybrid Systems (ARCH) in Summer 2025.
venue: Epic Series in Computing
human_qa_notes: This paper is NOT about software engineering -- it is a formal-verification/control-theory tool-benchmarking competition report for stochastic hybrid/cyber-physical systems (water distribution networks, autonomous vehicles, anesthesia, building automation); QA2 (SE context) is scored 0 because there is no software-engineering process content at all. Likely a false-positive inclusion in the SE-focused SLR corpus (matched on the 'stochastic models' keyword).
human_research_question: How do state-of-the-art tools for formal verification and control synthesis of stochastic (hybrid) systems compare on established and newly introduced benchmarks in the 2025 ARCH-COMP friendly competition?
human_main_finding: The report compares six stochastic-system verification/control-synthesis tools (three new: IMPaCT, IntervalMDP.jl, PRoTECT; three established: SySCoRe, hpnmg, AMYTISS) on established and newly introduced benchmarks (including a new water distribution network benchmark), showing e.g. that the IPS-FAS algorithm greatly outperforms plain Monte Carlo simulation for rare-event collision-probability estimation, and that hpnmg's new guided-simulation engine is faster than classical discrete-event simulation on the same hybrid Petri net model.
human_limitations: The authors identify ongoing open challenges for the field, including high-dimensional scalability, rare-event estimation, and handling expressive specifications, which remain unresolved for the compared tools.

title: A hybrid process-mining approach for simulation modeling
abstract: This paper presents a hybrid Modeling and Simulation framework to address business process challenges. The framework has integrated process mining techniques in the conceptual modeling phase to support developing simulation models that are unbiased and close reflection of reality in a timely manner. The hybrid approach overcomes the pitfalls of traditional conceptual modeling by using process mining techniques to discover valuable process knowledge from the analysis of event logs. The proposed hybrid framework has been applied to an Emergency Department (ED) in order to identify performance bottlenecks and explore improvement strategies in an attempt to meet national performance targets. A large number of unique process flows (i.e. patient pathways) within the ED were uncovered and deviations from process guidelines were accurately identified. Results show that unblocking of ED outflows have a significant impact on patients length of stay (over 80% improvement) rather than increasing the ED physical capacity.
venue: Proceedings Winter Simulation Conference
human_qa_notes: Text has garbled/mojibake character encoding throughout (font-encoding extraction artifact, not a scanned-OCR issue) but content remained fully readable; the real case study is a hospital Emergency Department, not a software engineering process, so QA2 scored low despite an SE-oriented example illustration early in the paper.
human_research_question: Can process mining techniques (applied to event logs) be integrated into the conceptual modeling phase of Modeling & Simulation studies to produce faster, less biased, more realistic simulation models than traditional interview/observation-based conceptual modeling?
human_main_finding: Applying fuzzy-miner-based process mining to real Emergency Department event-log data (20,521 events, ~20,000 patients) uncovered ~90 unique patient pathways and guideline deviations; a discrete-event simulation built from the mined process closely matched real KPIs, and simulation experiments showed that resolving inpatient-bed allocation bottlenecks reduced patient length-of-stay far more (~40% at some stages) than increasing physical ED capacity.
human_limitations: The authors note that a cost/financial analysis of the recommendations could not be performed due to lack of cost data, and that process knowledge mined from event logs can lead to wrong conclusions due to recording errors/inaccuracies, requiring cross-validation against traditional sources before use.

title: CoSMo: A Framework to Instantiate Conditioned Process Simulation Models
abstract: Process simulation is gaining attention for its ability to assess potential performance improvements and risks associated with business process changes. The existing literature presents various techniques, generally grounded in process models discovered from event log data or built upon deep learning algorithms. These techniques have specific strengths and limitations. Traditional data-driven approaches offer increased interpretability, while deep learning-based excel at generalizing changes across large event logs. However, the practical application of deep learning faces challenges related to managing stochasticity and integrating information for what-if analysis. This paper introduces a novel recurrent neural architecture tailored to discover COnditioned process Simulation MOdels (CoSMo) based on user-based constraints or any other nature of a-priori knowledge. This architecture facilitates the simulation of event logs that adhere to specific constraints by incorporating declarative-based rules into the learning phase as an attempt to fill the gap of incorporating information into deep learning models to perform what-if analysis. Experimental validation illustrates CoSMo's efficacy in simulating event logs while adhering to predefined declarative conditions, emphasizing both control-flow and data-flow perspectives.
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Rigorous ML/process-mining experimental paper with public code (GitHub: raseidi/cosmo) and public BPI benchmark datasets; limitations are discussed in a dedicated subsection (5.3) though not formally titled 'Threats to Validity'; QA2=0 because the evaluated event logs (BPI12/13/17/20, SEPSIS) are general business/healthcare processes rather than software-engineering-specific processes.
human_research_question: How can deep-learning-based process simulation models be conditioned on user-defined declarative (DECLARE/LTLf) constraints to overcome the inherent stochasticity and lack of controllability of existing DL-based simulation approaches, enabling what-if analysis?
human_main_finding: CoSMo, a novel conditioned recurrent neural architecture incorporating DECLARE/LTLf constraints into deep-learning process simulation, achieves high weighted precision (median 99% when replaying original rules, 81% under inverted/what-if constraints) across five real-world BPI event logs, substantially outperforming an unconstrained 'vanilla' stochastic baseline (~58% precision) in controlling simulated process behavior.
human_limitations: Authors note correlated DECLARE rules (e.g., existence/absence) may introduce redundant information, rule/activity selection was performed arbitrarily without domain-expert input, and the study only explored declarative/LTLf constraints rather than other constraint types (e.g., resource- or time-based), limiting real-world applicability so far.

title: Modeling the failure pathology of software components
abstract: Reliability prediction methods support early decision on software development by offering means for architects to reason and test their own designs. However, most of today's reliability prediction methods model the failure behavior as two states: functioning properly or failed, neglecting other failure modes. In addition, the lack of realistic case-studies and actual failure data make testing and validation difficult tasks. With this in mind, we propose a reliability modeling approach describing the behavior of a software component taking into account error occurrences and their associated impacts in terms of error masking, error propagation, error recovery and failures modes. To validate our approach we present a real case-study based on Xen where we injected faults at different virtualization layers. The experiments show close results between our modeling approach and the realistic values obtained from the experiment.
venue: Proceedings 2016 12th International ACM SIGSOFT Conference on Quality of Software Architectures Qosa 2016
human_qa_notes: Full QoSA 2016 text is clean and complete; QA6 scored 0 because there is no threats-to-validity discussion (fault-injection representativeness, workload, sequential-composition assumption are not treated as validity threats); QA8 scored 0 because validation uses reliability/%-diff tables, not fitness/precision/F1/MAPE/RMSE-style process-model quality metrics; raw data URL is given (QA7=1).
human_research_question: Can a discrete-time Markov chain that explicitly models error masking, propagation, recovery, and Avizienis multiple failure modes predict software-component reliability more accurately than classical two-state models, as validated by fault injection on Xen?
human_main_finding: An eight-state DTMC (OK/Error/Fail plus content/timing/hang/erratic and Halt) parameterized from Xen fault-injection runs (HVM n=1028, PV n=968, Dom0 Qemu/Watchdog) matches measured reliability within about 0–3.9% (mean absolute difference 0.69%), substantially closer than a classical no-recovery model (e.g. 85.22% vs real 97.86% on HVM); PV is more reliable than HVM, and Dom0 faults propagate to guest VMs while guest-to-guest isolation holds.
human_limitations: Only sequential component interaction is modeled (parallel/concurrent styles left as future work); faults are synthetic transient register bit-flips, not field failures; no dedicated threats-to-validity analysis; automated generation of the DTMC from an architecture is only planned.

title: Special panel: Software process simulation--at a crossroads?
abstract: Software Process Simulation (SPS) has been evolving in the last decades and gained researchers' and practitioners' interests in software process community. However, the growth of SPS seems slow down in recent years, and the evidence for its benefits to industrial practice is not commonly reported as expected. SPS still awaits a breakthrough success. This special panel aims to initiate a discussion on the challenges faced SPS and the solutions to tackling the problems, and to work out a research agenda for future advance of SPS.
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Software and System Process
human_qa_notes: This is a special-panel position/discussion paper about the state of Software Process Simulation research, not an empirical study; virtually all empirical-rigor QA criteria are inapplicable, so a uniformly low QA score is expected and appropriate.
human_research_question: What are the challenges facing Software Process Simulation (SPS) research and practice given its apparent stagnation, and what research agenda and collaborations could help SPS achieve broader industrial adoption and impact?
human_main_finding: This panel paper reports no empirical findings; it frames a discussion on SPS's slowing growth and sets goals to identify challenges, propose solutions, and develop a future SPS research agenda involving both academia and industry panelists.
human_limitations: Not applicable; this is a panel position paper rather than an empirical study, so no limitations of an empirical method are discussed.
