title: Software reliability
abstract: Abstract In this article, we present an overview of the state of the art in software reliability. We present some of the traditional software reliability models as well as recent advances in modeling. In so doing, we discuss use of hidden Markov models, as well as nonparametric models including mixtures of Dirichlet processes. Furthermore, we review decision problems in software reliability such as testing strategies and optimal stopping rules. We discuss computational issues associated with use of the models, their statistical analyses and development of optimal strategies. WIREs Comp Stat 2011 3 269–281 DOI: 10.1002/wics.159 This article is categorized under: Statistical and Graphical Methods of Data Analysis > Bayesian Methods and Theory Statistical and Graphical Methods of Data Analysis > Reliability, Survivability, and Quality Control Software for Computational Statistics > Software/Statistical Software Data: Types and Structure > Time Series, Stochastic Processes, and Functional Data
venue: Wiley Interdisciplinary Reviews Computational Statistics
human_qa_notes: Dense statistical/mathematical survey (technical report), not a typical empirical SE study; clean text extraction with math notation reasonably preserved; largely a literature review with one illustrative Bayesian analysis on public data.
human_research_question: The paper reviews the state of the art in software reliability modeling (parametric and nonparametric, including hidden Markov models and Dirichlet process mixtures) and decision-theoretic approaches to optimal software release/stopping time.
human_main_finding: The paper is primarily a literature survey; it illustrates a semiparametric Bayesian Dirichlet-process mixture model for time-between-failures using Musa's System 40 dataset, showing decreasing failure rates (reliability growth) over testing stages and about 9-10 distinct failure-rate groups.
human_limitations: not stated

title: Software reliability test case generation using temporal motifs recovery and configuration
abstract: In software updating process, software reliability test plays an important role. Test cases are the key to software test. To match real usage habit, log analysis becomes a hot way to generate reliability test cases. However, using log analysis can't cover new operations arising from software updating. In this paper, a reliability test cases generation method for updating software using temporal motifs recovery and configuration is presented in this paper. We tentatively introduce temporal network idea to abstract software usage log. Test cases adapting to software updating are generated using temporal motifs recovery and configuration. As a case study, the method is applied to an online application. The coverage frequency comparison experiment is designed. The proposed method can obtain similar results as log and Markov model. Thereby, the usability of the method is validated.
venue: International Journal of Performability Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text, encoded operation IDs in tables slightly cluttered but assessment straightforward; validation uses frequency-coverage comparison against log/Markov baselines rather than a formal fitness/precision/error metric, so QA8 scored 0; dataset is stated as freely available for research purposes (QA7=1).
human_research_question: Can a temporal-motifs recovery and configuration method generate software reliability test cases for updated software that adequately cover operations newly introduced by updates, compared with log-based Markov usage models that cannot cover such new operations?
human_main_finding: The proposed temporal-motifs recovery and configuration method generates reliability test cases whose operation-coverage frequencies are similar to those from a Markov usage model, while additionally covering operations newly introduced by software updates, which pure log-based Markov models cannot cover.
human_limitations: Authors note volatility from large changes in user behavior and cases where an operation absent from the immediately preceding version's log causes inaccurate coverage; they plan execution-based verification and use of more historical logs in future work.

title: Microflows: Enabling agile business process modeling to orchestrate semantically-annotated microservices
abstract: : Businesses and software development processes alike are being challenged by the digital transformation trend. Business processes are increasingly being automated yet are expected to be agile. Current business process modeling is typically labor-intensive and results in rigid process models, with larger process models unable to cope with all possible process variations and enactment circumstances. In software development, microservices have become a popular software architectural style for partitioning business logic into fine-grained services that can be rapidly and individually developed and (re)deployed while accessed via lightweight protocols, resulting in many more services and a much more dynamic service landscape. Thus, a more dynamic form of modeling, integration, and orchestration of microservices with business processes is needed. This paper describes agile business process modeling with Microflows, an automatic lightweight declarative approach for the workflow-centric orchestration of semantically-annotated microservices using agent-based clients, graph-based methods, and the lightweight semantic vocabularies JSON-LD and Hydra. A case study shows how Microflow constraints can be automatically extracted from existing Business Process Modeling Notation (BPMN) files, how Microflow execution log file process mining can be used to extract BPMN models, and demonstrates an automated error recovery capability during enactment.
venue: Bmsd 2017 Proceedings of the 7th International Symposium on Business Modeling and Software Design
human_qa_notes: Describes a microservice-orchestration architecture with generic process-mining-based log-to-BPMN extraction, but evaluation uses only a self-created illustrative example (not real data); authors explicitly list 'empirical and industrial usage' as future work, so no real empirical validation, no named PM algorithm, and no reproducibility/metrics.
human_research_question: How can agile, declarative orchestration of semantically-annotated microservices (Microflows) be integrated with BPMN-based business process modeling, including automatically extracting Microflow constraints from BPMN and mining BPMN models back from Microflow execution logs?
human_main_finding: Using a self-created travel-booking illustrative example, the authors show that Microflow constraint files can be automatically extracted from BPMN files (and are much smaller than the equivalent BPMN XML), that execution-log process mining can regenerate a BPMN model, and that automated error recovery (client state rollback plus cost-penalized replanning) works during microservice orchestration.
human_limitations: The evaluation is based on a self-created illustrative example rather than real industrial usage, which is explicitly listed as future work; several BPMN 2.0 constructs (multiple start/end events, swimlanes, artifacts, event subprocesses) are not yet supported by the prototype.

title: Guiding the discovery of open source software processes with a reference model
abstract: This paper describes a reference model for open source software (OSS) processes and its application towards discovering such processes from OSS project artifacts. This reference model is the means to map evidence of an enacted process to a classification of agents, resources, tools, and activities that characterize the process.
venue: IFIP International Federation for Information Processing
human_qa_notes: Short, clean OSS 2007 paper; QA3 scored 0 because the seven case studies name Apache/Mozilla/NetBeans public portals but give no artifact inventory, time window (beyond 'circa 2002' for the seed surveys), or coding protocol that would allow reproduction; qualitative application experiences support QA5=1, but there is no threats section, shared data/code, or model-quality metric.
human_research_question: Does a reference-model mapping from OSS project-artifact terms to a taxonomy of agents, resources, tools, and actions provide a systematic way to code evidence and discover OSS processes across projects and process types?
human_main_finding: A Mi–Scacchi-based reference-model dictionary guided discovery in seven case studies (NetBeans, Apache HTTPD, Mozilla): it was adequate for development/release/testing processes, too coarse for interorganizational process communication (missing proper names of shared libraries/tools and cross-project vocabularies), and useful for detecting role-migration tracks from shifts in an individual's action-taxonomy branches.
human_limitations: The reference model cannot eliminate discovery risk from cross-project lexical variance; usage-pattern data were especially limited; much interorganizational evidence lies outside public portals; full automated coding is judged not yet attainable; the model addresses only the data-analysis stage of process discovery.

title: GitProjectHealth: An Extensible Framework for Git Social Platform Mining
abstract: Git social platforms (such as Gitlab, Github, or Bitbucket) provide insight into a team’s workflow. Mining Software Repositories (MSR) provides methods and tools to extract data from these platforms. However, most tools lack connectivity and extensibility across multiple platforms. Moreover, they rarely connect to other project management platforms such as Jira. In this paper, we introduce GitProjectHealth (GPH), a framework to extract data from any Git repositories and social platforms. GPH is implemented inside a model-driven engineering framework in Pharo smalltalk, facilitating its extension to other social platforms. We demonstrate GPH features over 3 open-source organizations: Eclipse, MooseTechnology and Microsoft; as well as Berger-Levrault, a closed-source company. We extracted their activity to build distributions of commits by user and to determine which types of ticket were associated with each merge request.
venue: Proceedings 2025 IEEE ACM 22nd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories MSR 2025
human_qa_notes: Mining-software-repositories (MSR) tool paper (GitProjectHealth), not a process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique paper in the QA4/QA8 sense; reproducible via open-source Zenodo release, documented scripts, and public GitHub org data.
human_research_question: How can a unified, extensible model-driven framework be built to mine and connect data from multiple Git social platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket) and project-management platforms (Jira) to gain insight into software development team workflows and project health?
human_main_finding: GitProjectHealth (GPH), an MDE-based extensible tool built in Pharo/Moose, successfully extracts and connects data from multiple Git social platforms and Jira across both open-source (Eclipse, Microsoft, MooseTechnology) and industrial (Berger-Levrault) projects, enabling analyses such as commit distribution by user and classification of merge requests by associated ticket type (27% of merge requests were linked to bug-fixing 'Anomaly' tickets).
human_limitations: not stated

title: An integrated infrastructure using process mining techniques for software process verification
abstract: The verification of process implementations according to specifications is a critical step of process management. This verification must be practiced according to objective criteria and evidence. This study explains an integrated infrastructure that utilizes process mining for software process verification and case studies carried out by using this infrastructure. Specific software providing the utilization of process mining algorithms for software process verification is developed as a plugin to an open-source EPF Composer tool that supports the management of software and system engineering processes. With three case studies, bug management, task management, and defect management processes are verified against defined and established process models (modeled by using EPF Composer) by using this plugin over real process data. Among these, the results of the case study performed in a large, leading IT solutions company in Turkey are remarkable in demonstrating the opportunities for process improvement.
venue: Computer Systems and Software Engineering Concepts Methodologies Tools and Applications
human_qa_notes: Only the abstract and introduction (~2 pages) were retrievable; the source is a paywalled book-chapter preview whose remaining ~16 pages (case-study details, results, validity discussion, metrics) are not in the extracted text, so most criteria could not be positively assessed and are scored 0 for lack of evidence rather than confirmed absence.
human_research_question: Can an integrated infrastructure (a process-mining plugin for the open-source EPF Composer tool, combining process variants mining, conformance analysis, and statistical analysis) verify real software process implementations against their defined/established process models?
human_main_finding: Not determinable from the available excerpt — the abstract states that three case studies (bug management, task management, defect management) were verified using the plugin over real process data, and that the case study at a large IT company in Turkey was notable for revealing process-improvement opportunities, but the supporting results/analysis are in the paywalled remainder of the chapter not present in this extraction.
human_limitations: not stated (not present in the available excerpt)

title: Predicting data access patterns in object-oriented applications based on Markov chains
abstract: This work aims to create an innovative system for analyzing and predicting the behaviour of object-oriented applications, with respect to the domain objects they manipulate, based on Markov Chains. The results are validated by the execution of the TPC-W and oo7 benchmarks. The oo7 benchmark has been modelled as a stochastic process through Monte Carlo simulations. The system is sufficiently flexible to be applied to a broad spectrum of object-oriented applications. The results are precise, regarding the observed behaviour, and the overheads introduced by the data acquisition are low.
venue: Proceedings 5th International Conference on Software Engineering Advances Icsea 2010
human_qa_notes: Solid experimental validation using two well-known synthetic benchmarks (TPC-W, oo7) with statistical testing (Z-test) and runtime-overhead measurement; no explicit threats-to-validity section and the instrumentation tool/code is not stated to be publicly released.
human_research_question: Can Markov-chain models built from observed runtime data-access sequences in object-oriented applications accurately predict future data-access patterns, to support automated data prefetching/optimization?
human_main_finding: A Markov-chain-based system that instruments Java applications via bytecode rewriting to learn field-level data-access patterns achieves highly accurate predictions (Z-values near zero, within 95% confidence) on the TPC-W and oo7 benchmarks, with only about 9% runtime overhead and negligible extra memory cost.
human_limitations: Authors note the chosen type-based (vs. instance-based) analysis approach trades some specificity for scalability, and that it can be difficult to identify which specific object instances to target for optimization once predictions are available; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

title: Modelling and analysis of distributed software using GSPNs
abstract: This chapter discusses the role that Generalized Stochastic Petri Nets (GSPN) can play in the static analysis of distributed software. The material is organized along two main lines: the need and the advantages of studying both qualitative and quantitative aspects of a program, and the need for doing it in an automatic manner. The role of performance evaluation in the analysis of distributed software is illustrated through a small example, classical in the qualitative approach (the dining philosophers). Although small this example allows to point out the need and the requirements of automatic translation and to discuss the main hypothesis behind program performance evaluation through GSPN models. A procedure for the automatic generation of GSPN models starting from a distributed program written in a CSP-like language, and for the definition of program performance indices in terms of GSPN ones is then given and illustrated by means of a realistic example
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Text has some OCR noise/garbled symbols (mathematical notation, Greek letters) typical of a scanned book chapter, but core content and examples were legible; validation relies only on small illustrative/toy programs (dining philosophers, a distributed simulator), not a real-world empirical case study.
human_research_question: How can Generalized Stochastic Petri Nets (GSPN), automatically generated from CSP-like distributed program code, support combined qualitative (deadlock) and quantitative (performance) static analysis of distributed software?
human_main_finding: The chapter presents an automatic translation procedure from CSP-like distributed program code into GSPN models, demonstrated on the dining-philosophers problem and a distributed time-warp simulator, enabling combined deadlock detection and performance-index computation (throughput, communication graphs, resource interference) without manual model construction.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly discuss key modeling assumptions/limitations: activity delays are assumed exponentially distributed, physical resource contention (hardware/CPU) is not modeled, and explicit representation of program variables can cause state-space explosion or even model unboundedness.

title: Decomposed replay using hiding and reduction
abstract: In the area of process mining, decomposed replay has been proposed to be able to deal with nets and logs containing many different activities. The main assumption behind this decomposition is that replaying many subnets and sublogs containing only some activities is faster then replaying a single net and log containing many activities. Although for many nets and logs this assumption does hold, there are also nets and logs for which it does not hold. This paper shows an example net and log for which the decomposed replay may take way more time, and provides an explanation why this is the case. Next, to mitigate this problem, this paper proposes an alternative decomposed replay, and shows that this alternative decomposed replay is faster than the monolithic replay even for the problematic cases as identified earlier.owever, the alternative decomposed replay is often slower than the original decomposed approach. An advantage of the alternative decomposed approach over the original approach is that its cost estimates are typically better.
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Theoretical/algorithmic conformance-checking paper (PNSE'16) with formal proofs plus computational benchmarking on public BPI Challenge and other public event-log datasets; QA2=0 since it is a generic process-mining algorithms paper without a specific software-engineering process context; no code repository or threats-to-validity section provided.
human_research_question: How does decomposed replay for process-mining conformance checking behave computationally compared to monolithic replay, and can an alternative 'hide-and-reduce' decomposition avoid cases where decomposed replay is slower than monolithic replay while still providing better lower-bound cost estimates?
human_main_finding: Decomposed replay can, in some cases (especially with discovered nets containing subnets with several source transitions), take far longer than monolithic replay; the proposed 'hide-and-reduce' alternative decomposition avoids this misbehavior (finishing within 10 minutes for nearly all tested cases) and typically produces tighter (better) lower-bound cost estimates than the original decomposed replay, though it can be slower due to the added reduction step.
human_limitations: The reduction step itself can become a computational bottleneck (up to ~60 seconds in some cases even when the underlying replay takes only 2 seconds), and the proposed method is sometimes slower than the original decomposed replay; no formal threats-to-validity discussion is provided.

title: Effects of architecture and technical development process on micro-process
abstract: Abstract. Current software development methodologies (such as agile and RUP) are largely management-centred, macro-process life-cycle models. While they may include some fine-grained micro-process development practices, they usually provide little concrete guidance on appropriate micro-process level dayto-day development activities. The major factors that affect such micro-process activities are not well understood. We propose that software architecture and technical development processes are two major factors. We describe how these two factors affect micro-process activities. We validate our claim by mining micro-processes from two commercial projects and investigating relationships with software architecture and technical development processes
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Solid two-project case study with an explicit limitations discussion, but no formally named process-mining discovery algorithm, no shared/reproducible dataset, and no process-model quality metrics reported.
human_research_question: Do software architecture (module dependency) and technical development process factors significantly influence fine-grained micro-process activities, their cost, and recurring patterns, beyond what macro-process methodologies capture?
human_main_finding: Mining micro-processes from time sheets in two commercial projects, combined with architecture reconstruction (JDepend, SA4J) and structured interviews, confirmed that both architectural module dependency and technology-specific development processes strongly influence which micro-process activities occur, their cost, and recurring patterns.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly note that (1) only two of many possible influencing factors (Figure 1) were studied and other factors may play a more dominant role, and (2) the study only observed after-the-fact effects rather than actively using these factors in process planning.

title: Calculating the usage probabilities of statistical usage models by constraints optimization
abstract: The systematic generation of test cases from statistical usage models has been investigated recently for specific application domains, such as wireless communications or automotive applications. For Markov chain usage models, the expected usage of a hardware/software system is represented by transitions between usage states and a usage profile, meaning probability values that are attached to the state transitions.In this paper, we explain how to calculate the profile probabilities for the Markov chain usage model from a set of linear usage constraints and by optimizing a convex polyhedron that represents the constrained solution space. Comparing the computed probability distributions of our polyhedron approach with the maximum entropy technique, which is the main technique used so far, illustrates that our results are more obvious to the intented constraint semantics. In order to demonstrate the applicability of our approach, workflow testing of a complex RIS/PACS system in the medical domain was carried through and has provided promising results.
venue: Proceedings International Conference on Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction, mathematical notation well preserved; no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, and reproducibility limited by dependence on the proprietary Siemens TDE tool.
human_research_question: How can usage probabilities for Markov chain usage models (MCUM) be derived from linear usage constraints via constrained optimization (polyhedron approach), as an alternative to the maximum entropy method, for generating statistically representative test cases?
human_main_finding: The proposed polyhedron optimization approach for deriving MCUM transition probabilities from usage constraints produces distributions that better reflect intended constraint semantics than the maximum entropy approach; applied to a real RIS/PACS medical workflow testing case study, it yielded promising results and enabled meaningful usage-profile comparison via KL/JSD divergence.
human_limitations: not stated explicitly as a limitations section; the paper notes that KL divergence is undefined when some model arcs are never covered by test cases, requiring an approximation.

title: Mining balanced API protocols
abstract: API protocols can be used in many aspects of software engineering, such as software testing, program validation, software documentation, etc. Mining API protocols based on probabilistic models is proved to be an effective approach to achieve protocols automatically. However, it always achieves unbalanced protocols, that is, protocols described using probabilistic models have unexpected extremely high and low probabilities. In this paper, we discuss the unbalanced probability problem and propose to address it by preprocessing method call sequences used for training. Our method first finds tandem arrays in method call sequences based on the suffix tree. Then, it substitutes each tandem array with a tandem repeat. Since repeated sub method call sequences are eliminated, balanced API protocols may be achieved. In order to investigate the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach, we implemented it in our previous prototype tool ISpecMiner and used the tool to perform a comparison test based on several real-world applications. Experimental results show that our approach can achieve more balanced API protocols than existing approaches, which is essential for mining valid and precise API protocols.
venue: International Journal of Computational Science and Engineering

title: Warnings: Violation symptoms indicating architecture erosion
abstract: As a software system evolves, its architecture tends to degrade, and gradually impedes software maintenance and evolution activities and negatively impacts the quality attributes of the system. The main root cause behind architecture erosion phenomenon derives from violation symptoms (i.e., various architecturally-relevant violations, such as violations of architecture pattern). Previous studies focus on detecting violations in software systems using architecture conformance checking approaches. However, code review comments are also rich sources that may contain extensive discussions regarding architecture violations, while there is a limited understanding of violation symptoms from the viewpoint of developers
venue: Information and Software Technology
human_qa_notes: Text read in full including references; this paper does not employ any process-mining algorithm or stochastic model (it is a keyword-search plus manual qualitative-coding study of code review comments), so QA4 and QA8 scored 0 — likely a borderline/tangential inclusion for a process-mining + stochastic-modeling SLR; has a formal Threats-to-Validity section and a public replication package.
human_research_question: What are the characteristics (categories, linguistic patterns) of architecture violation symptoms discussed in code review comments, and how do developers address them?
human_main_finding: Analysis of 606 code review comments from four OSS projects (Nova, Neutron, Qt Base, Qt Creator) identified three categories/ten subcategories of architecture violation symptoms (mostly design-related, especially structural inconsistencies), expressed mainly via 'inconsistent'/'violate' terms and Problem-Discovery linguistic patterns, with about 90% of symptoms addressed through refactoring or code removal regardless of patch merge status.
human_limitations: Authors note limited generalizability since only four OSS projects (Python/C++, OpenStack/Qt) were studied, and a construct-validity threat around the completeness of the keyword set used to identify violation-related comments.

title: Reliability of task execution during safe software processing
abstract: This paper presents the reliability evaluation of task execution during safe software processing. The standard method of duplication in a safety-critical application can also be applied for tasks in a software system. But in addition to this, there is also the possibility for coded task processing to increase the reliability and availability of software. The presented analysis covers the reliability analysis of a single, a duplicated and a coded task by the technique of continuous time Markov processes. Markov processes are often used for the reliability evaluation of safety-critical systems. We introduce a method to describe the execution time of tasks by means of enhanced Markov models and their solution by numerical methods.
venue: Proceedings 15th Euromicro Conference on Digital System Design Dsd 2012
human_qa_notes: Purely analytical/theoretical reliability analysis (continuous-time Markov/Erlang model) using a literature-derived constant failure rate rather than a real dataset; no empirical case study, no threats-to-validity section, no shared data/code, and no PM-style quality metrics.
human_research_question: How can an n-staged (Erlang-enhanced) continuous-time Markov model be used to numerically evaluate and compare the reliability (undetected-failure probability, MTBF) of single, duplicated, and coded (diverse-redundant) task execution in safety-critical software, when the standard analytical Markov solution fails due to floating-point resolution limits?
human_main_finding: An n-staged continuous-time Markov model numerically overcomes the floating-point resolution problem of the standard analytical Markov solution for short task execution times; comparison of a single task, a duplicated (time/space-redundant) task, and a coded (information-redundant) task shows that coded/diverse task processing achieves better MTBF and lower undetected-failure probability than simple duplication.
human_limitations: Authors state the comparison does not account for the increased runtime overhead of coded operations (which would raise the fault probability), and further investigation is needed on the number and placement of synchronization points during task processing.

title: Kanban and Process Mining in the Task Management
authors: Mendes, Vitor; Faria Junior, Elio Ribeiro; Garcia, Cleiton; Malucelli, Andreia
abstract: In a world continuously changing with markets that are in permanent evolution and in contend, the companys must inovate, be more flexible, offer quality and respond swiftly. These factors do not apply for product manufacture processes only, but for software development processes aswell. This paper describes an account of experiences with the use of Kanban to improve the activities management in an ERP's development. To do this, a mapping of the current process was carried out, so to propose a set of improvements in the management of activities. As a result, a set of tools were implemented to enable a clear view and control over the activities, as well as to integrate the Issue Tracking System with the Kanban board. Furthermore, a process mining technique was used to estimate the time of conclusion of the activities and to detect performance problem.
venue: Proceedings of the XVII Brazilian Symposium on Software Quality (SBQS '18)
human_qa_notes: Brazilian Portuguese SBQS 2018 experience report; real industrial case study (AGEMED ERP maintenance) with explicit self-stated limitations, but proprietary data/commercial tools (no public dataset/code) and only descriptive-statistics-level metrics (no fitness/precision-type quality metrics).
human_research_question: How can Kanban combined with process mining (via the UPFLUX tool and fuzzy miner) improve the management, visibility, and lead-time control of software/ERP adaptation activities in an IT support/maintenance team?
human_main_finding: Integrating Kanban (via KanbanTool) with process mining (UPFLUX/fuzzy miner) on real ERP-maintenance ticket data improved visibility, lead-time control, and identification of bottlenecks/rework (e.g., the 'Em analise com Atendente' activity consumed the most rework), and a before/after comparative evaluation by three stakeholders scored the new approach substantially higher (120 vs 68 points) than the previous manual process.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly state that no quantitative data was collected after the improvements were implemented and that use of process mining was only initial/exploratory, with many possibilities left unexplored.

title: Understanding knowlegde-intensive processes: From traces to instance graphs
abstract: Enterprise information systems, while support daily activities, typically collect data on executed processes in event logs. These data describe the temporal sequence in which activities were carried out, hiding possible parallelism and other control flows. Representing the structure of each process execution in the form of an Instance Graph, enables managers to discover valuable knowledge on enterprise behaviors. In this work, we describe BIG4ProM, a tool which implements the Building Instance Graph (BIG) algorithm. BIG4ProM exploits filtering Process Discovery algorithms implemented in ProM in order to return the set of instance graphs related to the given event log. The plug-in is conceived to support both expert and standard users.
venue: 2016 International Conference on High Performance Computing and Simulation Hpcs 2016
human_qa_notes: Used ft_0016_decoded.txt (+29 ASCII shift). Prose is readable; punctuation/quotes remain noisy and some math tokens are garbled. QA2=0: motivating domain is knowledge-intensive / unstructured processes (healthcare guidelines, ERP/CRM/BPMS), not a software-engineering process. QA5=0: this paper only describes the BIG4ProM plug-in and a toy deletion-trace IG; empirical evaluation is deferred to prior ESWA 2016 [11]. QA7=0: implemented as a ProM plug-in but no release URL or availability statement.
human_research_question: How can instance graphs be built from minimal event logs of unstructured, knowledge-intensive processes (filtering discovery plus repair of irregular traces), and how can that Building Instance Graph (BIG) algorithm be delivered as a ProM plug-in for both standard and expert users?
human_main_finding: BIG4ProM implements BIG in ProM: causal relations from α-algorithm, Heuristics Miner or infrequent Inductive Miner; irregular traces detected via PNetReplayer cost-based fitness alignments; deleted/inserted events are repaired so IGs stay connected and more precise; two variants (log-only with defaults vs expert-supplied Petri net + alignment); graphs are visualized and exported as DOT.
human_limitations: Current implementation requires Petri-net models and PNetReplayer-format alignments; no empirical study or quality-metric numbers in this paper; default miner parameters for non-expert users; not evaluated on software-engineering logs.

title: Modeling Extraneous Activity Delays in Business Process Simulation
abstract: Business Process Simulation (BPS) is a common approach to estimate the impact of changes to a business process on its performance measures. For example, BPS allows us to estimate what would be the cycle time of a process if we automated one of its activities. The starting point of BPS is a business process model annotated with simulation parameters (a BPS model). Several studies have proposed methods to automatically discover BPS models from event logs via process mining. However, current techniques in this space discover BPS models that only capture waiting times caused by resource contention or resource unavailability. Oftentimes, a considerable portion of the waiting time in a business process is caused by extraneous delays, e.g. a resource waits for the customer to return a phone call. This paper proposes a method that discovers extraneous delays from input data, and injects timer events into a BPS model to capture the discovered delays. An empirical evaluation involving synthetic and real-life logs shows that the approach produces BPS models that better reflect the temporal dynamics of the process, relative to BPS models that do not capture extraneous delays.
venue: Proceedings 2022 4th International Conference on Process Mining Icpm 2022
human_qa_notes: Complete ICPM 2022 paper; two-column wrap artifacts but fully assessable; QA2 scored 0 because the contribution and all evaluation logs (pharmacy, insurance, loan, P2P, confidential CF, BPIC 2012/2017) are generic business-process simulation, not software engineering; QA8 credited for precision/recall, SMAPE, and Wasserstein/EMD between simulated and real temporal distributions.
human_research_question: Given an event log and a BPS model, can extraneous (non-resource-contention) activity delays be discovered and injected as timer events so that the enhanced model replicates the log's temporal dynamics more accurately than the original BPS model?
human_main_finding: Estimating each activity instance's optimal start (max of enablement time via a Heuristics Miner concurrency oracle and resource-availability time) and fitting timer-event delay distributions—optionally TPE-scaled—re-discovers injected extraneous delays (precision 1.00; recall 1.00 except 0.75 on P2P-4) and reduces cycle-time/timestamp EMD versus SIMOD baselines on BPIC 2012 and 2017.
human_limitations: Resource-contention waiting can partially or totally eclipse extraneous delays (missed P2P timer); first-activity delays are discarded because trace arrival is not estimated; delays are attached only to the succeeding activity; evaluation uses five simulated plus two real-life processes and as-is replay rather than what-if prediction; construct validity depends on the chosen discretized-distribution distances.

title: PoEM-Forum 2020 - Proceedings of the Forum at Practice of Enterprise Modeling 2020, co-located with the 13th IFIP WG 8.1 Working Conference on the Practice of Enterprise Modeling, PoEM 2020
abstract: The 13th IFIP WG 8.1 Working Conference on the Practice of Enterprise Modeling (PoEM 2020), is aimed at improving the understanding of the practice of Enterprise Modeling. The special focus in 2020 was on the role enterprise modeling in the digital age. Pollowing the tradition established in the previous PoEM editions, PoEM 2020 also featured the PoEM Forum. Its aim is to provide opportunities for presenting and discussing new ideas, challenges, methods, techniques, and tools relevant for Enterprise Modeling. The Forum was organized as an online session where the accepted papers were presented. In order to fuel the discussions, not only the audience could ask questions to the presenter, but also each presenter had the opportunity to raise questions to the audience in order to receive feedback directed to improve the presented research. In total, we received 11 submissions for the Forum. Based on three reviews by members of the Program Committee for the Forum, we selected 6 papers (54% acceptance rate). The seventh paper included in this volume is a summary of the panel discussion that took place at the conference on the topic of enterprise modeling in the digital age.</p
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings

title: A Systematic Literature Review on prioritizing software test cases using Markov chains
abstract: Test case prioritization (TCP) is deemed valid to improve testing efficiency, especially in regression testing, as retest all is costly. The TCP schedule the test case execution order to detect bugs faster. For such benefit, test case prioritization has been intensively studied. This paper reviews the development of TCP for regression testing with 48 papers from 2017 to 2020. In this paper, we present four critical surveys. First is the development of approaches and techniques in regression TCP studies, second is the identification of software under test (SUT) variations used in TCP studies, third is the trend of metrics used to measure the TCP studies effectiveness, and fourth is the state-of-the-art of requirements-based TCP. Furthermore, we discuss development opportunities and potential future directions on regression TCP. Our review provides evidence that TCP has increasing interests. We also discovered that requirement-based utilization would help to prepare test cases earlier to improve TCP effectiveness
venue: Information and Software Technology

title: Reconstructing meaningful workflow from transaction logs
abstract: Enterprises today rely on workflow more and more to accomplish business goals. A well designed process can contribute to better business operation and working efficiency. In practice, however, most organizations have no efficient workflow, either there is not at all from the very beginning, or lack domain experts who equip with the comprehensive landscape about the business. In order to conduct business more effectively, it is necessary to reconstruct workflows from transaction logs, and further, optimize the business via meaningful representations of these workflows. In this paper, we propose a method and corresponding toolbox to mine the workflows and vital patterns. Domain experts can use them in an interactive way to reconstruct meaningful business processes. We got very promising experimental results on two real applications datasets.
venue: Proceedings 2010 IEEE International Conference on Software Engineering and Service Sciences Icsess 2010
human_qa_notes: IEEE two-column extract is complete enough to judge (some math OCR such as s, for s′); QA2 scored 0 because both real logs are e-government property registration and hospital ambulatory care, not software engineering; QA7=0 because only a Java/GraphViz prototype is 'available on request' and the logs are not released; support/confidence and a visual Alpha comparison are not fitness/precision/MAPE-style model-quality metrics (QA8=0); no threats-to-validity section.
human_research_question: How can sequential pattern mining (GSP) plus redundancy filtering and outlier search reconstruct workflows that domain experts find meaningful, and expose both frequent patterns and affiliated rare tasks, from transaction logs?
human_main_finding: GSP-based sequence mining with length-based filtering, a confidence-range (RoC) control, and a second GSP pass for outliers produced expert-interpretable workflows on a one-year Chinese e-government log (656,952 entries / 150,853 instances / 568 tasks) and a hospital log (52,237 entries / 11,702 instances / 18 tasks); domain experts preferred these graphs to the ProM Alpha model, which they found too tangled to understand.
human_limitations: Meaningfulness is judged qualitatively by domain-expert feedback rather than process-model quality metrics; results depend on user-chosen support/RoC thresholds; the e-government and hospital logs and the prototype are not publicly deposited (prototype only 'on request').

title: Automated generation of test cases using a performability model
abstract: The authors present a new approach for the automated generation of test cases to be used for demonstrating the reliability of large industrial mission-critical systems. In this study they extend earlier work by using a performability model to track resource usage and resource failures. Results from the transient Markov chain analysis are used to estimate the software reliability at a given system execution time.
venue: Iet Software
human_qa_notes: Strong methodological paper with a discussion resembling threats to validity (accuracy of input parameters, validity of Markov modeling assumptions); the two 'empirical' case studies use illustrative/parametrized values modeled on real industrial systems rather than measured field data, and no dataset/code is shared.
human_research_question: How can an automated test-case-generation approach based on Markov-chain performability models (combining resource-usage and resource-failure sub-models) select a minimal set of most-probable test configurations to efficiently assess whether a large industrial system meets combined reliability and performance requirements?
human_main_finding: Extending prior Markov-chain-based test generation with performability theory, the paper shows on two illustrative industrial-like case studies (a distributed data-center system and a triple-redundant mission-critical system) how to select a minimal, most-probable set of resource configurations to test, computing a reliability/performance metric G(t) (fraction of time requirements are met) without exhaustively testing all configurations.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly note that model applicability depends on the accuracy of input parameter values and the validity of modeling assumptions, recommending sensitivity analysis as future work; full application to certify a real large mission-critical system is also left as future work.

title: Markovian reliability analysis for software using error generation and imperfect debugging
venue: Lecture Notes in Engineering and Computer Science
human_qa_notes: Clean text; purely theoretical/numerical study - authors explicitly state no real ("live") failure data was available, so illustrative default parameters were used instead.
human_research_question: Can a Markov-process-based software reliability growth model that accounts for two fault types, imperfect debugging, and error generation provide accurate predictions of software reliability and remaining fault content?
human_main_finding: Using Laplace transforms, matrix methods, and Runge-Kutta numerical solution, the proposed two-fault-type Markov reliability model with imperfect debugging and error generation shows reliability R(t) increasing and mean remaining faults E{D(t)} decreasing with testing time and with higher debugging/correction probabilities, supporting its use for release-time decision-making.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly state that no live/real failure data was available, so secondary/illustrative default parameter values were used instead of estimating parameters from actual field data.

title: 20th International Conference on Business Process Management, BPM 2022
abstract: Purpose Although Business Process Management (BPM) is a critical issue and small- and medium-sized family firms (SMFFs) frequently adopt process organization, very little literature focuses on the processes by which family firms remain distinctive (Chrisman et al. , 2016) or on their approach to BPM. The current research aims to fill this gap by analyzing dynamic companies’ attitudes to process-driven ability that concern exploitative as well as explorative processes. The purpose of this paper is to identify which kinds of dimensions may build an ambidextrous state in BPM in SMFFs, also favored by entrepreneurial IT capabilities and influenced by a stable but changeable context. Design/methodology/approach The authors referred to vom Brocke et al.’s (2014) study as it allows a focus on BPM research in the context of SMFFs. Then, the authors adapted the framework to the context of SMFFs. In addition, an empirical analysis has been made for applying the framework’s principles on effective BPM requirements to SMFFs. In the research, the authors applied grounded theory, according to which observation and theorization are linked by circularity, as they represent moments being managed simultaneously. The theorization emerged in different moments of the empirical surveys, influencing the next data gathering and the data gathering was the object of a de-structured matching and analysis process. Findings Specific cultural and cognitive aspects, values and abilities affect the company behavior of SMFFs in terms of BPM, and this is influenced by the connection between the family and the business. Therefore, it confirms that the family is a missing variable in organizational research (Dyer, 2006) also in BPM. A good BPM permits the definition of business abilities of running the current processes, along with of acclimatizing the company to a changeable context. In regard to the exploitative and explorative strengths typical of organizational ambidexterity, the research favors, respectively, transactional excellence with a focus on net cost reduction and transformational excellence based on net revenue generation. This approach requires consideration of the difference between external and internal contingencies as well as of the different processes to manage. However, despite IT-based BPM tools and the new era of IT-based process thinking, technology appropriation is only one of our dimensions, and each dimension plays a role in good BPM behavior; only a combination of dimensions favors effective and flexible BPM. Research limitations/implications The research contributes to the literature on BPM through theoretical implications, in particular two main implications. First, the research emphasizes the impact of familiness on good BPM practice. Family appears to be a missing variable in organizational research on BPM, even though familiness affects process specificity and mechanisms. Second, the research is based on certain category dimensions that characterize management models common in the literature, allowing the application of BPM in FFs by taking advantage of their confidence and adaptability. Limitations are related to different points of view on the model’s scope and design, the recipient and the research method. Practical implications The research has two main practical implications, representing managerial potential, that improve the significance and originality of the research in internal and external contexts. In the internal context, this permits a new BPM mind-set. Originality/value The research is original for the following two reasons. First, when FF complexity grows and/or new organizational issues emerge, FFs are faced with two challenges: an increased number of complex processes to handle, along with a lack of IT-based BPM for organizational ambidexterity. In such a context, this research can suggest a solution. Second, the research is based on dimensions that have been widely characterized in general management models. For this reason, FFs may already be familiar with these dimensions. In addition, the model strongly valorizes the familiness impact on BPM development and takes into consideration the context awareness of the company.
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics

title: Software Performance Analysis Using a Language Measure
abstract: This paper presents the software performance analysis using a finite state automation model. A signed real measure of formal languages has been used for quantitative evaluation of the software. This paper extends an earlier model based on a discrete time Markov chain to a semi-Markov process. As an example, a software rejuvenation policy is analyzed using the proposed approach.
venue: Proceedings of the American Control Conference
human_qa_notes: Theoretical control-theory/automata paper (American Control Conference 2003) applying semi-Markov reward processes and 'language measure' theory to a software rejuvenation example; the numeric illustration reuses parameter values from a cited prior study rather than original data collection, so there is no real empirical validation, reproducibility statement, or threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: How can a signed real 'language measure' of automata (extended from discrete-time Markov chains to semi-Markov reward processes) be used to formally analyze and optimize software rejuvenation (preventive restart) policies for improving software availability/performance?
human_main_finding: Extending the language-measure approach from discrete-time Markov chains to semi-Markov reward processes enables analytical comparison and optimization of software rejuvenation policies (level-1 partial restart vs level-2 full restart); applying sojourn-time estimates from prior literature, the analysis concludes the optimal policy is pure level-2 (full) restart, consistent with an earlier study's finding obtained via a different (deterministic) method.
human_limitations: The analysis is purely theoretical/illustrative, relying on numeric parameters borrowed from a prior paper rather than new empirical measurement; the paper provides no discussion of threats to validity or real-system validation.

title: Verification of lean-kanban processes with probabilistic model checking
abstract: Many software processes have been adopted in industrial practices. It is important to be able to understand whether a software process is efficient and effective. Many software process simulation methods have been proposed over the years to estimate and measure the processes. These measurements are highly effective at what they do but they are also highly inefficient in other terms. In this paper, we present a proposal for the application of probabilistic model checking in software process modelling, simulation and verification. Software processes are modelled using Markov chain models and the interested properties are specified as probabilistic temporal logic. We illustrate the proposal by a real case study of software maintenance of the lean-kanban process. The process requirements were validated by PRISM.
venue: International Journal of Computer Applications in Technology

title: Quantitative analysis of services
abstract: We show a number of applications of the tools which have been developed within the sensoria project to perform quantitative analysis of services. These tools are formally grounded on source calculi which allow the description of services at distinct levels of abstraction, and hence pose distinct challenges to both modelling and analysis. The reported applications refer to (suitable subcomponents of) the Finance Case-Study, and show instances of, respectively, exact model checking of MarCaSPiS against the both state-aware and action-aware logic SoSL, exact and statistical model checking of sCOWS against the state-aware logic CSL, querying of PEPA models by terms of the XSP language that expresses both state-aware and action-aware stochastic probes
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Illustrative application of multiple stochastic process-calculus verification tools to a fully specified synthetic Finance Case-Study; case study parameters are transparently given enabling reproduction of the formal analysis, but there is no real-world dataset, no explicit code repository link in this paper, and no formal threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: How can stochastic process calculi (MarCaSPiS, sCOWS, PEPA) and their associated quantitative analysis tools (exact and statistical model checking, stochastic probes) be used to analyze non-functional properties — performance, workload, and reactivity — of a service-oriented credit-request business process?
human_main_finding: Tools developed within the Sensoria Project successfully performed exact and statistical stochastic model checking and stochastic-probe querying on the Finance Case-Study credit request scenario, showing how client rating distributions affect system performance, quantifying supervisor/clerk workload and system reactivity, and demonstrating that statistical (simulation-based) model checking scales better than exact model checking as state spaces grow.
human_limitations: The analyzed scenario poses a 'stiff' multi-scale numerical problem because activity rates differ by several orders of magnitude (seconds vs. days), which the authors note challenges the underlying numerical routines of the quantitative analysis tools; no separate limitations section is otherwise given.

title: An Extended CompDepend-Algorithm to Discovery Duplicate Tasks in Workflow Process Mining System
authors: XiaoHui, Wang; WenQing, Zhao; FengJuan, Guo
abstract: The workflow mining technology had become a hot research field among computer application. In current mining algorithm, duplicated tasks are hard to be modeled. This paper proposes an extended CompDepend-Algorithm able to discovery duplicate tasks. Firstly, a new data structure based on sequence set is designed to describe duplicate tasks. Secondly, rules to discover duplicated tasks based on dependency relationship are proposed. Then the algorithm of workflow mining based these rules is given. At last, Experimental results prove that the algorithm is effective.
venue: 2009 International Conference on Research Challenges in Computer Science
human_qa_notes: Text extraction contains some garbled mathematical/set-notation OCR artifacts, but core content is legible; no real dataset or empirical validation beyond a synthetic illustrative example despite the abstract's claim of 'experimental results'.
human_research_question: How can duplicate tasks (activities with the same name occurring multiple times) be discovered and correctly modeled in workflow process mining, extending the CompDepend algorithm with a sequence-set-based data structure and new dependency rules?
human_main_finding: The paper proposes an Extended CompDepend-Algorithm using sequence sets and five new rules to identify duplicate tasks and their six possible relationship types (sequence, parallel, select combinations); illustrated on a synthetic workflow model example showing it reconstructs relationships the original algorithm could not distinguish for duplicate tasks.
human_limitations: not stated; the paper mentions future work will address multistep loops in workflow models but does not discuss limitations of the current approach or validate on real event log data.

title: Simplifying software metric models via hierarchical LASSO with incomplete data samples
abstract: Software metric models can be used in predicting the interested target software metric(s) for future software project based on certain related metric(s). However, during the construction of such a model, incomplete data often appear in data sample gained from analogous past projects. In addition, whether a particular continuous predictor metric or a particular category for a certain categorical predictor metric should be included in the model must be determined in practice. To solve these problems, this paper introduces a methodology integrating the k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) multiple imputation method, kernel smoothing, Monte Carlo simulation, and a latest variable selection method. Thus, a more flexible model is constructed. A case study is given to illustrate the proposed procedures.
venue: Proceedings 2010 2nd Wri World Congress on Software Engineering Wcse 2010
human_qa_notes: Readable IEEE extraction with some garbled math/operators but methods and tables remain assessable. QA6=0: no threats-to-validity discussion (conclusion is two sentences). QA7=0: ISBSG R9 is a licensed repository and authors only mention Zhu's unpublished R implementation of adaptive HLASSO, with no public data/code release.
human_research_question: How can software metric models with incomplete project samples be simplified (continuous-predictor omission and categorical-level collapse) by combining k-NN multiple imputation, Monte Carlo completion, and adaptive hierarchical LASSO, and does this outperform stepwise regression?
human_main_finding: On a preprocessed ISBSG R9 sample (669 of 3024 projects) predicting first-month extreme defects from major/minor defects, user-base locations, function points and development type, both stepwise and HLASSO drop the redundant locations predictor and merge enhancement with new-development; HLASSO keeps only the quadratic function-point term and reports lower K-fold CV MSE (71.51 vs 73.86) and MRE than stepwise.
human_limitations: Single ISBSG case; MRE is pathologically large because zero extreme-defect outcomes were replaced by 1e-6 in the denominator; no threats-to-validity section; licensed data and no released analysis code; theoretical properties of the imputation-plus-selection pipeline are not established.

title: Event logs for the analysis of software failures: A rule-based approach
abstract: Event logs have been widely used over the last three decades to analyze the failure behavior of a variety of systems. Nevertheless, the implementation of the logging mechanism lacks a systematic approach and collected logs are often inaccurate at reporting software failures: This is a threat to the validity of log-based failure analysis. This paper analyzes the limitations of current logging mechanisms and proposes a rule-based approach to make logs effective to analyze software failures. The approach leverages artifacts produced at system design time and puts forth a set of rules to formalize the placement of the logging instructions within the source code. The validity of the approach, with respect to traditional logging mechanisms, is shown by means of around 12,500 software fault injection experiments into real-world systems.
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Full text read including references; no process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique is used (the paper is about fault-injection-driven design of a rule-based logging mechanism, evaluated with recall/precision), so QA4 scored 0 — likely a borderline/tangential inclusion for a PM+stochastic-modeling SLR; LogBus framework code is publicly linked (sourceforge), supporting partial reproducibility.
human_research_question: Can a rule-based logging approach, derived from system design artifacts, significantly improve the ability of event logs to detect and report software failures compared to traditional ad-hoc logging mechanisms?
human_main_finding: Across roughly 12,500 fault-injection experiments on Apache webserver and TAO Open DDS, the proposed rule-based logging mechanism achieved much higher failure-detection recall (0.91-0.94 vs. 0.34-0.42 for traditional logs) with comparable or higher precision, while producing far more compact logs (up to ~275x smaller), at an acceptable runtime performance overhead (under about 16%).
human_limitations: Authors note rule-based logs may miss some failure-cause details (partially mitigated via a free-text complaint field) and that the approach's applicability depends on the availability of design artifacts, though reverse engineering can substitute for missing artifacts.

title: A business process simulation method supporting resource evolution
authors: Jimin Ling; Qi Feng; Li Zhang
abstract: Business process simulation is the procedure of planning, modeling and simulating enterprise process to analyze the features varying with time which guides the users to make decisions or important means of process improvement. In the existing simulation methods, they considered little about dynamic resource, which may lead to a large deviation. To solve the problem above, a business process simulation method supporting resource evolution that mainly focuses on human resource is proposed. Individual differences and personnel composition are analyzed to represent the dynamic feature of resources. Evolution of human capacity and personnel changes are described to meet the simulation requirements of human resource model. And then, process simulation mechanism and algorithm are realized. An experiment is conducted by simulating the software development process of a real-world software project using the system prototype we developed, and it shows that our method is closer to the practical project situation, thus the method effectiveness can be demonstrated to a certain extent. The main contribution of our work is a novel process simulation approach based on a dynamic resource model with configurable evolution rules.
venue: Proceedings of the 2014 International Conference on Software and System Process
human_qa_notes: Solid empirical validation against a real software project's actual duration using a discrete-event simulator (POMES) with configurable human-resource-evolution rules; no formal threats-to-validity discussion, no public data/code (proprietary in-house tool, single project), and no fitness/precision-style metrics (only total-duration comparisons).
human_research_question: How can business process simulation account for dynamic evolution of human resources (personnel ability growth, training, composition changes) to produce more realistic software-development-process simulation results than existing static-resource simulation methods?
human_main_finding: Incorporating configurable personnel-evolution rules (training, activity-driven ability growth, communication overhead) into a discrete-event business process simulator yielded a predicted project duration (483.6 days) much closer to the real project's actual duration (497 days) than a baseline simulation without resource evolution (411.3 days), validated on a real software development project (Ships Comprehensive Condition Assessment and Health Management System).
human_limitations: Authors state the approach was validated on only a single real-world project and future work will apply it to more industry software projects to further demonstrate effectiveness; measuring personnel ability more precisely across process phases and extending evolution modeling to non-personnel resources are noted as open issues.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Build Failures in the Continuous Integration Workflows of Java-Based Open-Source Software
abstract: Continuous Integration (CI) has become a common practice in both industrial and open-source software development. While CI has evidently improved aspects of the software development process, errors during CI builds pose a threat to development efficiency. As an increasing amount of time goes into fixing such errors, failing builds can significantly impair the development process and become very costly. We perform an indepth analysis of build failures in CI environments. Our approach links repository commits to data of corresponding CI builds. Using data from 14 open-source Java projects, we first identify 14 common error categories. Besides test failures, which are by far the most common error category (up to >80% per project), we also identify noisy build data, e.g., induced by transient Git interaction errors, or general infrastructure flakiness. Second, we analyze which factors impact the build results, taking into account general process and specific CI metrics. Our results indicate that process metrics have a significant impact on the build outcome in 8 of the 14 projects on average, but the strongest influencing factor across all projects is overall stability in the recent build history. For 10 projects, more than 50% (up to 80%) of all failed builds follow a previous build failure. Moreover, the fail ratio of the last k=10 builds has a significant impact on build results for all projects in our dataset.
venue: IEEE International Working Conference on Mining Software Repositories
human_qa_notes: Rigorous empirical MSR/CI study with an explicit threats-to-validity section (construct/internal/external), but relies on statistical hypothesis testing (Mann-Whitney, chi-square) rather than a process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique, so QA4/QA8 are not met; no public code/data link provided.
human_research_question: What types of errors cause CI build failures in Java-based open-source projects, and which development/process practices and CI-specific factors are correlated with build outcomes?
human_main_finding: Across 14 Java OSS projects, test failures, code-quality violations, and compile errors are the most common causes of CI build failures (over 80% combined with git/buildconfig errors), and build climate/previous build result is by far the strongest predictor of build outcome, with change complexity and author experience having weaker but significant effects; pull-request builds fail more often than direct push builds.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly discuss threats to validity: construct validity (possible misclassification during semi-automated error categorization), internal validity (correlational, not causal, findings; incomplete stratification), and external validity (results limited to high-profile Java/Maven/Gradle/GitHub/Travis-CI projects, not necessarily generalizable to smaller OSS or other VCS workflows).

title: Monte Carlo simulation based estimations: Case from a global outsourcing company
abstract: Effort estimation of various software project life cycle phases have been traditionally performed using deterministic methods. Deterministic methods fail to account for the variability inherent in the software engineering processes deployed in executing the project. We have developed stochastic notations and models that can represent these process variations. We have also constructed a Monte Carlo simulation tool that works using the stochastic model we have developed for software development projects. This tool has been tested in a mid-sized software services outsourcing (SSO) organization. The tool and results are described and reported in this paper.
venue: Proceedings of the 1st International Technology Management Conference Itmc 2011
human_qa_notes: Clean IEEE conference PDF text, no OCR issues; scored low on QA3/QA7/QA8 because the 70-project dataset is proprietary/not shared, no code released, and no fitness/precision-style model-quality metric is reported (only effort predictions and sensitivity bars).
human_research_question: How can Monte Carlo simulation and stochastic modeling of software development sub-phase efforts be used to produce confidence-based effort estimates that account for process variability, instead of deterministic estimation methods?
human_main_finding: Using stochastic notations and PDFs fitted from historical data of 70 real development projects, a Monte Carlo simulation tool (built on @Risk) can generate confidence-based effort estimates per SDLC phase/sub-phase, and sensitivity analysis identifies which sub-phases contribute most variability for targeted process improvement.
human_limitations: Authors state the model and notations were developed only for 'development' type projects (not other project types such as maintenance or migration), and that process performance varies across organizations, technologies, and personnel skills.

title: The economic impact of software process variations
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Strong methodological rigor with an explicit threats-to-validity discussion (transition-probability sensitivity analysis via the FAST method, and a memorylessness robustness check); underlying process model and calibration data are not shared due to company confidentiality.
human_research_question: What is the economic benefit (in effort and duration) of using isolated test/development environments (Caps) versus shared/non-isolated mainframe software development, and how can this be quantified when a controlled empirical study is infeasible?
human_main_finding: Using an absorbing-Markov-chain process-simulation model calibrated with empirical effort data and configuration-management-derived conflict probabilities, the BMW case study found that isolated test/development environments (Caps) save about 20% of total development effort versus non-isolated shared mainframe development for projects with average program dependencies; sensitivity analysis confirmed this relative conclusion is robust to parameter uncertainty and to relaxing the Markov memorylessness assumption.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly identify the two major threats to validity as the difficulty of precisely determining transition probabilities and the memoryless assumption of Markov chains, addressing both via sensitivity analysis, but note they lack formal external validation and instead rely on correspondence with practitioners' experience.

title: Nirikshan: Process Mining Software Repositories to Identify Inefficiencies, Imperfections, and Enhance Existing Process Capabilities
abstract: Process mining is to extract knowledge about business processes from data stored implicitly in ad-hoc way or explicitly by information systems. The aim is to discover runtime process, analyze performance and perform conformance verification, using process mining tools like ProM and Disco, for single software repository and processes spanning across multiple repositories. Application of process mining to software repositories has recently gained interest due to availability of vast data generated during software development and maintenance. Process data are embodied in repositories which can be used for analysis to improve the efficiency and capability of process, however, involves a lot of challenges which have not been addressed so far. Project team defines workflow, design process and policies for tasks like issue tracking (defect or feature enhancement), peer code review (review the submitted patch to avoid defects before they are injected) etc. to streamline and structure the activities. The reality may not be the same as defined because of imperfections so the extent of non-conformance needs to be measured. We propose a research framework `Nirikshan' to process mine the data of software repositories from multiple perspectives like process, organizational, data and time. We apply process mining on software repositories to derive runtime process map, identify and remove inefficiencies and imperfections, extend the capabilities of existing software engineering tools to make them more process aware, and understand interaction pattern between various contributors to improve the efficiency of project.
venue: Companion Proceedings of the 36th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE Companion 2014)
