title: A general modeling and analysis framework for software fault detection and correction process
abstract: Summary Software reliability growth modeling plays an important role in software reliability evaluation. To incorporate more information and provide more accurate analysis, modeling software fault detection and correction processes has attracted widespread research attention recently. In modeling software correction processes, the assumption of fault correction time is relaxed from constant delay to random delay. However, stochastic distribution of fault correction time brings more difficulties in modeling and corresponding parameter estimation. In this paper, a framework of software reliability models containing both information from software fault detection process and correction process is studied. Different from previous extensions on software reliability growth modeling, the proposed approach is based on Markov model other than a nonhomogeneous Poisson process model. Also, parameter estimation is carried out with weighted least‐square estimation method, which emphasizes the influence of later data on the prediction. Two data sets from practical software development projects are applied with the proposed framework, which shows satisfactory performance with the results. Copyright © 2016 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
venue: Software Testing Verification and Reliability

title: A markov error propagation model for component-based software systems
abstract: Component-based software engineering has proved itself as a strong pillar in software engineering community. Large number of factors are involved in the success of software product developed using Component-based software engineering, for instance, security, reliability, quality, safety, and testability. As the component-based software is made up of large number of components put together, therefore components’ reliability influence the reliability of the complete software. Numerous models and principles have been established to estimate the reliability of software by applying information regarding architecture, quality and security attributes of the software. Many researchers overlooked a major factor while estimating reliability of component-based software and that is error-propagation. Although it can be a case that the components are not dependent on each other and they are supplemented with the wrappers. However it is not true for many component-based applications. In this paper, a framework for reliability estimation has been proposed. In our proposal we have considered error propagation. We have analyzed the program structure and also presented how they are handled in estimation process. Further sensitivity analysis is done to identify the most sensitive component of the system. A numerical simulation is also presented for better understanding of the proposed framework.
venue: International Journal of Performability Engineering
human_qa_notes: Primarily a theoretical/simulation paper (MATLAB numeric example with assumed/simulated parameter values on a hypothetical component-based system) rather than an empirical case study with real measured data; no threats-to-validity section or code/data availability statement.
human_research_question: How can a Markov chain-based error propagation model, using only per-component and pairwise integration-testing data, estimate the reliability of an entire component-based software system without full system-level testing, while also supporting fault localization and critical-component protection?
human_main_finding: The proposed Markov-based error propagation model (using only 4n-2 states versus the exponential 2^n states of a comparable prior model) can estimate component and system reliability, localize the most likely fault-causing component, and identify critical components needing protection; demonstrated via a MATLAB simulation on a 7-component 'Make to Order' production-planning system example, achieving a computed path reliability of 0.8989.
human_limitations: Authors state the current model only considers transient states (future work will add absorbing states), compatibility across different system structures remains a challenge, and obtaining reliable probability distributions for path selection needs improved methods; no real empirical/industrial validation was performed, only a simulated numeric example with assumed parameters.

title: Linking software process modeling with Markov decision theory
abstract: Scheduling is a notoriously difficult task for managers of software projects. The time needed to complete some development activity in a software project is hard to estimate; feedback between activities causes rework and delays. The author presents a dynamic software process model and its formalization as a discrete-time Markov decision process. The model focuses on capturing how the feedback between development activities affects the cost and schedule of a software project. The model explicitly represents scheduling actions, component coupling, and rework caused by design changes. We use the MDP model to compute optimal strategies for several sample projects and analyze the resulting optimal strategies.
venue: Proceedings International Computer Software and Applications Conference
human_qa_notes: Rigorous formal/simulation study with fully specified synthetic input parameters (means, variances, coupling scenarios) enabling manual reproduction of the sample computations; no explicit code/data release, no formal threats-to-validity discussion, and no process-mining-style quality metrics (reports optimal cost/duration instead).
human_research_question: How can feedback between software development activities (rework caused by design changes and component coupling) be formalized as a Markov Decision Process to compute optimal team-scheduling strategies that minimize expected project cost/duration?
human_main_finding: Using an MDP-based software process scheduling model, optimal strategies were computed for a sample project via value iteration; results show optimal project cost/duration increases with the strength of inter-component coupling and decreases when teams are specialized on particular components.
human_limitations: Not explicitly stated as a limitations section; the model assumes an acyclic MDP state space and relies on statistical data about past projects plus high-level design coupling information as required inputs, which is presented as a modeling requirement rather than an acknowledged limitation.

title: Automatic Real-Time Mining Software Process Activities From SVN Logs Using a Naive Bayes Classifier
authors: Zhu, Rui; Dai, Yichao; Li, Tong; Ma, Zifei; Zheng, Ming; Tang, Yahui; Yuan, Jiayi; Huang, Yue
abstract: The abundance of event data in current software configuration management systems makes it possible to discover software process models automatically by using actual observed behavior. However, traditional process mining algorithms cannot be applied to event logs recorded in software configuration management (SCM) systems, such as SVN, because of missing activity attributes. To address this problem, a software process activity classifier is proposed to build event-activity mapping relationships from software development event streams, revealing activity attributes and associating the activity to the original SVN log. The proposed approach extracts activity from the SVN log based on semantic features and introduces a novel technique based on a naive Bayes approach to associate event activities dynamically. The approach has been applied to two real-world software development process logs, ArgoUML and jEdit, consisting of more than 80,000 events, covering development information from 1998 to 2015. With the application of our approach to such data, activities can be extracted from event logs and a classifier can be constructed for adding activity attributes to new events. The results of the classification are evaluated in terms of precision rate, recall rate, and the F-measure. Overall, two real-world software development process logs are used to validate the method, and the experimental results show that the approach can mine software process activities from SVN log events automatically and in real-time.
venue: IEEE Access
human_qa_notes: Clean, complete text; core technique (K-means/Word2Vec clustering plus naive Bayes classifier) is a machine-learning classification method that prepares SVN logs for process mining rather than a classic PM discovery/conformance algorithm or classic stochastic model; precision/recall/F-measure are reported (QA8=1) but no data/code availability statement is given (QA7=0).
human_research_question: Can a naive Bayes classifier, trained on K-means/Word2Vec-derived semantic clusters, automatically and incrementally map SVN log events to software process activities in real time, given the absence of native activity labels in software configuration management logs?
human_main_finding: The proposed K-means+Word2Vec clustering combined with a naive Bayes activity classifier accurately maps SVN log events to activities in real time (average precision/recall/F-measure of about 0.83-0.87 for ArgoUML and 0.68-0.84 for jEdit), outperforming a simpler fuzzy-clustering/path-name-based mapping baseline.
human_limitations: Authors note the size of the software process log sample is limited, the weighting of certain features used in event mapping lacks a standardized measure, and there is no standard method for evaluating unsupervised clustering results.

title: Assessing Agile Software Development Processes with Process Mining: A Case Study
authors: Marques, Rita; Mira da Silva, Miguel; R. Ferreira, Diogo
abstract: Software development is a growing industry with increasingly more complex projects. Agile methodologies, such as Scrum, have emerged in part to address this challenge. Agile focuses on a set of best practices rather than a standardized process, which makes it difficult to assess whether it is being properly implemented in an organization. In this work, we analyze the feasibility of using process mining to evaluate the implementation of Scrum practices based on event logs collected from a case-handling system. A case study was conducted in an IT organization that uses Jira Software to manage its projects. With process mining, it was possible to extract the workflow behaviour in two different projects. While Scrum standards like role distribution could be discovered, other practices like customer collaboration could not be detected in the log. This case study provided important insights regarding the application of process mining in case-handling systems and Scrum processes.
venue: 2018 IEEE 20th Conference on Business Informatics (CBI)
human_qa_notes: Solid SE case study following the PM2 methodology and comparing multiple process-discovery algorithms (alpha/heuristics/inductive/fuzzy miner) plus social-network analysis on two real Scrum/Jira projects; limitations are discussed thoroughly as lessons learned rather than a formal threats-to-validity section, and no data/code is shared (anonymized proprietary data).
human_research_question: Can process mining techniques be used to discover and assess the implementation of Scrum practices (roles, ceremonies, artifacts) from event logs recorded in a Jira case-handling system, and what issues arise when mining unstructured agile process data?
human_main_finding: Process mining (dotted charts, control-flow discovery with alpha/heuristics/inductive/fuzzy miners, organizational/social-network analysis, and performance analysis) on two real Scrum projects in Jira revealed that Scrum roles and issue-assignment practices could be discovered, while other practices (team self-organization, customer collaboration, sprint-artifact completion) could not be reliably detected; bottlenecks and non-agile rework loops were identified and confirmed with the project manager.
human_limitations: Authors note that process mining could not detect several Scrum practices from the event log alone (e.g., self-organization, artifact completion by sprint end), that alpha/heuristics miner produced spaghetti models and the inductive miner had control-flow inaccuracies, and that the degree (not just presence/absence) of Scrum practice implementation is hard to quantify from event logs.

title: Stochastic-aware precision and recall measures for conformance checking in process mining
abstract: Process mining studies ways to improve real-world processes using historical event data generated by IT systems that support business processes of organ-isations. Given an event log of an IT system, process discovery algorithms construct a process model representing the processes recorded in the log, while conformance checking techniques quantify how well the discovered model achieves this objective. State-of-the-art discovery and conformance techniques either completely ignore or consider but hide from the users information about the likelihood of process behaviour. That is, the vast majority of the existing process discovery algorithms construct non-stochastic aware process models. Consequently, few conformance checking techniques can assess how well such discovered models describe the relative likelihoods of traces recorded in the log or how well they represent the likelihood of future traces generated by the same system. Note that this is necessary to support process simulation, prediction and recommendation. Furthermore, stochastic information can provide business analysts with further actionable insights on frequent and rare conformance issues. This article presents precision and recall measures based on the notion of entropy of stochastic automata, which are capable of quantifying and, hence, differentiating, between frequent and rare deviations of an event log and a process model that is enriched with the information on the relative likelihoods of traces it describes. An evaluation over several real-world datasets that uses our open-source implementation of the measures demonstrates the feasibility of using our precision and recall measures in industrial settings. Finally, we propose a range of intuitive desired properties that stochastic precision and re-call measures should possess, and study our and other existing stochastic-aware conformance measures with respect to these properties.
venue: Information Systems
human_qa_notes: Full postprint text is clean and complete (no OCR garbling); QA2 scored 0 because the paper is a general business-process-mining/conformance-checking contribution (illustrated on healthcare, insurance, loan, and IT-incident logs) with no dedicated software-engineering context description.
human_research_question: How can classical precision and recall conformance-checking measures be lifted to account for the stochastic perspective of event logs and process models (e.g., Stochastic Petri nets), so that frequent versus rare deviations can be distinguished?
human_main_finding: The proposed entropy-based and gain-based stochastic precision/recall measures satisfy more of the desirable formal properties than existing techniques (EMSC, entropic relevance) and non-stochastic alignments, are computationally feasible on ten real-life public event logs, and successfully identified 48 pairs of near-duplicate stochastic process models in an industrial (German health insurer) repository of ~4,000 models.
human_limitations: The entropy measures only account for common prefixes (not postfixes) of traces, do not simultaneously consider the stochastic perspective of both log and model (the gain measures do, but ignore partial trace matches), and the approach does not yet extend to infinite-state/unbounded process models; the industrial case-study models could not be released publicly per the company agreement.

title: A Hybrid Approach to Process Mining: Finding Immediate Successors of a Process by Using From-To Chart
abstract: Process mining is a branch of data mining that aims to discover process model from the event logs. In this study, we propose a hybrid approach to process mining in such a way that, "from-to chart" is used as the frontend to monitor the transitions among activities of a realistic event log. Another novelty of this study is developed evaluation metrics, which are used for finding immediate successors in order to convert these raw relations into dependency/frequency graph.
venue: 2009 International Conference on Machine Learning and Applications
human_qa_notes: No software-engineering-specific context (the case is a general ERP/business travel-management process, not a software process) and no threats-to-validity or reproducibility discussion; validation is limited to a single case with a small reference model (7 activities).
human_research_question: Can an industrial-engineering 'from-to chart' technique, adapted with new confidence/support/modified-lift evaluation metrics, be used to discover immediate-successor relations between activities from event logs and reconstruct an accurate process model?
human_main_finding: A hybrid process-discovery method adapting the industrial-engineering 'from-to chart' technique (with new confidence/support/modified-lift metrics) correctly reconstructs the sequence of immediate-successor activities in a real ERP travel-management process log, achieving 100% correct identification of immediate successors relative to the reference model.
human_limitations: Not explicitly discussed by the authors; the only stated limitation (as future work) is that the current from-to-chart approach is limited to sequential/straight-line behavior and cannot yet capture branching or loop constructs in the process model.

title: Applying Process Mining: The Reality of a Software Development SME
abstract: One of the challenges the organizations confront is to extract data from the information systems to know the reality of their processes to improve their efficiency. In this study, the application of Process Mining is addressed as an opportunity in the specific context of an SME dedicated to software development, implementing the L* life cycle model methodology from a layered Software Engineering approach. This research is carried out based on process improvement in an initial SME project. Subsequently, it is compared with a second project, using different Process Mining perspectives such as control flow, case, organization, and time, with the aim of extending the process model. This holistic view allows not only to better understand the processes involved, but also to identify and analyze the similarities and differences between the two projects. As a result, the Process Mining analysis shows crucial aspects such as the representation of integrated models, traces on sequences of actions, and the interaction of activities with specific roles and deviations in the flow of activities that compromise the quality of the process and the product. At the same time, the challenges that emerged during the improvement cycle are highlighted. These challenges cover issues such as data extraction, fluid communication between those involved, and the documentation associated with the processes. This study contributes to the body of knowledge of Process Mining. Likewise, the case study results offer a vision for other SMEs seeking to incorporate Process Mining as part of their improvement strategies.
venue: Applied Sciences Switzerland
human_qa_notes: Clean text; one of the most rigorous papers in this batch - real dual-project case study, named algorithms, explicit fitness metrics, and a dedicated limitations/challenges discussion, though the underlying event-log dataset itself is stated as not publicly available.
human_research_question: What does applying process mining (inductive-miner discovery plus token-replay conformance checking, extended with case/organizational/time perspectives) reveal about the real software development process of an SME, and how do results compare across two of its projects?
human_main_finding: Applying the L* process-mining methodology to two real projects of a Mexican software-development SME produced overall process fitness of 93.5% (Project 1) and 89.4% (Project 2); analysis revealed inconsistencies (e.g., issues marked Done without prior Validation), role/staff-turnover differences, and common SME-specific challenges such as documentation gaps and tool-integration difficulties.
human_limitations: The paper discusses several challenges: lack of process documentation, difficulty integrating heterogeneous tool records (Jira, GitHub, SIMIo), staff turnover and inadequate communication affecting model interpretation in Project 2, and explicitly states the underlying event-log dataset is not publicly available due to privacy.

title: A vector Markov model for structural coverage growth and the number of failure occurrences
abstract: Most software reliability growth models specify the expected number of failures experienced as a function of testing effort or calendar time. However, there are approaches to model the development of intermediate factors driving failure occurrences. This paper starts out with presenting a model framework consisting of four consecutive relationships. It is shown that a differential equation representing this framework is a generalization of several finite failures category models. The relationships between the number of test cases executed and expected structural coverage, and between expected structural coverage and the expected number of failure occurrences are then explored further. A vector Markov model allowing for partial redundancy in sampling code constructs is developed. The model bridges the gap between setups related to operational testing and systematic testing, respectively. Two extensions of the partial redundancy model considering the development of the number of failure occurrences are discussed. The paper concludes with showing that the extended models fit into the structure of the differential equation presented at the beginning, which permits further interpretation.
venue: Proceedings International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering ISSRE
human_qa_notes: Purely theoretical/mathematical software-reliability-modeling paper (ISSRE 2002) with no empirical case study, real dataset, threats-to-validity discussion, or code/data availability; the paper explicitly defers practical parameter estimation and application to real data to future work.
human_research_question: How can a unifying differential-equation framework and a vector Markov model (extending existing software reliability growth models) formally relate test-case execution, structural code-coverage growth (allowing partial redundancy), and the expected number of failure occurrences?
human_main_finding: The paper develops a 'vector Markov model' for structural coverage growth that generalizes and bridges existing operational-testing (Piwowarski et al.) and systematic-testing (Rivers-Vouk) coverage models by allowing partial redundancy in code-construct sampling, and shows two extensions of this model (fault detection at first vs. repeated construct execution) both reduce to special cases of an overarching differential-equation framework unifying several classical software reliability growth models (Goel-Okumoto, Jelinski-Moranda, ENHPP).
human_limitations: The paper explicitly states it focuses only on theoretical model derivation; practical parameter estimation and application to real software development/testing data are described as 'the subject of the current research activities' (future work), with no dataset applied in this paper.

title: Using Monte Carlo simulation for assessing software reliability
abstract: Abstract Simulation is presented here as a mathematical and computational technique use to analyze probabilistic models. Monte Carlo simulation, where the passage of time does not play a significant role, is presented here, with an emphasis on reliability applications. Monte Carlo simulation methods are often used when analytic methods become intractable, and they typically give a modeler added insight into the structure of a problem. As reliability and lifetime models become less mathematically tractable, Monte Carlo methods will have increasing importance. The topics addressed in here are basic variate generation techniques, the generation of order statistics, the generation of lifetimes for the accelerated life and proportional hazards lifetime models, and variate generation of a renewal or nonhomogeneous Poisson processes. The generation of order statistics is useful for simulating the lifetime of a series, parallel, or k ‐out‐of‐ n system. The generation of lifetime in the accelerated life and the Cox proportional hazards lifetime models is used to account for the impact of covariates on failure. The generation of a renewal or nonhomogeneous Poisson processes is used to model the failure times of a repairable system.

title: Discovery and Simulation of Data-Aware Business Processes
abstract: Simulation is a common approach to predict the effect of business process changes on quantitative performance. The starting point of Business Process Simulation (BPS) is a process model enriched with simulation parameters. To cope with the typically large parameter spaces of BPS models, several methods have been proposed to automatically discover BPS models from event logs. Virtually all these approaches neglect the data perspective of business processes. Yet, the data attributes manipulated by a business process often determine which activities are performed, how many times, and when. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a data-aware BPS modeling approach and a method to discover data-aware BPS models from event logs. The BPS modeling approach supports three types of data attributes (global, case-level, and event-level) as well as deterministic and stochastic attribute update rules and data-aware branching conditions. An empirical evaluation shows that the proposed method accurately discovers the type of each data attribute and its associated update rules, and that the resulting BPS models more closely replicate the process execution control flow relative to data-unaware BPS models.
venue: Proceedings 2024 6th International Conference on Process Mining Icpm 2024
human_qa_notes: Strong empirical and reproducibility profile: public code/data repository, quantitative accuracy metrics (EMD, KS, 3-gram), and evaluation on both real (Traffic, Sepsis, BPIC19) and 150 synthetic event logs; no explicit threats-to-validity section, though scope limitations are stated as future work.
human_research_question: How can data-aware business process simulation models — including global, case, and event attribute update rules and data-driven branching conditions — be automatically discovered from event logs, and do they more accurately replicate real process control flow than data-unaware simulation models?
human_main_finding: The proposed discovery method accurately classifies data attribute types and their update rules (about 95% correct classification) and the resulting data-aware simulation models replicate process execution control flow more accurately than data-unaware baseline models, particularly for case-based attributes and OR-gateway scenarios.
human_limitations: The approach only discovers update rules where an attribute's new value depends on that same attribute's own previous value (not on multiple attributes jointly), does not model data-dependent activity durations, and does not handle multitasking behavior, all left as future work.

A Data-Centric Approach to Evaluate Requirements Engineering in Multidisciplinary Projects
authors: Salmani, Ali; Imani, Alireza; Bahrehvar, Majid; Duffett-Leger, Linda; Moshirpour, Mohammad
abstract: Multidisciplinary teams are often a necessity for software projects as they provide the required expertise to effectively solve complex problems. However, efficient collaboration between teams with different disciplines is challenging due to several factors such as considering gaps in knowledge areas, establishing a development process, and understanding different requirements from various groups or stakeholders. The agile methodology, such as scrum, offers a powerful approach to managing the software development process effectively. As part of the agile methodology, some techniques and tools are used to manage requirements change, which is a common practice in multidisciplinary teams. This research aims to leverage process-mining techniques to analyze data from Jira and GitHub to analyze the efficacy of software development process, particularly in multidisciplinary teams. This approach is applied to a case study of a virtual healthcare intervention system to measure the team’s productivity. The results indicate several deficiencies in the process with respect to requirements engineering task that cause loss of time and increase rework rates. Results indicate that there are some challenges in the development process that contribute to some deficiencies. The rework rate is high and the number of tasks that are intended to be completed is less than what was planned. These factors can contribute to the lengthening of the software development process. Most of these challenges can be addressed by improving the requirement engineering process in order to obtain the requirements and manage change requests more efficiently.
venue: 2022 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
human_qa_notes: Text extraction clean and complete; no formal threats-to-validity section; the study primarily used descriptive Jira/GitHub metrics rather than a specific process-discovery algorithm (ProM/Disco use is deferred to future work).
human_research_question: How can process mining techniques (analyzing Jira and GitHub data) be used to evaluate the efficacy of the software development process, particularly requirements engineering, in a multidisciplinary agile team?
human_main_finding: Applying process-oriented analysis of Jira/GitHub data (rework rate, time-to-market, backlog flow) to a real multidisciplinary healthcare software project (Robin's Nest) revealed significant requirements-engineering deficiencies, including high rework rates and delays caused by ineffective communication and insufficient shared domain knowledge.

title: Towards goal-oriented conformance checking
abstract: Constructing a business process is important area between requirements engineering and business process management. Goal-oriented requirements analysis method is widely researched in requirements engineering and useful for reflecting organizational requirements to business process models, but actual business processes deviate from defined process models. Therefore, it is not sufficient for business process analysis only using model’s information. It is important to analyze actual conducted business process logged data. Analyzing business process logged data is called process mining and detecting differences between models and logs is called conformance checking. A lot of conformance checking approaches mainly focus on process aspects of business process, but this is not sufficient for analysis whether actual business processes can satisfy organizational goals. In this paper, we propose a goal-oriented conformance checking approach which can detect deviations between logs and models, and can analyze the effects of the deviation. It is useful for evaluation of the detected deviation. We represent the effectiveness of our approach conducting a case study using the publicly available log.
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering Seke
human_qa_notes: Short 2-page SEKE conference paper; domain is a general business process (phone repair) rather than a software-engineering-specific process, so QA2 scored 0; no threats-to-validity discussion and no fitness/precision-style model quality metric (only statistical significance/effect-size values), so QA6 and QA8 scored 0; the event log used is publicly available (QA7=1).
human_research_question: Can conformance checking be extended with goal models (using linear temporal logic and statistical analysis) to detect deviations between event logs and organizational goals and evaluate whether such deviations have positive or negative effects on higher-priority goals?
human_main_finding: A two-phase goal-oriented conformance checking approach (LTL-based goal-trace filtering plus chi-squared/Fisher's exact statistical analysis) applied to a public phone-repair-process event log successfully detected significant deviations between goals and quantified their effects on higher-priority goals (e.g., failing the low-repair-numbers goal had a significant negative effect, effect=-0.903, on the repair-completion goal).
human_limitations: not stated

title: A CSP-Theoretic framework of checking conformance of business processes
abstract: In this paper, we tackle the problem of conformance checking which verifies if the event logs (observed) match/fit the reference (arbitrary) process. We use concepts from Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP), which facilitates automated analysis using PAT toolkit. By this technique one can identify all the logs which cannot be properly replayed on the process. We illustrate our approach with an example. Finally, we introduce some metrics based on conformance checking. They are related to fitness, closeness, and appropriateness of the event logs vis-a-vis reference process models.
venue: Proceedings Asia Pacific Software Engineering Conference APSEC
human_qa_notes: IEEE APSEC 2012 CSP/PAT conformance-checking paper; running example is bank account-opening and the 50 InFlux models are from general business domains, so QA2 scored 0 (not an SE-specific process context). QA4/QA8 scored 1 (named conformance checking via CSP trace refinement; fitness, closeness, structural/behavioural appropriateness in Table IV). QA6/QA7 scored 0: no threats-to-validity discussion and no public logs/code (in-house InFlux + PAT). FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (generic BPM conformance, not software-engineering processes).
human_research_question: How can Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) and automated trace-refinement checking in PAT verify whether MXML event logs conform to arbitrary/unstructured BPMN-style reference processes, and what fitness, closeness and appropriateness metrics can be derived from the resulting counterexamples?
human_main_finding: Translating BPMN processes and logs into trace-equivalent CSP processes reduces conformance to PAT trace-refinement, identifying all non-replayable traces; on 50 InFlux industrial models checking is fast (mean analysis time 0.034–0.044s); on the bank-account running example, logs 1–2 have fitness/closeness 1.0 while noisy log 3 has fitness 0.886 and closeness 0.389, with structural appropriateness 0.607.
human_limitations: Exceptions are not handled; checking whether the model conforms to the log fails on infinite traces; the 50-model experiment uses CPN-generated logs (with injected noise) rather than independently observed field logs; CSP encodings can be complex, though they are hidden from the end user.

title: An Approach for Face Validity Assessment of Agent-Based Simulation Models Through Outlier Detection with Process Mining
abstract: When designing simulations, the objective is to create a representation of a real-world system or process to understand, analyze, predict, or improve its behavior. Typically, the first step in assessing the credibility of a simulation model for its intended purpose involves conducting a face validity check. This entails a subjective assessment by individuals knowledgeable about the system to determine if the model appears plausible. The emerging field of process mining can aid in the face validity assessment process by extracting process models and insights from event logs generated by the system being simulated. Process mining techniques, combined with the visual representation of discovered process models, offer a novel approach for experts to evaluate the validity and behavior of simulation models. In this context, outliers can play a key role in evaluating the face validity of simulation models by drawing attention to unusual behaviors that can either raise doubts about or reinforce the model’s credibility in capturing the full range of behaviors present in the real world. Outliers can provide valuable information that can help identify concerns, prompt improvements, and ultimately enhance the validity of the simulation model. In this paper, we propose an approach that uses process mining techniques to detect outlier behaviors in agent-based simulation models with the aim of utilizing this information for evaluating face validity of simulation models. We illustrate our approach using the Schelling segregation model.</p
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Well-documented case study with explicit threats-to-validity discussion, but the application domain is agent-based social simulation (Schelling segregation model), not software engineering, so QA2 is not met; fitness/precision are mentioned only as generic selection criteria, not reported as actual computed values, and no code repository is given for the modified implementation.
human_research_question: Can process mining techniques (e.g., Fuzzy Miner discovery, filtering/outlier analysis) be used to detect outlier behaviors in agent-based simulation (ABS) models and thereby support human-expert face validity assessment of such models?
human_main_finding: Applying process mining (Fuzzy Miner via Disco) to event logs from the Schelling segregation ABS model enabled animation, output, and immersive assessment techniques that helped a human expert identify both plausible and implausible model behaviors (e.g., unrealistic movement timing, simultaneous agent moves), demonstrating that process-mining-based outlier detection can meaningfully support face validity assessment of ABS models.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly state the study relied on a single expert's subjective judgment, covered only a limited set of scenarios and techniques (restricting generalizability), and that iteration/refinement plus application to a real-world dataset remain future work.

title: Assisting developers towards fault localization by analyzing failure reports
abstract: Large software applications encompass many components with complex interdependencies. When a failure occurs, developers usually have limited information and time in their disposal for localizing the root cause of the observed failure. The most common information developers have readily access to includes failure reports, stack traces, and event logs. In this context, a major challenge is to devise techniques that assist developers utilize this information in order to zero-in their focus on specific methods that have a high probability of containing the root cause of the observed failure. Once such an initial set of methods has been identified, other more elaborate, complex, and computationally expensive data flow analyses could be applied. In this paper, we present a technique which aims to identify such an initial set of suspicious methods by first, retrieving information from failure reports obtained from Bugzilla repositories, second by combining this information with graph models that denote actual dependencies obtained from the subject system's source code in order to create an hypothesis space and third, by applying a ranking score to identify methods that have high likelihood of containing the root cause. The technique is shown to be tractable when applied to systems with several thousands of source code methods and the results exhibit high accuracy.
venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual International Conference on Computer Science and Software Engineering Cascon 2017

title: Interactive creation, visualization, and exploration of process model collections
venue: Software and Systems Modeling

title: A method for stochastic modeling the software development process in constrained resource environments
abstract: Process Improvement requires a formal process definition and associated measures of performance. Processes can then be diagnosed in order to formulate hypotheses on where changes should be made. Subsequently, new processes can be conceived, and developers can check whether the desired improvements have actually been achieved. Simulation is a powerful low-cost tool for diagnosis and test of several improvement alternatives, prior to field tests. This paper presents a UML-based method to obtain the probability distribution of the execution time of a large variety of business processes, including software development. Such a method, which is based on Monte Carlo simulation, allows for the identification of factors that most strongly influence process execution time, favoring changes that increase process efficiency with considerable impact on the deployment of business tactics and strategies.
venue: Proceedings of the 2008 IEEE Systems and Information Engineering Design Symposium Sieds 2008
human_qa_notes: IEEE two-column extract is complete and readable (minor hyphenation); QA3/QA5 scored 0 because Section V is only a constructed Incremental-Development illustration with assumed triangular PDFs, not a real project log; no threats-to-validity discussion, no shared data/code, and the KS bound is a Monte Carlo sample-size rule rather than a process-model quality metric.
human_research_question: How can a UML Activity-Diagram well-formed process model, combined with Monte Carlo sampling of resource-constrained deterministic activity networks, yield the probability distribution of software-development-process duration when resources are constrained and activities may loop?
human_main_finding: A restricted UML Activity-Diagram WFP plus Monte Carlo GenerateDAN/ScheduleDAN (heuristic RCPSP scheduling) produces an empirical PDF/CDF of SDP duration; on an illustrative four-package Incremental Development example, 4,649 scenarios give 1,810 ± 36.2 hours (227 ± 5 calendar days) at 95% confidence and 2% KS error.
human_limitations: Assumes the SDP can be expressed as a well-formed process and that business allocation policy maps to a single priority heuristic; uses a restricted UML subset; demonstrated only on a constructed example with assumed activity PDFs, with no comparison of predicted versus observed durations.

title: COLORED PETRI NETS SIMULATION ON THE CLOUD WITH PYTHON: A FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW
venue: Icic Express Letters Part B Applications
human_qa_notes: Framework-overview paper for a container-terminal (manufacturing/logistics) use case, not software engineering, so QA2 is not met; no public dataset/code and no formal threats-to-validity section, though the paper does state key assumptions/limitations and uses an explicit distribution-fitness test (KS-test).
human_research_question: How can an automatic, modular, cloud-based Colored Petri Net simulation model generator be built in Python that discovers process flow and resource assignment from event logs using process mining techniques, while allowing flexible plug-in of custom (e.g., machine-learning) components?
human_main_finding: The proposed Python/CoreUI-React cloud framework can automatically generate a Colored-Petri-Net-based discrete-event simulation model from an uploaded event log (process flow via process mining, resource assignment via organizational/social-network mining, KS-test-based time distributions) with a modular plug/unplug mechanism; applied to container-terminal operation data, simulated container throughput under default settings was within about 5% of the real baseline, and resource-configuration experiments correctly identified the bottleneck resource.
human_limitations: Authors note a security limitation of the plug-in mechanism (loading arbitrary pickled Python objects without safety checks) and that the approach assumes the input event log fully and accurately represents real operations; no dataset/code availability is provided.

title: Monitoring a CI/CD Workflow Using Process Mining
venue: SN Computer Science
human_qa_notes: Full text (Springer SN Computer Science article) reads cleanly with no OCR noise; QA6/QA7/QA8 scored 0 because there is no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, the industrial CI/CD event data and code are not released, and no fitness/precision/F1-style model-quality metric is reported (only frequency counts of pipeline stage transitions).
human_research_question: How can Apache Kafka be used to integrate and normalize heterogeneous CI/CD event logs in near real time so that process mining (discovery/conformance) techniques can be applied to monitor and improve an organization's CI/CD workflow?
human_main_finding: Applying the heuristics miner to Kafka-normalized CI/CD event logs from a large e-commerce company's Jenkins/GitLab pipelines revealed a 'deceiving perception' of CI/CD as an orderly sequence: it exposed pipeline misconfigurations, undocumented/anomalous stages (e.g., builds bypassing QA/UAT), and missing metadata, demonstrating that process mining plus streaming integration gives actionable observability of real-world DevOps pipelines.
human_limitations: The study covers only discovery-based monitoring (Jan-May 2020) at one company's specific tool stack; full real-time conformance checking is explicitly left as future/ongoing work, and metrics such as feature-branch lead time are only available for Git/GitLab projects, not for SVN-based trunk development.

title: Architecture of process mining based business process optimization
abstract: The optimization of processes of business guarantees the successes of informationization project. Although its importance is fully recognized, it never obtains sufficient study. This paper first discuss the current business process optimization methods, they are classified into three type: participation-type, principle-type and analytical-type. Then, architecture of process mining based business process optimization is proposed. According to this architecture, the subset of information that is relevant for process mining or analysis is extracted from a variety of business process system. This information is then modelled in certain of expression. Based on the model, hidden relationship and unknown knowledge about business processes are extracted and stored in the form of business knowledge model. With the help of the acquired business knowledge, business process can be optimized both on macro structure level through case based reasoning and on micro parameter level through process simulation and linear programming. Business process performance measurement system is employed in the architecture to check effect of optimization. Finally, key issues in this architecture are discussed.
venue: Iet Conference Publications
human_qa_notes: Purely conceptual/position paper proposing an architecture, with no implementation, dataset, case study, or empirical validation, and no SE-specific context (general business-process-management/ERP focus); consequently almost all QA criteria score 0.
human_research_question: What architecture is needed to integrate process mining into business process optimization (BPO), spanning data extraction, business-knowledge representation, and both macro- and micro-level process optimization?
human_main_finding: The paper proposes a conceptual architecture for process-mining-based business process optimization, integrating an adapter layer for extracting business-process data, a business-knowledge representation model, and a performance-measurement system, combining macro-level (case-based reasoning) and micro-level (simulation, linear programming) optimization; no implementation or case study is provided.
human_limitations: The authors frame several core issues (business-process data modelling, the knowledge representation model, and the process mining method itself) as open research challenges/future work rather than presenting them as limitations of an implemented system.

title: Discovering simulation models
abstract: Process mining is a tool to extract non-trivial and useful information from process execution logs. These so-called event logs (also called audit trails, or transaction logs) are the starting point for various discovery and analysis techniques that help to gain insight into certain characteristics of the process. In this paper we use a combination of process mining techniques to discover multiple perspectives (namely, the control-flow, data, performance, and resource perspective) of the process from historic data, and we integrate them into a comprehensive simulation model. This simulation model is represented as a colored Petri net (CPN) and can be used to analyze the process, e.g., evaluate the performance of different alternative designs. The discovery of simulation models is explained using a running example. Moreover, the approach has been applied in two case studies; the workflows in two different municipalities in the Netherlands have been analyzed using a combination of process mining and simulation. Furthermore, the quality of the CPN models generated for the running example and the two case studies has been evaluated by comparing the original logs with the logs of the generated models.
venue: Information Systems
human_qa_notes: Clean text; rigorous methodological paper with an open, downloadable running-example dataset and tool (ProM) and two real-life case studies, but the empirical case studies are municipal government processes (complaint/invoice handling), not a software engineering process, so QA2 scored low.
human_research_question: Can multiple process-mining perspectives (control-flow, data, performance, organizational) be automatically discovered from event logs and integrated into a single Colored Petri Net simulation model that accurately reproduces the original process's behavior?
human_main_finding: Combining control-flow, decision, performance, and organizational-perspective process mining into an integrated Colored Petri Net simulation model (via the ProM/CPN Tools pipeline) allowed automatic simulation-model discovery; a "second pass" evaluation on an artificial running example and two real-life Dutch municipality case studies (complaint handling, invoice handling) showed the generated models reproduced the original control-flow, data, and performance characteristics with high fidelity (e.g., 100% fitness).
human_limitations: The authors note that human/resource behavior is imperfectly captured because people work part-time across multiple concurrent processes, requiring an ad hoc addition of extra waiting time that does not truly reflect real working patterns; they also note the evaluation approach does not address the validity of the underlying log data itself.

title: Process mining framework for software processes
abstract: Software development processes are often not explicitly modelled and sometimes even chaotic. In order to keep track of the involved documents and files, engineers use Software Configuration Management (SCM) systems. Along the way, those systems collect and store information on the software process itself. Thus, SCM information can be used for constructing explicit process models, which is called software process mining. In this paper we show that (1) a Process Mining Framework can be used for obtaining software process models as well as for analysing and optimising them; (2) an algorithmic approach, which arose from our research on software processes, is integrated in the framework
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science Including Subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics
human_qa_notes: Well-known process-mining/software-engineering paper demonstrating the ProM framework on real ArgoUML SVN logs; tools (ProM, ProMImport) and the ArgoUML repository are publicly available, but no explicit numeric process-model quality metrics (fitness/precision) or dedicated threats-to-validity section are reported.
human_research_question: How can process mining techniques and the ProM framework be applied to Software Configuration Management (SCM) system logs (e.g., Subversion/CVS) to automatically discover, analyze, and verify explicit software development process models across control-flow, organizational, and informational perspectives?
human_main_finding: Applying the ProM process mining framework (via a two-step transition-system-generation-and-Petri-net-synthesis approach, plus Alpha/Heuristics/Genetic Miner alternatives) to real Subversion commit logs from the ArgoUML open-source project produced plausible software-development process models, and enabled further performance analysis, conformance checking, LTL-based rule checking, and social network analysis of developer collaboration (e.g., detecting a developer who both wrote source code and tests, violating a separation-of-duties constraint).
human_limitations: The generation-and-synthesis approach struggles to handle noise (incorrectly logged events/exceptions) in the log; the paper demonstrates the tool/methodology on a single project rather than providing a broad empirical validation, and no formal threats-to-validity discussion is included.

title: Predicting Issue Handling Process using Case Attributes and Categorical Variable Encoding Techniques
abstract: Software development process deals with the increasing complexity, needs for enhancement, and the reduction of bugs. The software project managers have a responsibility to maintain the software quality, e.g., by establishing Service Level Agreement (SLA) to the software development. However, there are difficulties to monitor SLA and to predict the software quality, due to a lot of issues should be handled. This work proposed prediction techniques for handling issues in the software development by using historical data from software repositories. There are two types of predictions in this work, namely 1) prediction of the remaining duration, and 2) prediction of the next activities. Event logs extracted from historical data in the software repositories exploited case and event attributes as predictors. Furthermore, the categorical variable encoding technique used in the preprocessing data phase. Some categorical variable encoding techniques also proposed in this study. The results showed that the use of case attributes as predictors could improve performance by 8.57% in the next activity prediction and 1.9% in the remaining duration prediction. Of the 4 (four) categorical variable encoding techniques used, one-hot encoding and sum encoding techniques can provide the best remaining duration prediction with a MAE of 19.72 and one-hot encoding technique can provide the best next activity prediction with an accuracy of 65.38%. All of these methods are widely evaluated using datasets from the Google Chromium Project. Further work including utilization of other attributes outside case and event attributes, e.g., component attributes, as predictor variables.
venue: 2019 International Conference on Data and Software Engineering (ICoDSE)
human_qa_notes: Empirically solid study using a real, citable open-source dataset (Google Chromium issue log) with clear quantitative metrics (MAE, accuracy); no explicit threats-to-validity discussion and no stated code/data release for the extended (crawled) dataset used in this specific study.
human_research_question: Does incorporating case attributes (in addition to event attributes) and different categorical variable encoding techniques improve prediction of remaining issue-handling duration and next activity in software issue-tracking processes?
human_main_finding: Using case attributes alongside event attributes improves next-activity prediction accuracy by 8.57% and remaining-duration prediction by 1.9%; one-hot encoding (and sum encoding) achieved the best overall predictive performance (MAE 19.72 days for duration; 65.38% accuracy for next activity) on the Google Chromium issue-tracking log.
human_limitations: The original public dataset lacked case attributes, requiring the authors to supplement it via manual web crawling; future work is suggested to use additional predictor attributes (e.g., component, resource) and to evaluate on other data sources.

title: Remaining activity sequence prediction for ongoing process instances
abstract: Remaining activity sequence prediction (i.e. activity suffix prediction) aims at recommending the most likely future behaviors for ongoing process instances (i.e. traces), which enables process managers to rationally allocate resources and detect process deviations in advance. Recently, techniques of neural networks have found promising applications in activity suffix prediction by training a prediction model for next activity and iteratively performing the model to achieve the whole sequence prediction. However, the iterative prediction accumulates the deviations of each iteration and the result also lacks interpretability. In this paper, we propose a novel method to predict activity suffixes from the perspective of control flow and data flow for ongoing traces, where process discovery and trace replay techniques are employed to simulate executions of traces under real conditions and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is applied to characterize the correlation between executed information and future execution. Sequence matching between historical prefix traces and ongoing traces is performed based on the above information to select the optimal-matched (i.e. most similar) activity suffix for ongoing process instances. Experiments on real-life datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms other methods.
venue: Proceedings of the International Conference on Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering Seke
human_qa_notes: Clean text extraction with math notation reasonably preserved (minor OCR artifacts in special symbols); no explicit threats-to-validity discussion, typical of a short SEKE conference paper.
human_research_question: How can the remaining activity sequence (activity suffix) for ongoing process instances be predicted more accurately and interpretably than existing iterative next-activity-prediction methods, by combining process discovery/trace replay with LSTM-based data-context prediction and sequence matching?
human_main_finding: The proposed method, combining Inductive-Miner-based trace replay (control flow) with LSTM-predicted data context, outperforms most state-of-the-art neural-network-based activity suffix prediction methods on real-life event logs (Helpdesk, Sepsis, BPIC2012W) as measured by Damerau-Levenshtein similarity, though performance degrades on datasets with low trace diversity or many self-loops.
human_limitations: Authors note performance depends on dataset characteristics (low Coincidence Degree, self-loops reduce accuracy, e.g. BPIC2012W_Complete), and the current work addresses only activity suffix prediction, leaving prediction of other attributes (resource, time) as future work.

title: Detecting Bottleneck and Fraud in Agile Development by using Petri net Performance and Trace Clustering
authors: Razi, Muhammad Ar; Sungkono, Kelly Rossa; Sarno, Riyanarto; Wahyuni, Cahyaningtyas Sekar
abstract: Software Development Life Cycle model is one of the basic idea of the software development. SDLC is a continuous process, the cycle starts from the moment when it is decide to release the project, and it ends when its full remove from the exploitation. Agile is one of the mostly used SDLC models. Combination of incremental and iterative process models with a focus on process customer satisfaction and can adapt to rapid delivery of working sofware is called Agile SDLC. This contribution of this paper is evaluating the performance, such as occurring bottleneck and fraud, of an Agile model to handle the management of the project. This paper uses Petri net to analyze Agile SDLC model performance. The petri net use to detect the bottleneck that occur in the model. If an event has longer waiting time tahen others, it can identify that the bottleneck occur in that task. Then, the fraud is detected based on trace clustering. Based on the experiment, the cluster which has lowest member is indicates as fraud processes.
venue: 2019 International Seminar on Application for Technology of Information and Communication (iSemantic)
human_qa_notes: Short 5-page conference paper with clean text; dataset is a small simulated/synthetic Agile-model event log (21 traces total) generated via ProcessMaker rather than real project data, which limits empirical strength despite the case-study framing; no threats-to-validity discussion, no data/code availability, and no fitness/precision-style metric reported.
human_research_question: Can Petri-net-based performance analysis (bottleneck detection) combined with alpha-algorithm process mining and trace clustering (fraud detection) identify bottlenecks and anomalous traces in an Agile software development process event log?
human_main_finding: Applying the Alpha mining algorithm and Petri net performance analysis to a simulated Agile SDLC event log identified bottlenecks concentrated around decision-making/validation stages (especially the development stage), while trace clustering separated the 21 traces into a 16-trace 'complete process' cluster and a 5-trace cluster of short/incomplete traces flagged as likely fraud.
human_limitations: not stated

title: Generating transition probabilities for automatic model-based test generation
abstract: Markov chains with Labelled Transitions can be used to generate test cases in a model-based approach. These test cases are generated by random walks on the model according to probabilities associated with transitions. When these probabilities correspond to a usage profile, reliability may be estimated. However, in early stages of development, such probabilities are not easy to determine, thus default profiles must be considered. In such a case it may be interesting to target some coverage criteria rather to use classical uniform probability generation approach. In this paper we enrich an existing industrial tool based on usage profile with 3 possibilities to create default profiles that improve transition coverage. We report experiments that compare the improvement of the coverage rates by our approaches with respect to uniform probabilities on transitions from a given state, which is the current default profile.
venue: Icst 2010 3rd International Conference on Software Testing Verification and Validation
human_qa_notes: Solid industrial experiment on a real client model comparing Markov-chain-based test-profile generation algorithms; no formal threats-to-validity section, no shared data/code (proprietary MaTeLo tool and client model), and reported results are test coverage rates rather than PM fitness/precision-style metrics.
human_research_question: How can default transition-probability profiles be automatically generated for Markov-chain-based model-based test generation (in the MaTeLo tool) to improve state/transition coverage compared to the current uniform-probability default, especially for models containing cycles?
human_main_finding: Three proposed profile-generation algorithms (adapted Chinese Postman Problem, adapted Chow's algorithm, and a new cycle-aware traversal method) all achieved significantly better state and transition coverage than the existing uniform-probability default on a real 1500-state/2500-transition industrial client model (e.g., 80% transition coverage with 15,000 tests vs. 30,000+ for the baseline), with the Chinese-Postman variant converging fastest but producing fewer, longer test cases.
human_limitations: The paper notes the Chinese Postman solution's longer test cases are impractical for some clients with constraints on test length, and that the difference between the three proposed solutions is not very significant.
