title: Stochastic actor-oriented modeling for studying homophily and social influence in OSS projects
venue: Empirical Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Rigorous, well-documented empirical SE paper explicitly targeting homophily vs. social-influence in OSS developer networks using stochastic actor-oriented models (SIENA); public data/scripts, explicit 'Threats to Validity' section, and goodness-of-fit validation of the stochastic model.
human_research_question: Can stochastic actor-oriented models (SAOMs) be used to disentangle social selection (homophily) from social influence (contagion) in the co-evolution of developer social networks (email communication) and technical behaviors (commit rate, code ownership, minor contribution) in OSS projects?
human_main_finding: Using SAOMs (via SIENA) on two Apache Software Foundation projects (Ant, Axis2/Java), the authors found significant social selection (homophily) effects for code-ownership and productivity behaviors in both projects (positive in Axis2/Java, negative in Ant), but found no evidence of social influence (behavior spreading through network ties) for any behavior in either project.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly discuss threats to validity: case studies limited to ASF (a tightly-knit community, likely capturing less variance than the full OSS space), simplifying assumptions in constructing email networks (e.g., only thread-response pairs counted as ties, ignoring other communication channels like IRC), and uncertainty in SAOM-specific modeling choices (wave count/spacing, social-interaction decay function) given SAOM's novel application outside traditional sociological survey data.

title: Simod: A tool for automated discovery of business process simulation models
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Short, digital-native LNCS tool-demo paper, no OCR issues; QA2 scored 0 because the tool and its three evaluation logs (purchase-to-pay, academic credentials recognition, manufacturing production) are generic business processes, not software engineering; QA8 credited because Simod quantifies similarity between simulated and real logs via a (Damerau-Levenshtein + time-penalty) distance metric functioning as a model-quality score.
human_research_question: Can a tool (Simod) automatically discover an accurate business process simulation model directly from an event log, by combining automated process discovery, conformance-based log repair, simulation-parameter extraction, and Bayesian hyperparameter optimization?
human_main_finding: Simod automatically produces BIMP-executable simulation models from an XES/MXML event log by combining SplitMiner-based control-flow discovery, trace-alignment-based conformance repair, and Bayesian-optimized parameter extraction, and was shown on one synthetic and two real-life logs to reproduce process performance measures similar to those observed in the original logs.
human_limitations: The accuracy of the generated simulation model is inherently limited by the accuracy of the discovered process model and by the pre-processing parameters chosen; this first version supports only the SplitMiner discovery algorithm and the BIMP simulator, with the use of multiple mining algorithms left as future work.

title: The review linkage graph for code review analytics: A recovery approach and empirical study
abstract: Modern Code Review (MCR) is a pillar of contemporary quality assurance approaches, where developers discuss and improve code changes prior to integration. Since review interactions (e.g., comments, revisions) are archived, analytics approaches like reviewer recommendation and review outcome prediction have been proposed to support the MCR process. These approaches assume that reviews evolve and are adjudicated independently; yet in practice, reviews can be interdependent. In this paper, we set out to better understand the impact of review linkage on code review analytics. To do so, we extract review linkage graphs where nodes represent reviews, while edges represent recovered links between reviews. Through a quantitative analysis of six software communities, we observe that (a) linked reviews occur regularly, with linked review rates of 25% in OpenStack, 17% in Chromium, and 3%–8% in Android, Qt, Eclipse, and Libreoffice; and (b) linkage has become more prevalent over time. Through qualitative analysis, we discover that links span 16 types that belong to five categories. To automate link category recovery, we train classifiers to label links according to the surrounding document content. Those classifiers achieve F1-scores of 0.71–0.79, at least doubling the F1-scores of a ZeroR baseline. Finally, we show that the F1-scores of reviewer recommenders can be improved by 37%–88% (5–14 percentage points) by incorporating information from linked reviews that is available at prediction time. Indeed, review linkage should be exploited by future code review analytics.
venue: Esec Fse 2019 Proceedings of the 2019 27th ACM Joint Meeting European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean ESEC/FSE'19 extraction; six Gerrit communities with Table 1 counts, GitHub replication package, and an explicit Threats to Validity section. QA4 scored 0: review-linkage-graph recovery plus TF-IDF classifiers is MSR/traceability, not a named process-mining or stochastic-modeling technique. QA8 scored 1 for reported precision/recall/F1/AUC of link-category classifiers and reviewer recommenders. FLAG: borderline SLR inclusion (code-review analytics / artefact linkage, not PM or stochastic process models).
human_research_question: To what degree are modern code reviews linked, why are they linked, can link categories be recovered automatically from surrounding text, and does using linked-review information available at prediction time improve reviewer recommendation and review-outcome prediction?
human_main_finding: Among 1.47M Gerrit reviews, linkage rates range from 3% to 25% (25% OpenStack, 17% Chromium) and 16 link types fall into five categories; classifiers recover categories with F1 0.71–0.79 (more than double ZeroR); adding linkage awareness improves cHRev reviewer-recommender F1 by 37–88% (5–14 percentage points), while outcome predictors misclassify 35–39% of linked reviews.
human_limitations: Regex recovery may miss or falsely extract links (manual false-positive rate <0.1% in the coded sample); open coding is subjective despite dual-coder agreement; classifiers and impact analyses focus on OpenStack Nova/Neutron and may not generalise to all Gerrit or non-Gerrit review environments.

title: Software reliability modelling and prediction with hidden Markov chains
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to use the framework of hidden Markov chains (HMCs) for the modelling of the failure and debugging process of software, and the prediction of software reliability. The model parameters are estimated using the forward-backward expectation maximization algorithm, and model selection is done with the Bayesian information criterion. The advantages and drawbacks of this approach, with respect to usual modelling, are analysed. Comparison is also done on real software failure data. The main contribution of HMC modelling is that it highlights the existence of homogeneous periods in the debugging process, which allow one to identify major corrections or version updates. In terms of reliability predictions, the HMC model performs well, on average, with respect to usual models, especially when the reliability is not regularly growing.
venue: Statistical Modelling
human_qa_notes: CRITICAL CAVEAT: this fulltext extraction is severely corrupted (garbled font/encoding throughout most of the mathematical and prose body, not a clean OCR), so most equations and detailed argumentation could not be read directly; assessment relies on the readable abstract, section headers, figure/table captions (named 'M' and 'C' series real software-failure datasets, 'restored hidden states', AIC comparison table) and partially legible discussion/conclusion text, so QA1-QA8 judgments are lower-confidence than for cleanly extracted papers.
human_research_question: Can a Hidden Markov Chain model of the software fault-detection process, which explicitly represents homogeneous 'debugging phases' via hidden states, provide better reliability predictions than standard (non-hidden) software reliability growth models when applied to real software failure datasets?
human_main_finding: A Hidden Markov Chain (HMM) model of software reliability, with parameters estimated via a forward-backward EM algorithm and AIC-based model selection, is compared against standard software reliability growth models (Goel-Okumoto, Musa-Okumoto, Littlewood-Verrall, etc.) on roughly 20 real software failure datasets; the HMM approach best reveals homogeneous debugging phases via its restored hidden states and gives the best predictive validity for datasets with irregular/non-monotonic reliability growth, though it performs only comparably to standard models on average and can have poor predictive validity in some cases.
human_limitations: The (partially legible) discussion notes that HMM predictive validity can be very poor in some cases because, in the Q-Q-plot predictive method, parameter/model estimates are computed sequentially and the selected hidden-state model can change as more data becomes available; usual (non-hidden) models perform comparably or better except when real homogeneous debugging periods and imperfect debugging are present.

title: Enhancing information technology project portfolio management with agile principles and Kanban practices
abstract: PurposeThis study addresses the challenges in information technology project portfolio management (IT PPM) organizations face, particularly in dynamic and competitive markets. It proposes a customized model inspired by agile principles and Kanban practices to improve IT PPM processes in a case study bank in Türkiye. The research seeks to enhance responsiveness, efficiency and alignment with business objectives, filling gaps in existing literature.Design/methodology/approachThe study employed a design science research approach. Initial issues were identified through process mining and focus group discussions with IT and business experts. The solution model was iteratively developed and refined based on agile principles and Kanban practices, with benchmarking with other organizations and expert feedback. The evaluation involved multiple stakeholders, including high-level managers and quality teams.FindingsThe proposed model demonstrated improvements in demand visibility, prioritization and capacity management. Key solutions included work-in-progress (WIP) limits, frequent evaluations and the integration of Kanban for enhanced transparency and adaptability. The model also addressed reduced bottlenecks and increased flexibility in managing IT project demands, although challenges like cultural shifts and complexity remained.Originality/valueThis research contributes to the literature on agile IT PPM by proposing a practical model that integrates agile principles and Kanban practices. It highlights the applicability of Kanban at the portfolio level and provides insights into addressing common IT PPM issues in large organizations, offering a replicable framework for similar sectors globally.
venue: International Journal of Managing Projects in Business

title: Mining reuse processes
venue: Cibse 2014 Proceedings of the 17th Ibero American Conference Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Clean text; the most thorough and rigorous document in this batch (full MSc dissertation) - real open-source case studies, explicit precision/recall metrics, dedicated threats-to-validity and limitations sections, and open-source underlying tools/data.
human_research_question: Can a process-mining-based approach (Reuse Miner) automatically discover object-oriented framework instantiation processes from existing application source code, represented executably in the Reuse Description Language (RDL)?
human_main_finding: Reuse Miner, applying heuristics-miner process discovery and RPST-based translation to event logs mined from GEF and Graphiti framework applications (including GitHub-sourced repositories), successfully generated executable RDL instantiation processes with generally high precision/recall against manually created reference processes, though results degraded (overfitting/"spaghetti" processes) when input applications were too few or too heterogeneous.
human_limitations: The dissertation includes a dedicated Threats to Validity section covering the manual construction of reference RDL scripts, a small/non-diverse sample of input applications causing overfitting, and the subjectivity of the precision/recall penalty factor; the Limitations/Future Work section also notes the pipeline requires substantial manual interaction with the ProM tool and does not fully automate repeated process discovery across sub-processes.

title: Intelligent agile method framework
abstract: Abstract: The paper addresses the problem of the low usage of software development methods in software development practice. This has been recognized as one of the key reasons for failures in software development projects and a contributor to the low quality of software. We introduce a novel approach that could help to improve the maturity of software development processes. The approach is based on the method engineering principles taking into account the limitations that hinder its use in practice. The main objective of our research is to show that the method engineering concepts are applicable in real settings and that could contribute to the higher quality of software development processes and their products. 1
venue: Enase 2013 Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Evaluation of Novel Approaches to Software Engineering
human_qa_notes: Forward-looking position/proposal paper (ENASE 2013) describing planned future research phases (initiation, implementation, testing, evaluation) rather than reporting completed empirical work; the authors explicitly state drawing conclusions now would be 'premature and risky', so most QA criteria requiring data, validation, or reproducibility are unmet by design.
human_research_question: How can a novel 'Intelligent Agile Method Framework' (iAMF) — combining situational method engineering with process/intention mining of developers' real actions via revision-control-system logs — help software companies capture, follow, and continuously improve the development methods they actually use in practice, raising process maturity and reducing project failures?
human_main_finding: This position/research-proposal paper introduces the 'Intelligent Agile Method Framework' (iAMF) concept and toolset architecture, which aims to mine developers' actual revision-control-system actions to document a company's real 'base method,' detect and guide deviations from it, and iteratively raise software process maturity toward CMMI levels 3-5; no empirical results are reported, as evaluation had not yet been conducted at time of writing.
human_limitations: The authors explicitly acknowledge the research is longitudinal and evaluation-dependent, with no empirical results available at time of publication; the framework had not yet been tested or evaluated with real companies, and hypotheses (H1-H4) about developer adoption and maturity improvement remain unconfirmed.

title: Optimal test profile in the context of software cybernetics
abstract: Software cybernetics explores the interplay between software theory/engineering and control theory/engineering Following the idea of software cybernetics, the controlled Markov chains (CMC) approach to software testing treats software testing as a control problem. The software under test serves as a controlled object, and the (optimal) testing strategy determined by the theory of controlled Markov chains serves as a controller. The software under test and the corresponding (optimal) testing strategy constitute a closed-loop feedback system, and the software state transitions behave as a Markov chain. The paper analyzes the behavior of the corresponding optimal test profile determined by the CMC approach to software testing. It is shown that in some cases the optimal test profile is Markovian, whereas in some other cases the optimal test profile demonstrates a different scenario. The analyses presented in the paper deepen our understanding of the CMC approach to software testing and are related to software operational profile modeling.
venue: Proceedings 2nd Asia Pacific Conference on Quality Software Apaqs 2001
human_qa_notes: Purely theoretical/mathematical paper with only illustrative toy numeric examples (no real testing data or empirical case study); no reproducibility artifacts or threats-to-validity discussion.
human_research_question: Under the controlled Markov chains (CMC) approach to software testing, does the resulting optimal test profile (the sequence of chosen test actions) itself form a Markov chain, given that the corresponding software state transitions do?
human_main_finding: The paper proves that while software state transitions under an optimal CMC testing strategy always form a Markov chain, the optimal test profile (sequence of actions) is Markovian only under specific structural conditions (e.g., a contiguous block of states at the start or end mapping to one identical action while all other states map to unique actions); otherwise it is generally non-Markovian.
human_limitations: The authors state that the general non-Markovian conclusion for cases not satisfying the identified structural conditions 'needs further mathematical justification,' indicating the analysis is not fully proven for all cases.

title: Static and dynamic architecture conformance checking: A systematic, case study-based analysis on tradeoffs and synergies
venue: Ceur Workshop Proceedings
human_qa_notes: Clean, well-structured full paper; explicit (though informally labeled) discussion of generalizability limitations in the conclusion serves as a threats-to-validity statement.
human_research_question: What are the relative strengths and weaknesses of static versus dynamic architecture conformance checking approaches (RQ1), and how can the two be combined to obtain complementary synergies (RQ2)?
human_main_finding: Based on a theoretical comparison and a six-month industrial case study (125k-LOC Java OSGi system), static and dynamic architecture conformance checking are complementary: static (Sonargraph-Architect) is complete, fast and low-effort but limited to static structure, while dynamic (ARAMIS/Dynatrace) captures run-time behavior but is incomplete and resource-intensive (13-33 hours vs. under a minute); authors recommend static as baseline with dynamic on demand.
human_limitations: Authors explicitly note that their practical results are based on a single software system case study, so findings cannot be generalized, and recommend studying additional industrial cases in future work to validate the results.

title: Predicting release time based on Generalized Software Reliability Model (GSRM)
abstract: Development environments have changed drastically, development periods are shorter than ever and the number of team members has increased. Especially in open source software (OSS), a large number of developers contribute to OSS. OSS has difficulties in predicting or deciding when it will be released. In order to assess recent software developments, we proposed a generalized software reliability model (GSRM) based on a stochastic process, and compared GSRM with other models. In this paper, we focus on the release dates of OSS and the growth of faults (issues).
venue: Proceedings International Computer Software and Applications Conference
human_qa_notes: Short workshop-style paper; text is readable with minor formula/layout glitches. QA6=0: no threats-to-validity section (only a brief future-work caveat). QA7=0: Foundation GitHub is public but extracted issue time series and GSRM fitting code are not released. QA8=1: RSS and AIC are reported (RSS treated as closely analogous to RMSE).
human_research_question: Can a generalized software reliability model (GSRM) based on an Ito stochastic differential equation, applied after splitting OSS history by version, predict release dates and issue counts better than a classical NHPP reliability-growth model?
human_main_finding: On Zurb Foundation versions 2–4 (GitHub issues), GSRM obtains better AIC/RSS than NHPP and is claimed to predict release timing/issue volume better, but NHPP tracks the observed growth curve more closely and GSRM badly over-predicts (e.g. v2: 899 issues / 854 days vs actual 536 / 258). Time-independent growth rate was imposed so NHPP could be compared.
human_limitations: Single OSS project; growth-rate time-dependence was disabled for comparability, which the authors say prevented GSRM from fitting well; no threats-to-validity discussion; no released analysis code or extracted series; Table II predictions are far from actuals despite the 'successfully predict' claim in the conclusion.

title: Automated method for verification of stochastic graph transformation systems
abstract: Stochastic Graph Transformation Systems (SGTS) have been introduced to model dynamic distributed systems. To insure correctness of a SGTS, we should employ verification concept. There are different methods for verifying such systems, for example simulation, test, deductive verification and model checking of which the most common is model checking. But most of the researches in the field of model checking come back to construct of a suitable model from SGTS and there is not done a complete research and a practical work in the field of model verification methods. Therefore, in this paper, we have implemented a SGTS to PRISM (a stochastic model checker) translator to automatically verify SGTS.
venue: Icsess 2011 Proceedings 2011 IEEE 2nd International Conference on Software Engineering and Service Science
human_qa_notes: Theoretical/algorithmic formal-methods paper illustrated only with a small toy example (mobile network), not real data, and no conclusion/limitations section is present after the case study; domain is general distributed-systems verification rather than a software-engineering process, so QA2 and QA5 scored 0; text extraction is clean overall though some algorithmic notation/symbols render oddly, typical of PDF-to-text conversion of formulas.
human_research_question: Can stochastic graph transformation systems (SGTS) be automatically translated into the PRISM probabilistic model-checking language to enable automated verification (e.g., safety and liveness properties) of dynamic distributed systems modeled as continuous-time Markov chains?
human_main_finding: The paper presents an algorithm that automatically translates SGTS models (nodes, edges, rules) into PRISM's continuous-time Markov chain input language, demonstrated on a toy mobile-network case study where safety and liveness properties were specified in CSL and successfully verified via PRISM model checking.
human_limitations: not stated
